A variety of sensitivity analyses were conducted, including policy effect sise, mortality rate assumptions, capital depreciation rates, and a 1000-iteration bootstrap to assess parameter uncertainty. Further details regarding the model structure and parameters were provided in . Role of the funding source The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report. Results Eight schools were contacted, of which six met the eligibility criteria and agreed to participate in the study. From 6 to 30 September, 2022, 394 students were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 331 met the inclusion criteria and were enrolled in the study (145 in the intervention group and 186 in the control group), 63 children in the intervention group declined before the intervention began, citing the high commitment for additional exercise and the demands of meal photography required for the multifaceted program. No significant differences were observed between included and excluded participants in either the intervention group ( , ) or across all six schools ( , ). Baseline characteristics were comparable between the two groups ( ). Among the participants, 120 (36.3%) were female, with a mean age of 8.5 years (SD 0.3). The study population was predominantly Han Chinese (n = 324, 97.9%), with only seven participants (2.1%) identifying as ethnic minorities (one Hui, five Tujia, and one Bouyei). The mean BMI was 20.4 (SD 2.2), corresponding to BMI Z score of 2.0 (SD 0.7). All participating schools completed the trial. No adverse events were reported throughout the trial. Six children (1.9%) were lost to follow-up by the end of the trial ( ). Missing data for primary outcomes was minimal (1.6–9.1%) and primarily attributed to non-systematic factors such as fear of blood sampling, competing examinations or sports events, and specific test refusals (e.g., VCTE in 15 control-group participants). Statistical comparisons confirmed that baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between participants with and without missing endline assessments ( , ), supporting the assumption that data were missing at random. After one academic year, a reduction in mean BMI was observed in the intervention group, whereas an increase was noted in the control group, resulting in a mean difference of −0.38 (95% CI −0.59 to −0.16; p < 0.0001; A). A similar trend was observed for CAP, with a mean difference of −15.73 (−22.39 to −9.07; p < 0.0001; B). LSM increased in the control group but remained stable in the intervention group, leading to a mean difference of −0.69 (−0.89 to −0.48; p < 0.0001; C). Sensitivity analyses using the LOCF and PP approaches yielded results consistent with the primary analysis. Furthermore, additional adjustment for family socioeconomic status did not alter these findings ( , ). At the 3-month follow-up (mid-intervention), favourable although non-significant trends were observed in BMI and CAP in the intervention group compared with the control group ( , ). Subgroup analyses revealed no significant differences in treatment effects according to sex, baseline BMI status, maternal education level or household per-capita disposable income ( , ). Mediation analyses revealed that changes in BMI and BMI Z score accounted for 11.9% and 9.1%, respectively, of the improvements in CAP (both p < 0.05, , ). However, no significant mediation effect was observed for LSM. Compared with the control group, the intervention group had significantly lower prevalence of MASLD (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.12–0.87; p = 0.025) and liver fibrosis (0.10, 0.12–0.87; p = 0.032) after the intervention ( ). A lower prevalence of obesity was also observed in the intervention group, although this difference was not statistically significant. In addition, the intervention group demonstrated improvements in several secondary outcomes, including reductions in BMI Z score (mean difference −0.13, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.06; p < 0.0001), body fat percentage (−1.30, −2.58 to −0.01; p = 0.047), fasting insulin (−0.36, −0.50 to −0.23; p < 0.0001) and triglyceride levels (−0.27, −0.42 to −0.12; p < 0.0001). Post hoc analyses for other obesity-related indicators also indicated consistent beneficial effects associated with the intervention ( , ). No significant between group differences were observed in waist circumference, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, total cholesterol, ALT levels, or performance on CRF. In terms of knowledge and behaviours ( , ), the intervention group showed significant improvements

Z score (mean difference −0.13, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.06; p < 0.0001), body fat percentage (−1.30, −2.58 to −0.01; p = 0.047), fasting insulin (−0.36, −0.50 to −0.23; p < 0.0001) and triglyceride levels (−0.27, −0.42 to −0.12; p < 0.0001). Post hoc analyses for other obesity-related indicators also indicated consistent beneficial effects associated with the intervention ( , ). No significant between group differences were observed in waist circumference, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, total cholesterol, ALT levels, or performance on CRF. In terms of knowledge and behaviours ( , ), the intervention group showed significant improvements in healthy lifestyle knowledge scores (mean difference 0.49, 95% CI 0.18–0.79; p = 0.0020) and Global Dietary Recommendation scores (0.63, 0.12–1.14; p = 0.015). More students in the intervention group reached the action stage of behavioural change (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.25–4.66; p = 0.091), ate out less frequently (0.52, 0.30–0.90; p = 0.018) and had more days of MVPA (>1 h/day; mean difference 0.90, 95% CI 0.40–1.41; p < 0.0001). No significant differences were observed between two groups in depression, social anxiety, or sleep quality scores. In three intervention schools, the intervention was delivered with high fidelity (>88%) for health education activities for students, parents and school staff. Regarding mHealth engagement, 139 of 145 caregivers (95.9%) accessed the platform, and 99 (71.2%) uploaded dietary photos. Adherence rates were 78.6% for weight monitoring and 66.2% for dietary behaviour monitoring. Student attendance at weekly extracurricular physical activities ranged from 77% to 82%. At the school level, all intervention schools allocated curriculum time for health education and physical activity, implemented restrictive food policies, while two schools expanded exercise spaces and facilities ( , ). In the baseline scenario in post-hoc macroeconomic analyses, which assumes no intervention and a continuation of current MASLD epidemiological trends, the projected total economic burden of MASLD is Chinese RMB (¥) 2004.98 billion (US$ 281.20 billion) at constant 2025 prices (based on the 2025 exchange rate of US $1 = RMB ¥7.13; ). This corresponds to approximately 0.038% of the cumulative GDP between 2026 and 2050. In contrast, under a steady-state policy scenario simulating a nationwide MASLD intervention in primary school with full population coverage, the projected cumulative macroeconomic gains reach RMB 694.96 billion (US$ 97.47 billion). This is equivalent to RMB 493.48 (US$ 69.21) per capita, accounting 0.013% of the cumulative GDP over the same period. Panels B–E in reported the results of sensitivity analyses for economic gains. Panel B, showed that under the lower and upper estimates of policy effectiveness, cumulative gains ranged from 0.003% to 0.017% of GDP. When a gradual effect onset was assumed, the estimated gain decreased to 0.006% of GDP. Panel C reported the sensitivity to the 95% CIs of MASLD-related mortality rates, with projected GDP gains ranging between 0.012% and 0.015% of GDP. Panel D examined sensitivity to capital depreciation rate, yielding gains between 0.010% and 0.016% of GDP. In Panel E, a bootstrap simulation with 1000 iterations was conducted by resampling key parameters between 50% and 150% of their original values, and the mean gain was 0.013% (95% CI 0.003%–0.021%) of total GDP. Discussion This mHealth-assisted multifaceted lifestyle intervention effectively reduced BMI, CAP, and LSM in 8- to 10-year-old children with overweight or obesity after one academic year. The intervention also demonstrated significant reductions in metabolic outcomes, including body fat percentage, fasting insulin, and triglycerides, alongside improvements in several diets and physical activity knowledge and behaviours. Furthermore, the post-hoc, health-augmented macroeconomic model projects that these health improvements could translate into substantial long-term economic dividends, estimated at approximately 0.013% of cumulative GDP by 2050. To our knowledge, this study represents the first cluster RCT addressing both pediatric obesity, MASLD and their economic implications through a multifaceted intervention approach. Dietary habits play an essential role in obesity and hepatic steatosis pathogenesis. In this study, clinical nutritionists guided dietary changes both at school and home, resulting in improved dietary quality and a reduction in eating out frequency among students. Previous research indicated that nutrition literacy alone may be insufficient to drive behaviour changes in patients with MASLD. However, with professional guidance, our intervention group presented improved Global Dietary Recommendation scores and reduced rates of eating out. Such professional support is crucial to translating knowledge into action, which aligns with US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations for intensive behavioural interventions in children aged 6 years or older with high BMI (>95th percentile, children with obesity). Given China's vast territory and diverse culinary cultures, nutritionists' familiarity with regional dietary habits allows them to adapt recommendations to local, seasonal foods, making the guidance both practical and culturally relevant. Moreover, the mobile application facilitated communication between parents and nutritionists, enabling parents to receive timely, practical guidance on healthy food substitutions. The effect of the intervention on BMI

of eating out. Such professional support is crucial to translating knowledge into action, which aligns with US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations for intensive behavioural interventions in children aged 6 years or older with high BMI (>95th percentile, children with obesity). Given China's vast territory and diverse culinary cultures, nutritionists' familiarity with regional dietary habits allows them to adapt recommendations to local, seasonal foods, making the guidance both practical and culturally relevant. Moreover, the mobile application facilitated communication between parents and nutritionists, enabling parents to receive timely, practical guidance on healthy food substitutions. The effect of the intervention on BMI in this study (mean difference −0.38, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.16) was smaller than that observed among children with overweight or obesity in DECIDE-Children study (−0.76, −1.02 to −0.50), although the 95% CIs overlapped. Several factors may explain this disparity. The COVID-19-related early winter break reduced the duration of school-based moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. This temporary reduction in intervention intensity likely led to an underestimation of the true intervention effect sise. Participants in the present study were also younger (Grade 3) than those in the DECIDE-Children study (Grade 4). Although biological maturation can influence adiposity measures, recent data from the Chinese National Surveys on Students' Constitution and Health indicate that the median ages at menarche and spermarche are 12.0 and 13.9 years, respectively. Given our participants’ age and the observed annualised growth velocity of ∼5.4 cm/year, which aligns with prepubertal norms, it is unlikely that a significant proportion of participants had entered the rapid pubertal growth phase. This limits the potential confounding effect of maturation. Furthermore, consistent intervention effects were observed across supplementary outcomes (BMI Z score, body fat percentage, and waist circumference), all of which were adjusted for age and sex, suggesting that the results are robust to maturational variations. Although the reduction in BMI is modest, evidence indicates that even small improvements can bring meaningful clinical benefits in school-aged children. In the study, the decrease in BMI Z score exceeded thresholds (0.1-unit) previously linked to cardiometabolic improvements and favorable changes in liver enzymes, and was accompanied by favorable changes in body fat percentage, fasting insulin, triglycerides, and hepatic steatosis. Importantly, intervening at 8–10 years of age, before pubertal metabolic changes, may help redirect long-term obesity trajectories and potentially reduce risks of future chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and premature mortality. Previous evidence demonstrated that such interventions were likely to be more effective for girls. Nonetheless, we did not find any difference in sex subgroup analyses, which is in line with the findings of the DECIDE-Children study. The possible reason is the higher level of family involvement and relatively high fidelity of the intervention delivery. As parents playing a central role in executing dietary and physical activity strategies, potential sex-related differences in behavioural responses may have been attenuated. Despite the significant burden of pediatric MASLD, its awareness and treatments remain limited. A recent review of 10 RCTs (one school-based, 9 hospital-based) on childhood MASLD, which focused on diet or exercise, showed promising results but were limited by small sample sises and a lack of cluster RCTs. In this study, while the absolute mean reductions in CAP and LSM may appear modest compared to intensive therapeutic trials in severe disease, their clinical relevance is underscored by the “prevention of progression”. Most importantly, this shift in continuous variables translated into tangible clinical benefits: a significant reduction in MASLD risk (OR 0.32) and a marked decrease in the proportion of children exceeding pediatric liver stiffness thresholds (5.1 kPa, , ). Although primarily focused on a childhood obesity intervention, this study provides exploratory insights into the primary prevention of hepatic health. Clinically, variations within this low CAP range (<248 dB/m) do not represent current pathology; however, evidence suggests that rising CAP levels increase diabetes risk, and elevated LSM serves as a predictor for metabolic syndrome. Ectopic fat deposition driven by sustained adiposity is a continuous pathophysiological process. While the categorical prevalence of overweight and obesity in our cohort did not dramatically reverse, the intervention successfully induced a concurrent reduction in both continuous adiposity metrics (BMI and BMI Z scores) and hepatic fat content. This demonstrates that even before children completely transition out of overweight/obesity categories, lifestyle modifications can effectively intercept the upward trend of early subclinical fat accumulation, essentially shifting the population's long-term risk curve to the left before pathological thresholds are reached. Moreover, compared with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), VCTE has limited sensitivity for quantifying subtle changes in hepatic steatosis, particularly when steatosis is below 20%, but its low cost and portability are essential for translating public health research into large-scale practice. A weight reduction (>5%) has been shown to lead to steatosis remission in adults, with 10% needed for fibrosis improvement. Our study observed a 6.5% reduction in BMI Z

of overweight/obesity categories, lifestyle modifications can effectively intercept the upward trend of early subclinical fat accumulation, essentially shifting the population's long-term risk curve to the left before pathological thresholds are reached. Moreover, compared with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), VCTE has limited sensitivity for quantifying subtle changes in hepatic steatosis, particularly when steatosis is below 20%, but its low cost and portability are essential for translating public health research into large-scale practice. A weight reduction (>5%) has been shown to lead to steatosis remission in adults, with 10% needed for fibrosis improvement. Our study observed a 6.5% reduction in BMI Z score, correlating with liver steatosis and fibrosis improvement. However, BMI explained a limited proportion of the improvement in CAP, suggesting that other factors might have contribution to the intervention effect, such as improved dietary quality, increased physical activity, and metabolic changes including better insulin sensitivity and lower triglycerides. Although the intervention showed some effect on LSM, no mediation effect for BMI was found, possibly due to the limited BMI change or short intervention duration. In contrast, ALT did not show significant inter-group differences. Given the relatively low baseline ALT levels across the intervention, there was minimal room for further reduction. Furthermore, reduction in hepatic fat content can occur independently of significant alterations in ALT, particularly when baseline ALT levels are not markedly elevated. Building upon the observed reduction of prevalence of MASLD, we translated these clinical improvements into long-term societal impacts using a health-augmented macroeconomic model. Our projections estimate cumulative economic gains of approximately 0.013% of GDP (¥694.96 billion) by 2050. Notably, this magnitude aligns with other population-level public health policies, falling between the projected gains of sugar-sweetened beverage taxation (∼0.0016% of GDP) and alcohol excise tax increases (∼0.034% of GDP), underscoring the substantial economic potential of early MASLD prevention. However, these health-economic findings must be interpreted as a scenario-based exploration rather than a definitive macroeconomic forecast. The model used national-level demographic and epidemiological parameters combined with effect sizes from a specific regional sample (Ningbo, China). Given the limited sample size and regional focus of the trial, extrapolating these results requires caution regarding real-world scalability. These estimates serve as a proof-of-concept for future cost-effectiveness studies. Second, regarding sustainability, although the one-year timeframe inherently captured the impact of the winter break, potential “behavioural wash-out” during the longer summer hiatus remains unassessed. To address these uncertainties, we conducted extensive sensitivity analyses adjusting for sex, income, and applying a conservative 62.5% disease persistence rate from childhood to adulthood ( , ). Results indicated that even under the most conservative assumptions, the intervention consistently generated positive economic returns (ranging from 0.003% to 0.017% of GDP). Thus, while local adaptation is necessary, the current evidence suggests that a nationwide rollout would likely generate meaningful and robust macroeconomic benefits. This study has several strengths. First, clinical nutritionists were involved in delivering dietary guidance, which helped translate weight management knowledge into practical skills, benefiting not only the students’ health but also dietary practices among parents and school cafeterias. Second, the purposely designed mobile application effectively facilitated timely and convenient communication among schools, nutritionists, and parents, aligning with the communication preferences of modern families. Third, the adequate sample sise and cluster-RCT design strengthen the reliability of our findings. A post hoc power analysis based on the observed effect sises suggested moderate to adequate statistical power ( , ). Fourth, the economic modelling suggests that interventions targeting childhood MASLD may bring considerable economic returns. Nonetheless, several limitations should be noted. First, this study focused on one city, Ningbo, and included six public primary schools in eastern China, the findings are likely generalisable to similar urban contexts, but should be cautiously extended to regions with different economic or medical conditions. Second, COVID-19 pandemic restrictions and an early winter break confined children to their homes, significantly reduced extra school-based MVPA in the intervention groups, which likely underestimate the effect sise in the intervention group. Third, due to the nature of the lifestyle intervention, blinding of participants was infeasible, which may introduce performance bias. However, this risk was mitigated by the use of objective primary outcomes and blinded outcome assessment. Finally, the intervention covered only one academic year, and longer-term sustainability of the observed effects could not be evaluated. This cluster-randomised trial demonstrated that an mHealth-assisted, multifaceted lifestyle intervention effectively improved in BMI, liver health, and metabolic outcomes among children with overweight or obesity. These findings support the incorporation of such interventions into national child health strategies, particularly for mitigating obesity and preventing non-communicable disease. Ultimately, this study highlights the potential of multifaced interventions to yield both immediate clinical benefits and substantial long-term macroeconomic gains. chunks.content: Abbreviations 340B 340B drug pricing program AASLD American association for the study of liver diseases ALT alanine aminotransferase anti‐HBc hepatitis B core antibody anti‐HBs hepatitis B surface antibody ART antiretroviral therapy AST aspartate aminotransferase CDC centers for disease control and prevention CDS clinical decision support CKD chronic kidney disease CME continuing medical education DAA direct‐acting antiviral DNA deoxyribonucleic acid ECHO extension for community healthcare outcomes ED emergency department eGFR estimated glomerular filtration rate EHR electronic health record ESRD end‐stage renal disease FDA U.S. food and drug administration FFS fee‐for‐service FIB‐4 fibrosis‐4 index HBsAg hepatitis B surface antigen HBV hepatitis B virus HCC hepatocellular carcinoma HCV hepatitis C virus HepCCATT hepatitis C care, access, treatment, and testing HIV human immunodeficiency virus IDSA infectious diseases society of America KDIGO kidney disease improving global outcomes MCO managed care organization MINMON minimal monitoring NS3/4A nonstructural protein 3/4A PA prior authorisation PHBPP perinatal hepatitis B prevention program POC point of care PWID persons who inject drugs RNA ribonucleic acid SU substance use SVR sustained virologic response SVR12 sustained virologic response at 12 weeks USG ultrasonography WHO World Health Organization 1 Introduction In 2016, the World Health Organization set an ambitious target of eliminating hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection by 2030. Nearly a decade later, it is clear that the mere availability of a cure is insufficient to bridge aspiration to reality. The discovery of direct‐acting antivirals (DAAs) transformed HCV infection from a disease managed over decades to one curable in 8 weeks with a daily oral regimen. Unfortunately, deployment of this cure remains suboptimal. The HCV care cascade defines sequential steps from screening and diagnosis, linkage to care, treatment initiation, ongoing monitoring, culminating in sustained virologic response (SVR) which signifies a cure. There is significant fracture in the continuum of care, with progressive attrition at each step. A large meta‐analysis found that among persons screened positive for HCV, only 62% attended their first care appointment, 41% initiated treatment, 38% completed treatment, and only 29% achieved cure [ ], highlighting the magnitude of this problem. The emergency department (ED) serves as a vital access point for patients and encounters a higher prevalence of HCV infections compared to other care settings [ ]. Given the frequency with which HCV‐infected individuals interact with the ED, re‐conceptualising the care cascade to integrate screening and treatment initiation within this setting, could represent a crucial step toward addressing this public health challenge. This manuscript proposes a pragmatic framework for ED‐based HCV elimination within the United States healthcare system. The challenges and solutions described reflect the structure of U.S. care delivery, payer models and regulatory conditions. It may not directly translate to settings with different coverage or access constraints. The framework is intended to highlight the need for region‐specific strategies to address gaps in the care cascade. Five domains are addressed: point‐of‐care diagnostics, simplified treatment initiation and eligibility screening, policy and financial barriers, operational considerations and post‐treatment surveillance. The proposed pathway from ED presentation to SVR confirmation is summarised in Figure . 2 Point of Care Testing Innovations A critical requirement for any ED‐based model is the ability to establish a definitive diagnosis during the encounter itself. Point of care (POC) POC HCV RNA testing offers solutions to current, often cumbersome diagnostic pathways. Many facilities currently use a two‐step testing process: an initial antibody screening via rapid or lab‐based immunoassay, followed by confirmatory RNA testing if positive. These assays are conducted in separate laboratory sections, such as immunology and molecular diagnostics, or sent to external reference laboratories [ ], creating turnaround times on the order of days. POC fingerstick testing delivers results in ~1 h [ ], allowing diagnosis to be made within the critical window of opportunity where patient retention is most practical and intervention can be initiated promptly. Multiple studies have demonstrated strong diagnostic performance for these platforms [ , ]. On June 27th 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted market authorisation to the first of these products [ ]. The ability to perform and interpret these tests without training in laboratory techniques makes them ideally applicable in ED settings. Widespread implementation, however, would require solutions to existing cost barriers. The Global Fund has successfully negotiated pricing and procurement agreements with Cepheid, the developer of the only FDA‐approved POC HCV RNA test to subsidise the cost of its tuberculosis testing products. Expansion of these agreements to include HCV testing products should also be pursued. Negotiation of bulk pricing by state or federal agencies, provision of subsidies for departments implementing these tests and advocacy for universal coverage of POC HCV RNA testing under Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurance are reasonable funding considerations. 3 Simplified Treatment Initiation The initiation of DAAs by non‐specialist providers may seem intimidating, and the concern is not unfounded. Expecting ED physicians to counsel patients on

procurement agreements with Cepheid, the developer of the only FDA‐approved POC HCV RNA test to subsidise the cost of its tuberculosis testing products. Expansion of these agreements to include HCV testing products should also be pursued. Negotiation of bulk pricing by state or federal agencies, provision of subsidies for departments implementing these tests and advocacy for universal coverage of POC HCV RNA testing under Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurance are reasonable funding considerations. 3 Simplified Treatment Initiation The initiation of DAAs by non‐specialist providers may seem intimidating, and the concern is not unfounded. Expecting ED physicians to counsel patients on DAA side effect profiles, recognise drug interactions, and independently navigate serologic and fibrosis workups is a genuine cognitive burden in an already compressed clinical environment. Experience from other settings, however, suggests this barrier is surmountable when the right infrastructure surrounds the clinician. The HepCCATT study demonstrated meaningful improvement across the HCV care cascade. This was not achieved by training physicians to function as hepatitis C specialists. Instead, it relied on embedding ECHO‐Chicago tele‐mentoring support and providing frontline clinicians with expert backup [ ]. Critically, HepCCATT also illustrates the ceiling of workforce training alone. Despite gains in screening and diagnosis, only 7.7% of confirmed cases were ultimately treated. This finding underscores that individual clinician capacity is not the binding constraint. In the proposed ED model, this limitation is addressed through a different approach. EHR‐embedded clinical decision support (CDS) automates eligibility assessment, reflex laboratory ordering, and DAA prescription generation, reducing the physician's role to confirming eligibility and overriding the system when clinical judgement requires it. On June 11th, 2025, the FDA approved an expanded indication for glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Mavyret), making it the first and only oral, pan‐genotypic, 8‐week regimen for the treatment of acute HCV in patients ≥ 3 years without or with compensated cirrhosis [ ]. This decision, grounded in the findings of the M20‐350 trial, further strengthens the rationale for ED‐based treatment models. While most cases of acute HCV infection are asymptomatic, up to 20% of individuals develop clinically apparent illness, often severe enough to prompt evaluation in the ED [ ]. However, the majority of HCV diagnoses made in the ED represent undiagnosed chronic infection. Distinguishing between these two is often clinically impossible. The stronger argument for ED‐based treatment rests not on the acute indication but on the well‐established efficacy of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. The ED encounter however brief, represents a rare and often unrepeatable opportunity for intervention. Supporting this simplified treatment paradigm is the MINMON trial, which enrolled even compensated cirrhotics and HIV‐infected individuals with suppressed viral loads. Adopting a minimalist strategy, researchers omitted pre‐treatment genotyping, scheduled office visits, laboratory monitoring and dispensed the entire treatment course (84 tablets) to participants on enrolment. 91% of participants completed the 84 tablet course, SVR rate was 95% and safety was exceptional with no adverse events necessitating treatment discontinuation or death [ ]. The pragmatic approach of MINMON suggests that DAAs can be dispensed from the ED both safely and in a manner that delivers strong value for societal resources. Particularly compelling were SVR rates, which rival those reported in large outpatient and real‐world DAA cohorts [ ]. 4 Eligibility and the Minimal Safety Screen Based on the updated HCV test‐and‐treat algorithm, treatment can be safely initiated during an ED encounter in patients who are DAA‐naïve, not known to be HBsAg‐positive, have no history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and who lack clinical features of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, or varices) [ ]. In this model, each of these criteria is operationalised within the ED encounter through EHR‐embedded CDS to reduce cognitive burden on ED clinicians. 5 Hepatitis B Virus Status Before DAA initiation, consideration must be given to coinfection with HBV owing to potential for seroconversion or HBV viral reactivation during therapy [ ]. Standard protocols involve assessing serum HBsAg, anti‐HBs, and anti‐HBc prior to DAA therapy initiation to assess whether a patient is immune to HBV, previously exposed, or actively infected. To alleviate cognitive burden on ED physicians, EHR‐based CDS tools should prompt these HBV serologic tests when HCV RNA positivity is confirmed, with reflexive ordering if results are not previously documented. A similar automated workflow has been successfully implemented in EDs, reflexing HCV RNA testing for positive HCV antibody testing on the same specimen [ ]. Those HBV‐immune from vaccination [HBsAg (−), anti‐HBc (−), anti‐HBs (+)] can proceed with ED‐based DAA initiation without additional precautions. Patients with resolved HBV infection [HBsAg (−), anti‐HBc (+), anti‐HBs (+)], although at theoretical risk of HBV reactivation, absolute risk is low. In a systematic review of 1317 HBsAg‐negative, anti‐HBc‐positive patients treated with DAAs for HCV across six studies, the occurrence of HBV DNA reappearance and clinical reactivation was 0.91% [ ]. Prospective 1‐year surveillance data further address concerns regarding late reactivation, showing zero reactivations

EDs, reflexing HCV RNA testing for positive HCV antibody testing on the same specimen [ ]. Those HBV‐immune from vaccination [HBsAg (−), anti‐HBc (−), anti‐HBs (+)] can proceed with ED‐based DAA initiation without additional precautions. Patients with resolved HBV infection [HBsAg (−), anti‐HBc (+), anti‐HBs (+)], although at theoretical risk of HBV reactivation, absolute risk is low. In a systematic review of 1317 HBsAg‐negative, anti‐HBc‐positive patients treated with DAAs for HCV across six studies, the occurrence of HBV DNA reappearance and clinical reactivation was 0.91% [ ]. Prospective 1‐year surveillance data further address concerns regarding late reactivation, showing zero reactivations among 108 patients with resolved HBV infection. Some 16.7% did experience transient ALT elevations [ ], hence a strategy of post‐treatment ALT monitoring is prudent. Those with active hepatitis B infection [HBsAg (+)] are at risk too high to proceed with simplified treatment. In a pooled analysis of 17 studies, the risk of HBV reactivation in HBsAg positive patients was computed at 24% [ ]. Such cases of coinfection require HBV antiviral prophylaxis extending 6–12 months beyond DAA completion [ ]. This duration and monitoring burden is fundamentally incompatible with a single‐encounter treatment model. 6 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">HIV</styled-content> And Antiretroviral Interactions While MINMON supports DAA initiation in HIV positive individuals, caution is required. The central concern is that of pharmacologic interaction between DAA regimens and antiretroviral therapy (ART). The proposed model addresses this by stratifying HIV patients into three operational tiers. Patients with documented HIV virologic suppression on a compatible ART regimen may proceed with ED‐initiated DAA therapy. Compatibility can be determined automatically through EHR‐embedded interaction checks. Those with viral suppression but on an interacting ART regimen are not started on DAAs in the ED. They are flagged for expedited referral to an infectious disease specialist. Patients with unsuppressed or undocumented HIV viral load are deferred from ED‐initiated treatment owing to the degree of clinical complexity such management entails. 7 Renal Impairment Renal impairment warrants brief consideration given its high prevalence in the ED population and relationship with HCV. HCV infection promotes renal disease through various mechanisms including membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, direct cytopathic injury to podocytes and tubular cells, and cryoglobulinemia [ ]. An internal inconsistency exists within current AASLD/IDSA guidance. While instruction regarding renal impairment endorses DAA therapy without dose adjustment across all CKD stages, the simplified treatment algorithm excludes patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . It reflects historic caution around sofosbuvir's metabolite GS‐331007 which is renally cleared and putatively associated with cardiac toxicity in animal models [ ]. Contemporary data supports the safety and efficacy of both sofosbuvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir regimens in advanced CKD and dialysis [ ]. In the current proposed model, ESRD is not an exclusion. Patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 who otherwise meet criteria proceed with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, whose biliary clearance removes renal pharmacokinetic concerns. 8 Cirrhosis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma The early DAA era furnished signals suggesting accelerated hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) occurrence/recurrence after therapy, particularly in those with cirrhosis or prior history of HCC [ ]. Contemporary consensus holds that DAA treatment in cirrhotic patients reduces long‐term HCC risk compared to untreated cirrhosis but does not eliminate it [ ]. Ongoing surveillance therefore remains necessary. Decompensated cirrhosis further complicates treatment selection. NS3/4A protease inhibitor‐containing regimens are contraindicated due to impaired hepatic metabolism and the risk of drug accumulation. Instead, management requires sofosbuvir‐based regimens with ribavirin, introducing monitoring demands that are incompatible with a simplified low‐touch framework. Cirrhosis exclusion in the ED is operationalised through a combinatorial assessment of FIB‐4 and ultrasonography (USG). In the context of HCV infection, a FIB‐4 of < 1.45 has a negative predictive value exceeding 90% for ruling out advanced fibrosis [ , ]. Patients with FIB‐4 score elevated above this threshold or sonographic features of cirrhosis (surface nodularity, splenomegaly, ascites) would be ineligible for ED‐initiated treatment and should be triaged to expedited specialist referral. FIB‐4 requires only AST/ALT and the patient's age which are already routinely obtained in ED evaluation. Formal USG is available in most US ED's, particularly those affiliated with hospitals where radiology services are staffed. In rural hospitals or freestanding EDs, imaging acquisition is typically performed locally with interpretation support through teleradiology. Together, these modalities represent an immediately implementable cirrhosis exclusion strategy. History of HCC is addressed through history taking and EHR review at the time of eligibility determination. Patients with known prior HCC would also be excluded and referred. Soon, formal USG may be replaced with transient elastography. Palm‐sized wireless systems capable of B‐mode imaging and liver stiffness measurements have been developed, clinically validated [ ], and have already crossed FDA regularly threshold as of February 2024. Patients with known prior HCC would also be excluded and referred. Soon, formal USG may be replaced with transient elastography. Palm‐sized wireless systems capable of B‐mode imaging and liver stiffness measurements have been developed, clinically validated [ ], and have already crossed FDA regularly threshold as of February 2024. Scepticism toward this progress would be akin that once directed at POC ultrasound; a technology once doubted as feasible outside of radiology suites but is now a mandated Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education milestone competency in every academic emergency medicine training programme in the United States [ ]. 9 Active Case Management for Those Ineligible for Simplified Treatment Simplified treatment ineligibility should not be conflated with therapeutic abandonment. Patients excluded from ED‐initiated DAA therapy whether due to HBsAg positivity, decompensated cirrhosis, unsuppressed HIV viremia, a history of HCC or complex drug interactions represent the highest risk individuals within the HCV‐infected population. For these patients, an appropriate response is a distinct, high‐priority active case management protocol, modelled on the infrastructure of the CDC's Perinatal Hepatitis B Prevention Program (PHBPP). The PHBPP is a currently functioning nationally funded programme in which HBsAg positivity in the specific clinical context of pregnancy triggers active case management rather than passive surveillance. This entails proactive outreach, household contact tracing, needs assessment, care coordination and eliminates patient self‐navigating and follow‐up [ ]. Spanning 2009 to 2017, the PHBPP case‐managed 100,372 infants born to HBsAg‐positive women across 56 jurisdictions, and over this time, increased timely administration of post‐exposure prophylaxis rates from 94.7% to 97%. Similar improvements were recorded for post‐vaccination serologic testing which increased from 58.8% to 66.8% ( p = 0.002), ultimately declining perinatal transmission from 0.9% to 0.4% ( p = 0.0006) [ ]. However, the PHBPP does not map perfectly to the ED HCV context. The heterogeneity of ineligibility criteria, absence of a third party harm imperative (i.e., risk of harm to a neonate), and lack of a dedicated federal funding mechanism represent important structural differences. It does however establish a key principle. A clearly defined high risk clinical trigger can justify an active case management infrastructure rather than passive referral. Applying this principle to treatment‐ineligible ED HCV patients would ensure that exclusion from the simplified pathway consistently initiates proactive specialist referral and coordinated follow‐up, rather than discharge with instructions alone. 10 Policy & Systemic Barriers A review of publicly available Medicaid HCV coverage policies across all 52 U.S. jurisdictions reveals a heterogeneous and frequently restrictive policy landscape (Table ). As of 2025, 18 jurisdictions (35%) require prior authorisation for initial DAA therapy, including most states that have not expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. In these settings, 62% of non‐expansion jurisdictions maintain prior authorisation requirements compared with 24% of expansion states. Prescriber restrictions persist in 12 jurisdictions (23%), ranging from “specialist‐only” mandates to continuing medical education (CME) based credentialing requirements. Substance‐use related requirements remain in 6 jurisdictions (12%), now uniformly framed as counselling attestation rather than sobriety mandates. Taken together, at least one barrier directly relevant to DAA‐naive patients presenting to the ED is present in 24 jurisdictions (46%). (Table ) Therefore, approximately half of U.S. Medicaid programmes would require additional policy navigation before the proposed model could be implemented without modification. Additionally, seven jurisdictions (14%) exhibit Managed Care Organization (MCO) parity gaps in which private insurance companies that administer Medicaid benefits on behalf of the state impose more restrictive HCV coverage criteria than the state fee‐for‐service programme. Given that a majority of Medicaid beneficiaries in most states are enrolled in MCOs rather than fee‐for‐service [ ], parity gaps represent a particularly insidious form of access restriction. The full state‐by‐state policy data are reported in Table . Feasible ED‐based HCV treatment initiation will therefore require targeted policy interventions alongside clinical implementation. Although prior authorisation removal has been shown to increase treatment rates [ ], abrupt universal rollback is a financially non‐viable strategy for most payers given anticipated surges in treatment demand. A more durable approach would be advocacy for ED‐specific prior authorisation exemptions. A useful precedent is noted in the liberation of buprenorphine prescription requirements during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Prior to 2020, the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act of 2008 required an in‐person evaluation before prescribing controlled substances via telemedicine. This barrier is structurally akin to the specialist‐only prescribing requirement for DAAs. Federal regulators temporarily waived this requirement for buprenorphine initiation in defined telehealth settings while maintaining prescriber oversight. The impact was immediate. Within the Veterans Health Administration, a national interrupted time series analysis showed an increase of 265 patients receiving buprenorphine in the first month, with continued growth thereafter, even as overall substance use

noted in the liberation of buprenorphine prescription requirements during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Prior to 2020, the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act of 2008 required an in‐person evaluation before prescribing controlled substances via telemedicine. This barrier is structurally akin to the specialist‐only prescribing requirement for DAAs. Federal regulators temporarily waived this requirement for buprenorphine initiation in defined telehealth settings while maintaining prescriber oversight. The impact was immediate. Within the Veterans Health Administration, a national interrupted time series analysis showed an increase of 265 patients receiving buprenorphine in the first month, with continued growth thereafter, even as overall substance use disorder care declined by 6% [ ]. Importantly, safety did not worsen. In a propensity score–matched study of more than 23,000 adults, telehealth initiation was associated with a 36% lower risk of opioid overdose, along with better treatment engagement and refill rates, without increases in ED visits or hospitalisations [ ]. Though these data are derived from commercially insured patients, the principle remains. Removing a categorical prescribing barrier in a defined clinical setting can expand access without compromising safety. A structured ED‐based protocol can justify exemption from requirements that were designed for routine outpatient care. 11 Financial Access Barriers and Mechanisms for Cost Mitigation DAA therapies are now significantly more affordable than their initial entry into the HCV treatment armamentarium. When introduced in 2013, sofosbuvir was priced at $1000 per pill, totalling $84,000 for an 8 week course. Yet, meaningful cost barriers persist across insurance strata and are most acute precisely where HCV burden is highest. Patients with commercial insurance may have out‐of‐pocket costs as little as $5/month. However, patients relying on Medicare Part D historically faced average out‐of‐pocket costs approaching $5351 prior to recent legislative reforms, while uninsured individuals continue to encounter list prices for generic regimens ranging from $22,000 to $36,000 [ ]. The Inflation Reduction Act sought to ease this burden by implementing a $2000 annual cap and closing the long‐problematic coverage gap, which left patients exposed to substantial coinsurance after initial benefits [ ]. While these provisions are now in effect, recent policy shifts under the current administration introduce some uncertainty regarding the broader trajectory of federal drug pricing reform. This magnitude of cost is not driven by the complexity of drug manufacturing. Generic price modelling that incorporates active pharmaceutical ingredient costs, excipients, and production in India at a 10% profit margin estimates that a full course of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir can be produced for approximately $85 [ ]. In contrast, wholesale acquisition prices for preferred generic regimens have historically exceeded $20,000 per course, with no universal cost mitigation mechanism available outside insured and 340B‐eligible settings [ ]. These realities illustrate that cost barriers to HCV elimination in the United States stem from modifiable regulatory and policy constraints. One promising mechanism to offset DAA costs in the ED is the federal 340B drug pricing programme. If HCV treatment is prescribed and dispensed through an ED affiliated with a 340B‐eligible Disproportionate Share Hospital, medications can be acquired at steeply discounted prices. These savings may be passed on through sliding‐scale pricing or free dispensing to qualifying uninsured patients. Even in rural areas without owned outpatient facilities, 340B pricing can be accessed via contract pharmacy arrangements. While few existing bridge clinic models explicitly leverage 340B pricing, this presents an opportunity for innovation. EDs affiliated with 340B‐eligible hospitals could explore partnerships with nearby pharmacies to extend discounted DAA access beyond the ED encounter. Operationalising this model would require integrated electronic health record systems and dedicated care navigators. The federal 340B Drug Pricing Program offers a potential solution, but its reach is limited by structure. Under 340B, covered entities can purchase outpatient medications at significantly reduced prices. These savings can be passed on to uninsured or underinsured patients, potentially reducing DAA costs. Eligibility is uneven however. Rural critical access hospitals, freestanding emergency centres, and many community hospitals do not qualify. These are often the same settings where uninsured patients are concentrated. Even within eligible institutions, passing savings to patients depends on local policy and is not guaranteed or mandated [ ]. In addition, contract pharmacy arrangements, which have extended 340B pricing into community settings, face ongoing legal challenges following manufacturer restrictions introduced in 2020. This creates additional uncertainty, particularly for rural implementation strategies [ ]. For institutions outside the 340B system, no reliable same‐encounter cost mitigation mechanism currently exists for uninsured patients. Manufacturer patient assistance programmes, including AbbVie's myAbbVie Assist, offer free medication to qualifying uninsured patients but require income documentation, provider attestation, and a processing timeline of days to weeks. Addressing this gap will require policy‐level solutions: expansion of 340B covered entity eligibility, federal bulk purchasing mechanisms, or Medicaid expansion in the 13 states where uninsured adults below poverty remain categorically ineligible. At the systems level, subscription‐based procurement models implemented by Louisiana

Manufacturer patient assistance programmes, including AbbVie's myAbbVie Assist, offer free medication to qualifying uninsured patients but require income documentation, provider attestation, and a processing timeline of days to weeks. Addressing this gap will require policy‐level solutions: expansion of 340B covered entity eligibility, federal bulk purchasing mechanisms, or Medicaid expansion in the 13 states where uninsured adults below poverty remain categorically ineligible. At the systems level, subscription‐based procurement models implemented by Louisiana and Washington show that structural cost reform is achievable when payer infrastructure and political will align. Under these agreements, states pay a fixed annual amount in exchange for broad access to DAAs across Medicaid and incarcerated populations. A synthetic control analysis of Medicaid prescription data found that Louisiana experienced a 534% increase in HCV prescription fills following implementation [ ]. Despite this, neither state reached its elimination targets, indicating that improving affordability alone is not sufficient. These findings highlight the need for both care delivery and financial access reform. 12 Operational Considerations Beyond regulatory and financial prerequisites, feasibility depends on workflow integration within an already capacity constrained environment. Integrating HCV treatment into ED workflows adds modest physician workload if tasks are appropriately distributed. Serologic and radiographic tests run passively within the existing visit and physician involvement is limited to eligibility confirmation and prescription authorisation which are achievable in minutes with EHR‐embedded CDS. The downstream burden of patient counselling, insurance verification, prior authorisation navigation, and follow‐up coordination is best assigned to pharmacists and care navigators. Phlebotomy access warrants specific attention in persons serving PWID where poor venous access can extend intake time and impede concurrent patient management [ ]. Phlebotomy support and POC fingerstick compatible assays should be incorporated where available. Staffing requirements for ED‐based HCV initiation have not been prospectively defined and will likely vary by institution. Estimates depend on expected RNA positivity rates, the proportion of patients who meet simplified treatment criteria, and the non‐physician workload required per patient. Data from outpatient programmes provide a useful reference point. The Boston Medical Center primary care HCV programme reported annual staffing costs of $282,770, corresponding to approximately $940 per patient referred and $4160 per SVR [ ], with most of the workload carried by non‐physician staff. Across implementation studies, a consistent finding is that successful programmes require protected and dedicated time for pharmacists and care navigators. Dispensing logistics will vary by institutional context. Large urban emergency departments affiliated with health systems that have on‐site pharmacies offer the most straightforward implementation pathway. In these settings, EHR‐based screening alerts, co‐located pharmacist or navigator support during clinical shifts, and in‐house dispensing can function as a fully integrated model. When an on‐site pharmacy is unavailable, partnerships with community pharmacies provide a practical alternative. Electronic prescription transmission with same‐day or next‐day dispensing can preserve the central goal of minimising the gap between diagnosis and treatment initiation. Rural emergency departments operate under different constraints, including lower patient volumes, limited specialist access, and smaller staffing models. A hub‐and‐spoke telehealth approach is a reasonable adaptation. Point‐of‐care testing and eligibility screening can be performed locally, while treatment evaluation and authorisation are completed through real‐time telemedicine consultation. Although same‐visit dispensing may not always be feasible in this setting, same‐visit eligibility determination with rapid electronic prescribing and pharmacy dispensing within 24–48 h still represents a meaningful improvement over current pathways that often result in no treatment. 13 Post‐Treatment Surveillance and Cure Confirmation SVR12, defined as an undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment completion, is the accepted endpoint of cure and the target for post‐treatment follow‐up. For patients started on therapy in the ED, reaching this endpoint depends on two steps. A confirmatory sample must be obtained, and the result must be delivered to a patient who may no longer be connected to traditional care. Dried blood spot testing offers a practical solution for sample collection. A simple fingerstick applied to filter paper avoids venipuncture, does not require refrigeration, and remains stable for months [ ]. This allows collection in settings where these patients already engage, including harm reduction sites, opioid treatment programmes, and needle exchange services. For patients with stable housing, mail‐in or community drop‐off options can eliminate the need for a return visit altogether. In real‐world settings, dried blood spot testing has shown high accuracy, with reported specificity of 100% and sensitivity approaching 96% [ ]. There are limitations. Variability in sample volume, drying conditions, and processing can affect reliability at very low viral levels, where false negatives are the main concern [ , ]. These issues can be reduced with standardised collection techniques and validated processing protocols. When feasible, venous sampling remains preferred, but dried blood spot testing is

In real‐world settings, dried blood spot testing has shown high accuracy, with reported specificity of 100% and sensitivity approaching 96% [ ]. There are limitations. Variability in sample volume, drying conditions, and processing can affect reliability at very low viral levels, where false negatives are the main concern [ , ]. These issues can be reduced with standardised collection techniques and validated processing protocols. When feasible, venous sampling remains preferred, but dried blood spot testing is an appropriate alternative when it is not. The second challenge is ensuring that results reach the patient and that non‐responders are identified. Telemedicine has shown benefit, with studies demonstrating improved SVR rates and engagement compared to standard referral pathways [ , ]. However, its reach is limited in the same populations that rely on the ED. Access to smartphones, stable internet, and the ability to attend scheduled visits cannot be assumed. Simpler approaches may be more reliable. Asynchronous text messaging programmes have been associated with improved adherence and reduced treatment‐related distress in VA‐based HCV programmes [ ]. For patients without dependable digital access, in‐person follow‐up through harm reduction or opioid treatment programmes remains essential. Reinfection should be anticipated in populations with ongoing injection drug use. SVR does not confer immunity, and recurrence is not uncommon. This does not represent treatment failure. Reinfection can be managed with the same DAA regimens, with preserved efficacy. The appropriate response is retreatment alongside renewed engagement in harm reduction services. Follow‐up encounters for SVR confirmation provide an opportunity to reassess risk, reinforce counselling, and link patients to treatment for opioid use disorder when appropriate. No single follow‐up strategy will reach all patients. Effective post‐treatment care requires flexibility and selection of the approach that best fits the individual. 14 Conclusion This framework represents a deliberate shift in how the HCV care cascade is approached. Rather than relying on delayed linkage to outpatient care, it begins at the point of ED contact. Point‐of‐care RNA testing, simplified eligibility assessment, same‐visit treatment initiation, decentralised SVR confirmation, and flexible follow‐up together form a model grounded in the realities of the populations most affected by hepatitis C, particularly those with inconsistent access to traditional care. The barriers are real. Regulatory requirements vary across states. Financial access remains uneven and, in some settings, legally contested. Staffing these programmes requires institutional investment that cannot be secured through a single policy change. These constraints do not undermine the model. They define the areas where advocacy, pilot implementation, and prospective evaluation should be focused. Hepatitis C is curable. The tools to diagnose infection within an hour, treat it in weeks, and confirm cure without a clinic visit already exist. What remains is a delivery system that continues to lose patients at each step. The downstream consequences of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and their socioeconomic burden rest like an anvil on the healthcare system. Addressing this will require more than incremental change. It will require rethinking where and how care is delivered. The emergency department is not traditionally designed for chronic disease management, but for a condition defined by silent progression and concentrated among patients who rely on the ED for care, it may be the most consequential place to intervene. documents.title: Autoimmune hepatitis

chunks.content: Introduction La périartérite noueuse (PAN) est une vascularite segmentaire focale nécrosante affectant les artères de calibre moyen (artères rénales, hépatique, coronaires, cœliaque et mésentérique) ou petit (artères intraparenchymateuses) sans glomérulonéphrite ni vascularite des artérioles, des veinules ou des capillaires [ ]. La première observation a été rapportée par Kussmaul et Maïer en 1866, correspondant sur le plan histologique à une panartérite avec infiltration de l’adventice par des polynucléaires neutrophiles et des lymphocytes, une nécrose fibrinoïde de la média, et une prolifération endothéliale de l’intima. Sur le moyen et/ou long terme peuvent apparaitre des anomalies de la paroi vasculaire à type de microanévrisme, de sténose, et/ou de thrombose in situ. Les manifestations cliniques diverses qui en découlent dépendent des territoires et organes irrigués ou drainés par ces vaisseaux. Le caractère systémique de cette affection suscite de multiples diagnostics différentiels, et fait qu’elle reste encore mal connue des praticiens d’Afrique subsaharienne. L’atteinte neurologique représenterait 50 à 75% des atteintes au cours de la PAN avec de façon prédominante une atteinte du système nerveux périphérique [ ]. Nous rapportons deux observations avec déficit majeur: l’un à type de tétraplégie et l’autre de paraplégie, réversible sous traitement spécifique. Observation 1 Mademoiselle BMDF, gabonaise sans emploi, âgée de 25 ans consulte en janvier 2025. Elle signale des antécédents essentiellement obstétricaux (une fausse couche dans le premier trimestre, un accouchement prématuré à 24 semaines d’aménorrhée avec naissance d’une fille âgée actuellement de 2 ans). Elle présente 3 ou 4 jours après un épisode fébrile, une douleur abdominale invalidante avec arrêt des matières et des gaz, suivie de rétention d’urine et de paraplégie brutale, motivant son hospitalisation dans le service de médecine interne. Avant cet épisode, elle avait successivement présenté pendant huit à neuf mois des épisodes de migraine à bascule difficilement contrôlable par du paracétamol et des douleurs des extrémités des mains et des pieds. Cependant, ces troubles ne s’accompagnaient pas de myalgie, de syndrome de Raynaud, de syndrome sec oculo-buccal, ou de troubles de la vision. L’état général était conservé malgré une perte de poids de 5 kilogrammes sur trois mois. Elle était apyrétique, normotendue, et eupnéique. Les éléments pertinents cliniques se résumaient à une main tombante droite, une paraplégie avec troubles sphinctériens, et nouures des 2 faces internes des avant-bras. Sur le plan biologique, la protéine C réactive (CRP) était normale (< 6 mg/l). La vitesse de sédimentation n’a pas été réalisée. Les leucocytes étaient à 10 510/mm 3 à prédominance neutrophiles, le taux d’hémoglobine à 11,7 g/dl, et les plaquettes normales. Le bilan rénal, hépatique, la glycémie, le cholestérol et ses sous-fractions, l’hormonologie thyroïdienne, la bandelette urinaire et le temps de céphaline activé (TCA) étaient normaux. Les sérologies hépatitiques B et C, VIH 1,2, et syphilitiques étaient négatives. Sur le plan immunologique, le test de Coombs et l’anticoagulant circulant du lupus étaient positifs, les anticorps anticardiolipine (IgM et IgG), antinucléaires, anti DNA natifs et anticytoplasmiques des neutrophiles (ANCA) négatifs. Sur le plan morphologique, la tomodensitométrie abdominopelvienne était normale, et l’IRM médullaire objectivait une myélite extensive jusqu’à la 5 e vertèbre thoracique mesurant 201 millimètres de hauteur (Fig. ). La biopsie cutanée d’une lésion purpurique de la face postérieure de la cuisse, apparue à 48 heures de l’hospitalisation, retrouvait une vascularite leucocytoclasique. Sur la présence de 6 des 15 critères de Guillevin (Tableau ) (fièvre, altération de l’état général, paraplégie, nodules sous cutanés, arthralgies distales et douleur abdominale inaugurale), était retenu le diagnostic de périartérite noueuse. Sur le plan thérapeutique, la patiente était traitée par bolus de méthyl prednisolone à raison de 1 g/jour pendant 3 jours. Ce traitement a été relayé par de la prednisone à 1 mg/kg/jour (soit 50 mg/jour) et à des perfusions de cyclophosphamide de 1 gramme/mois pour un total de 6 cures, relayées par de l’azathioprine à 150 mg/jour, couplée à une kinésithérapie intensive. Ce trépied thérapeutique permettait à 5 mois la reprise de verticalisation de la patiente avec une autonomie de marche limitée aux gestes du quotidien, et à 7 mois d’une récupération optimale avec discrets troubles persistants de la sensibilité superficielle. Observation 2 Mademoiselle OMC, de nationalité gabonaise, fonctionnaire, âgée de 45 ans, présentait en décembre 2023, des épisodes de myalgies des membres d’aggravation progressive, se compliquant à trois mois de tétraplégie. Avant l’installation de ce déficit de traumatisme, il n’existait pas de contexte fébrile ou grippal, de prise médicamenteuse ou de décoctions traditionnelles, ni de consommation d’alcool. Depuis 4 ans, elle présentait des épisodes d’asthénie invalidante spontanément régressive, avec douleur abdominale spasmodique postprandiale améliorée alternativement par antiinflammatoires non stéroïdiens et inhibiteur de la pompe à proton. Ses antécédents se résumaient à des épisodes de bleus spontanés des membres inférieurs, une migraine à bascule évoluant depuis près de 20 ans, et un épisode d’amaurose en novembre 2020 spontanément résolutif. Elle n’avait jamais été jusque-là hospitalisée ni opérée.

Avant l’installation de ce déficit de traumatisme, il n’existait pas de contexte fébrile ou grippal, de prise médicamenteuse ou de décoctions traditionnelles, ni de consommation d’alcool. Depuis 4 ans, elle présentait des épisodes d’asthénie invalidante spontanément régressive, avec douleur abdominale spasmodique postprandiale améliorée alternativement par antiinflammatoires non stéroïdiens et inhibiteur de la pompe à proton. Ses antécédents se résumaient à des épisodes de bleus spontanés des membres inférieurs, une migraine à bascule évoluant depuis près de 20 ans, et un épisode d’amaurose en novembre 2020 spontanément résolutif. Elle n’avait jamais été jusque-là hospitalisée ni opérée. Sur le plan obstétrical, elle rapportait 3 fausses couches spontanées dans le premier trimestre, n’avait pas d’enfants, et présentait depuis 2 mois une aménorrhée non gravidique. L’état général était conservé avec un indice de masse corporel de 23 kg/m 2 malgré une perte de poids de 6 kg. Elle était apyrétique, normotendue et eupnéique. Les éléments de l’examen clinique se résumaient à une tétraplégie, avec des réflexes ostéotendineux, cutanéo-abdominaux et cutanéo-plantaires absents. Il existait des hématomes spontanés de la face antérieure du genou gauche et du tiers supérieur de la jambe, ainsi que de multiples nouures des membres inférieurs prédominant à la face interne des jambes et des cuisses. Sur le plan biologique les leucocytes étaient à 12 750/mm 3 avec une prédominance neutrophile, le taux d’hémoglobine à 13,5 g/dl, et les plaquettes normales, la vitesse de sédimentation à 35 mm, la CRP à 98 mg/l. Créatine phosphokinase, ionogramme sanguin, glycémie à jeun, cholestérol et sous-fractions, calcémie, phosphorémie, transaminases, taux de prothrombine et temps de céphaline activée étaient normaux. La protéinurie était positive à une croix avec nitrites, sans hématurie, ni leucocytes. Les sérologies des virus hépatotropes (Ag Hbs et anticorps anti VHC) et HTLV1 étaient négatives; la sérologie Borrelia burgdorferi positive en IgG. La ponction lombaire ramenait un liquide clair normotendu paucicellulaire avec de rares macrophages, une absence de polynucléaires, de lymphocytes, et de cellules atypiques. Le test de Coombs (direct et indirect), les autoanticorps antinucléaires, anti DNA natifs, autoanticorps nucléaires solubles, anticardiolipine (IgM et IgG), anti-béta 2 glycoprotéine 1, ANCA, étaient négatifs. L’anticoagulant circulant du lupus était positif. L’IRM médullaire retrouvait une myélite transverse longitudinalement étendue de C2 à C6 (Fig. ). La tomodensitométrie abdominopelvienne, et l’angioscanner rénal et des artères digestives étaient normaux. L’électromyogramme n’avait pu être réalisé faute de disponibilité. Avec la conjonction de 7 critères de Guillevin sur 15 (altération de l’état général, multinévrite, nodules sous cutanés, myalgies, crises douloureuses abdominales, néphropathie glomérulaire et syndrome inflammatoire), le diagnostic de périartérite noueuse était envisagé. Elle était traitée par bolus de méthylprednisolone (Solumédrol ® ) (960 mg/jour pendant 3 jours) relayés par une corticothérapie de 1 mg/kg/jour de prednisone (Cortancyl ® ) soit 80 mg/jour, perfusions de cyclophosphamide (Endoxan ® ) à raison de 1 g/mois pendant 6 mois suivi de relai oral, antiagrégant plaquettaire à la dose de 100 mg/ jour, rosuvastatine 20 mg/jour et kinésithérapie intensive. Devant la récupération lente, la patiente était évacuée, après trois mois de ce traitement, vers l’Europe, pour réalisation de plasmaphérèses et poursuite de la rééducation fonctionnelle. À six mois, elle retrouvait une autonomie des quatre membres. Discussion La PAN demeure le prototype de vascularite nécrosante systémique. Il y a encore deux décennies, la PAN était rapportée en association avec l’hépatite B dans 36 à 50% des cas [ ], affection sévissant à l’état endémique en Afrique subsaharienne. En 2020, l’Afrique recensait 26% des cas mondiaux d’hépatite B [ ]. Paradoxalement, en tenant compte de ce contexte, on peut se poser la question de savoir si la PAN n’est pas sousdiagnostiquée en Afrique subsaharienne. Très souvent, il s’agit de cas uniques rapportés. Ndongo et al., dans une étude au Sénégal portant sur 27 vascularites, retrouvait 2 PAN associées au virus de l’hépatite B (VHB) [ ]. Le VHB au cours de la PAN induit une réaction de « type III » où les complexes immuns sont piégés dans les parois vasculaires, provoquant des lésions vasculaires [ , ]. Des complexes immuns antigènes Hbs et anticorps anti-Hbs ont été mis en évidence dans ces lésions vasculaires. Grâce à la vaccination contre le VHB, et l’amélioration des conditions d’hygiène, la fréquence de la PAN due au VHB est en voie de diminution passant de 30% à 7% [ ]. En effet, nous retrouvons dans nos observations une négativité de l’antigène Hbs, sans remise en cause du diagnostic de PAN. Nous avons retenu le diagnostic de PAN devant l’existence de 6 et 7 critères de Guillevin. Pour le diagnostic, nous n’avons pas choisi les critères ACR du fait de la difficulté à réaliser chez nos patientes un bilan artériographique à la recherche d’anévrismes et une biopsie d’une artère de petit ou moyen calibre à la recherche de polynucléaires dans la paroi artérielle. la PAN due au VHB est en voie de diminution passant de 30% à 7% [ ]. En effet, nous retrouvons dans nos observations une négativité de l’antigène Hbs, sans remise en cause du diagnostic de PAN. Nous avons retenu le diagnostic de PAN devant l’existence de 6 et 7 critères de Guillevin. Pour le diagnostic, nous n’avons pas choisi les critères ACR du fait de la difficulté à réaliser chez nos patientes un bilan artériographique à la recherche d’anévrismes et une biopsie d’une artère de petit ou moyen calibre à la recherche de polynucléaires dans la paroi artérielle. En outre, les critères de l’ACR présentent une moins bonne spécificité (86% contre 92,3%) (Tableau ). Nos patientes ont en commun une histoire de migraine, de fausses couches, et une positivité des anticoagulants circulant du lupus, qui constituent des stigmates du syndrome des anti-phospholipides (SAPL). Elles présentent également une myélite transverse avec déficit neurologique majeur (tétraplégie et paraplégie) et un contexte de survenue en saison sèche, saison où les températures sont les plus basses sur l’année au Gabon. Le SAPL se définit par l’association des signes obstétricaux et thrombotiques, couplés à la positivité d’anticorps antiphospholipides (anticoagulants circulant lupiques, anticorps anticardiolipine (IgM et IgG) et d’anticorps anti-β2 glycoprotéine-1 (IgM et IgG) [ ]. Certains auteurs ont émis l’hypothèse que les anticorps antiphospholipides favoriseraient le développement d’une vascularite, déclenchée par une inflammation vasculaire révélant des antigènes cryptiques stimulant des anticorps anti-cellules endothéliales [ , ]. Chez certains patients, ces anticorps persisteraient dans le sérum, et ce même en l’absence d’activité de la maladie [ ]. Les vasa nervorum qui assurent l’apport artériel du système nerveux périphérique, sont l’un des sites les plus fréquemment touchés au cours de la PAN. Ces vasa nervorum pénètrent dans le nerf et se divisent en réseaux microvasculaires anastomosés complexes qui passent en grande partie dans l’épinèvre, le tissu conjonctif (qui recouvre les nerfs périphériques) et comble l’espace interfasciculaire [ ]. Cela pourrait expliquer pourquoi jusqu’à 85% des patients atteints de PAN développent une neuropathie périphérique de survenue brutale, avec un déficit complet, ou moins souvent partiel, à type de mononévrite, de multinévrite et de polyradiculonévrite ascendante [ ]. Les anomalies du système nerveux central sont moins fréquentes que celles du système nerveux périphérique et ont tendance à survenir plus tardivement au cours de la maladie [ ]. L’apparition rapide d’une paraparésie/paraplégie ou d’une tétraparésie/tétraplégie associée à un déficit sensitif bilatéral ayant un niveau supérieur précis et à des troubles sphinctériens, définit cliniquement les myélopathies aiguës transverses totales. Dans les myélopathies aiguës transverses partielles, l’atteinte médullaire est asymétrique, parfois unilatérale; le déficit sensitif peut être au premier plan. La réalisation d’une IRM médullaire en urgence est indispensable pour éliminer une myélopathie aiguë d’origine compressive [ ]. La survenue de PAN en période de basse température sur l’année pourrait faire discuter dans notre étude de son rôle comme déclencheur dans l’expression de cette maladie. Cependant, aucun profil saisonnier n’a été observé pour cette vascularite dans la littérature [ ]. Les étiologies des myélites transverses sont nombreuses, réparties en cause primitive et secondaires. Les premières sont responsable de 2/3 des atteintes. Les données génétiques déterminent la susceptibilité génétique, et les facteurs environnementaux déclenchent la maladie. Les causes secondaires sont responsables d’un tiers des cas. Elles comprennent les causes infectieuses, en particulier les causes virales telles que l’hépatite B et C, l’infection par le VIH, le parvovirus B19 et le virus d’Epstein-Barr dans sa forme active. Parmi les autres causes, on trouve des causes hématologiques telles que la leucémie à tricholeucocytes, la leucémie myélomonocytaire et le syndrome myélodysplasique. Les causes auto-immunes comprennent le lupus, le syndrome des antiphospholipides, la sclérose en plaques et la neuromyélite optique. Dans ce cas, un test de Coombs positif et un nombre suffisant de critères de Guillevin, nous a orienté vers une cause immunologique, conduisant au diagnostic de PAN. Nous avons constaté chez nos deux patientes une récupération neurologique lente ayant nécessité plusieurs mois en raison du caractère axonal des lésions. La récupération est souvent de bonne qualité mais parfois incomplète, avec sur le plan sensitif, des douleurs résiduelles pouvant persister comme chez une de nos patientes [ ]. Des thérapies novatrices (biothérapies) ont été utilisées dans les cas de PAN récidivante ou réfractaire: tocilizumab, anti-TNF alpha et rituximab, permettant une rémission complète dans respectivement 50%, 40% et 33% des cas, avec des profils de sécurité comparables [ ]. les cas de PAN récidivante ou réfractaire: tocilizumab, anti-TNF alpha et rituximab, permettant une rémission complète dans respectivement 50%, 40% et 33% des cas, avec des profils de sécurité comparables [ ]. Au Gabon, l’assurance maladie nationale (encore appelée Caisse nationale d’assurance maladie et de garantie sociale) prend en charge 80% du coût effectif du médicament pour les affections courantes et 90% concernant les affections à longue durée [ ]. La périartérite noueuse est la 21 e /30, au même titre que le lupus systémique et la sclérodermie systémique [ ]. Pour le rituximab qui est à ce jour la seule biothérapie prise en charge, le patient paie 145,3 €. Conclusion La PAN est une vascularite nécrosante autoimmune très peu connue des praticiens africains, dont le pronostic peut être redoutable en l’absence de diagnostic. Il importe de vulgariser ce groupe d’affections dans les programmes universitaires des facultés de médecine d’Afrique subsaharienne, et de façon plus globale les maladies auto-immunes, étiquetées à tort par les praticiens d’Afrique subsaharienne, de « maladies des occidentaux ».
