documents.title: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF)

chunks.content: Introduction Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is a severe clinical syndrome characterized by acute hepatic decompensation, extrahepatic organ damage, and high short-term mortality, [ , ] which occurs on the basis of chronic liver diseases. The concept of ACLF was first proposed by Ohnishi et al [ ] in 1995, to describe two simultaneous lesions or insults to the liver, namely, an acute and rapid deterioration in liver function in individuals with preexisting chronic liver disease that was characterized by decompensated liver failure, high incidence of organ failure, and extremely high short-term mortality. In the nearly 30 years since the concept was proposed, it has been widely accepted by scholars all over the world. However, there is still no unified standard clinical definition for the diagnosis of ACLF worldwide. To better understand ACLF, the continuous comprehension and development of the clinical definition of ACLF is reviewed in this study. Furthermore, we have consolidated the current understanding of ACLF pathogenesis and summarized the therapeutic targets for ACLF that are currently under investigation. Last, we propose an experimental mouse model that can contribute to the mechanistic understanding of ACLF and the evaluation of potential new therapies. Disease Definition of ACLF Since the concept of ACLF was first proposed in 1995, its definition has been a subject of ongoing debate for nearly 30 years. Nevertheless, with the advancement of large-scale, well-characterized ACLF cohort studies conducted by different organizations and institutions, the definition of ACLF has progressively been clarified and refined. In 2006, the Chinese Society of Infectious Diseases and the Chinese Society of Hepatology of the Chinese Medical Association (CMA) described ACLF as: acute decompensation of liver function on the basis of chronic liver diseases. [ ] In 2009, the ACLF working group of Asian-Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL) published the first expert consensus on ACLF for the Asia-Pacific region. ACLF was defined as: acute deterioration of liver function manifested by jaundice (total bilirubin [TBil] ≥5 mg/dL or ≥85.5 μmol/L) and coagulopathy (international normalized ratio [INR] ≥1.5 or prothrombin activity [PTA] <40%), and complicated clinical ascites and/or encephalopathy within 4 weeks, regardless of whether the patient has previously diagnosed or undiagnosed chronic liver disease (including cirrhosis). [ ] In 2012, the CMA released the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2012 Edition)”, which also updated the definition of ACLF, pointing out that ACLF is a clinical syndrome of acute or subacute decompensation of liver function that occurs within a short period, usually within 4 weeks, on the basis of chronic liver diseases. [ ] Also in 2012, the APASL–ACLF Research Consortium (AARC) was formed to collect prospective data of patients with ACLF. [ ] In 2013, based on the results of a prospective multicenter study (Consortium for the Development of Criteria for Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure [CANONIC]) involving 1343 patients from eight European countries, the Chronic Liver Failure Consortium (CLIF-C) of the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) described ACLF as an acute deterioration of liver cirrhosis, usually correlating with a preceding disease characterized by organ failure and high short-term mortality (28-day mortality ≥15%). [ ] They proposed the CLIF–sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score to define ACLF and used SOFA score to diagnose organ failures. [ , ] According to the number of organ failures, ACLF is divided into three different grades (ACLF grades 1, 2, and 3), with 28‑day mortality rates of 22%, 32%, and 76% and 90‑day mortality rates of 40%, 52%, and 79%, respectively. The EASL–CLIF ACLF score (or CLIF–C ACLF score) does not reflect the severity of liver failure itself but provides useful information for predicting mortality and transplant inefficiency in Western patients with ACLF. In July 2014, the North American Consortium for the Study of End-stage Liver Disease (NACSELD) observed the outcomes of 507 hospitalized patients with decompensated cirrhosis caused by alcohol or hepatitis C and complicated with infection from 18 centers of liver diseases in the United States and Canada. They proposed the concept of infection-related ACLF (I-ACLF), which was defined as acute deterioration of a patient with cirrhosis due to infection presenting with two or more extrahepatic organ failure, such as grade III or IV hepatic encephalopathy, circulatory shock, need for mechanical ventilation, dialysis or other forms of renal replacement therapy, with high short-term mortality. [ ] This disease definition does not include changes in liver function and coagulation function. In October 2014, APASL updated the expert consensus based on the prospective study cohort data (AARC data) from the Asia–Pacific region. The cohort was constituted with 1363 patients from 14 countries. The updated definition of ACLF adopted some of the concepts of EASL–CLIF–C, and the characteristic of “high short-term (28-day) mortality” was added. [ ] Also in 2014, to bridge the gap between the disease definitions of

circulatory shock, need for mechanical ventilation, dialysis or other forms of renal replacement therapy, with high short-term mortality. [ ] This disease definition does not include changes in liver function and coagulation function. In October 2014, APASL updated the expert consensus based on the prospective study cohort data (AARC data) from the Asia–Pacific region. The cohort was constituted with 1363 patients from 14 countries. The updated definition of ACLF adopted some of the concepts of EASL–CLIF–C, and the characteristic of “high short-term (28-day) mortality” was added. [ ] Also in 2014, to bridge the gap between the disease definitions of ACLF from different agencies in the East and the West, the World Gastroenterology Organisation (WGO) proposed a new consensus, integrating existing concepts and ideas, defining ACLF as a syndrome that occurs in patients with chronic liver diseases with or without cirrhosis, characterized by acute liver failure (ALF) (jaundice and INR prolongation) caused by acute liver decompensation, single or multiple extrahepatic organ failures, resulting in an increased mortality rate within 3 months. In addition, ACLF was divided into three types: (1) type A, ACLF without cirrhosis; (2) type B, ACLF with compensated cirrhosis; and (3) type C, ACLF with decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] In 2018, the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2018 Edition)” of the CMA was updated, further improving the definition of ACLF as: on the basis of chronic liver diseases, a syndrome characterized by acute jaundice deepening and coagulation dysfunction as manifestations of liver failure caused by various precipitating factors, which may be combined with complications such as hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, electrolyte disorders, infections, hepatorenal syndrome, and hepatopulmonary syndrome, as well as other extrahepatic organ failure. [ ] At the same time, the update in this guideline also included the different ACLF types as proposed by the WGO, dividing ACLF into three types: (1) type A, ACLF occurring on the basis of chronic noncirrhotic liver diseases; (2) type B, ACLF occurring on the basis of compensated cirrhosis, usually within 4 weeks; and (3) type C, ACLF occurring on the basis of decompensated cirrhosis. In 2018, through the establishment of Chinese Group on the Study of Severe Hepatitis B (COSSH), Chinese scholars completed a study involving 1322 hospitalized patients with acute decompensation of hepatitis B cirrhosis or acute injury of chronic hepatitis B from 13 centers of liver diseases. Considering the fact that the clinical characteristics of hepatitis B virus infection-related ACLF (HBV–ACLF) in the East are different from those of alcoholic liver disease-related ACLF (ALD–ACLF) in the West, they summarized the clinical characteristics of HBV–ACLF in the East and defined HBV–ACLF as: in patients with chronic liver disease due to HBV infection, acute decompensation with liver or extrahepatic organ failure is associated with high short-term mortality. When TBil ≥12 mg/dL and prothrombin time (PT)–INR ≥1.5, ACLF should be diagnosed. This approach refines the HBV-related ACLF definition, filling the gap in EASL–ACLF criteria, which are not fully applicable to patients with hepatitis B in China. [ ] In 2019, based on the prospective multicenter study cohort data of 5228 patients from 43 centers in 15 countries in the Asia–Pacific region, the APASL–AARC once again updated the APASL consensus on ACLF, adding the description that “ACLF is a reversible syndrome” to the original disease definition, taking the reversibility of the disease as an important feature of ACLF, and pointing out that this reversibility is manifested as the decrease of TBil and PT–INR, as well as the improvement of hepatic encephalopathy or ascites. [ ] In 2022, the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) released the “Clinical Guidelines for Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure” for the first time based on the three international ACLF guidelines launched by APASL, EASL, and NACSELD, pointing out that ACLF is a potentially reversible disease that occurs in patients with chronic liver diseases with or without cirrhosis, and may lead to multiorgan failure and death within 3 months in the absence of basic treatment for liver disease, liver support treatment, or liver transplantation. ACLF is identified by chronic liver diseases, elevated serum TBil, and prolonged INR, and the occurrence of kidney, respiratory, circulatory, or brain function failure during the course of the disease, which is a further basis for ACLF diagnosis. The disease description of ACLF by the ACG is similar to the definitions of the CMA and APASL guidelines, and emphasizes more on the reversibility of the disease. In April 2023, the EASL once again updated the clinical practice guidelines for ACLF, evaluating and comparing the disease definitions and standards of ACLF proposed by APSAL, NACSELD, and COSSH, pointing out the deficiencies in APSAL and NACSELD, and emphasizing that the update of this guideline aims to help clinicians identify ACLF, rationally allocate treatment resources, and develop management strategies. The disease definition of ACLF described in

further basis for ACLF diagnosis. The disease description of ACLF by the ACG is similar to the definitions of the CMA and APASL guidelines, and emphasizes more on the reversibility of the disease. In April 2023, the EASL once again updated the clinical practice guidelines for ACLF, evaluating and comparing the disease definitions and standards of ACLF proposed by APSAL, NACSELD, and COSSH, pointing out the deficiencies in APSAL and NACSELD, and emphasizing that the update of this guideline aims to help clinicians identify ACLF, rationally allocate treatment resources, and develop management strategies. The disease definition of ACLF described in this version of the guideline is adjusted and improved from the 2013 version to: ACLF is a severe form of acute decompensation of cirrhosis, associated with a high 28-day mortality rate (≥20%), manifested as the failure of one up to six organ system (including the liver, kidney, brain, coagulation, circulation, and respiration), and the onset of acute factors that lead to systemic inflammation (SI), including intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic damage. [ ] In June 2023, during the 12th National Conference of the China Network for Severe Liver Diseases (CNSLD) held in Dalian, China, we proposed that ACLF could be divided into two types, based on the characteristics of intrahepatic and extrahepatic organ failures at the onset of ACLF [Figure ]. [ ] Type I ACLF: liver failure without extrahepatic organ failures Acute liver injury on the basis of chronic liver diseases, mainly manifested as jaundice and coagulation dysfunction. At the onset of ACLF, the affected organ is the liver, and some patients have hepatic encephalopathy. Liver failure is the first manifestation, and other organ failures do not occur simultaneously, and the disease definition is close to the content of APASL and CMA. [ , ] Type II ACLF: liver failure with extrahepatic organ failures Mostly acute decompensation of liver function on the basis of cirrhosis, manifested as elevated TBil, prolonged PT–INR, and the occurrence of complications of cirrhosis, accompanied by liver and at least one extrahepatic organ failure within 1 week, and the disease definition is close to the content of EASL–CLIF, COSSH, and NACSELD. [ , ] This classification and disease definition are of positive significance for bridging the gap between different associations in the East and the West regarding ACLF. However, it is worth further carrying out prospective multicenter studies to expand and confirm this classification and disease definition. In November 2023, the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) released a practice guideline proposing that any definition of ACLF needs to include the presence of hepatic dysfunction as well as the presence of extrahepatic organ failure. They recognized ACLF as multiorgan failure in patients with chronic liver disease, emphasizing its reversibility and the role of liver transplantation and supportive care. [ ] In March 2024, similar classification for ACLF (types A and B) was proposed in India. [ ] Moreover, at the APASL annual meeting held in Kyoto in March 2024, the “Kyoto APASL Consensus” proposed a unified ACLF definition based on the two-type classification (types A and B) and further refined the specific content of this definition. Type A ACLF excludes patients with earlier decompensation or those experiencing extrahepatic organ injury, and its course is considered reversible. Type B ACLF is defined similarly to the COSSH definition of ACLF and may include patients with earlier decompensation and organ failure caused by intra- or extrahepatic injuries (including infections), which is associated with increased mortality. Type A ACLF encompasses definitions from APASL and Japanese definitions, while Type B ACLF corresponds to the AASLD, EASL–CLIF, NACSELD, and COSSH definitions. Type A ACLF can be further stratified into grades A1, A2, and A3 based on the AARC score. ACLF defined by NACSELD can be reclassified into B2 and B3 based on the number of organ failures. [ ] This has made certain contributions to unifying the definitions of ACLF between the East and the West. In December 2024, the CMA released the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2024 Edition)”, incorporating key concepts from the COSSH standards. [ ] In April 2025, the Chinese Society of Hepatology of CMA released the first “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF) (2025 Edition)” in China, which builds upon the content related to ACLF from the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2024 Edition)”. It systematically classifies ACLF into type I (liver failure without extrahepatic organ failure) and type II (liver failure with extrahepatic organ failure) for separate description in clinical practice. [ ] By sorting out the descriptions for the disease definition of ACLF by various societies or organizations in recent years, we can clearly recognize the research progress that has been made in the field of ACLF [Table ]. The

and Treatment of Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF) (2025 Edition)” in China, which builds upon the content related to ACLF from the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2024 Edition)”. It systematically classifies ACLF into type I (liver failure without extrahepatic organ failure) and type II (liver failure with extrahepatic organ failure) for separate description in clinical practice. [ ] By sorting out the descriptions for the disease definition of ACLF by various societies or organizations in recent years, we can clearly recognize the research progress that has been made in the field of ACLF [Table ]. The APASL definition is simple and easy to use, emphasizing liver failure itself, which aligns with the epidemiological trend in the Asia–Pacific region, where viral hepatitis is predominant. This definition facilitates early diagnosis and treatment of ACLF, helping prevent progression to multiorgan failure. However, it pays insufficient attention to other organ failures and is not suitable for patients outside the Asia–Pacific region. Compared to the APASL definition, the EASL–ACLF includes patients with decompensated cirrhosis in its definition, emphasizing multiorgan failure and SI. It is more comprehensive and suitable for patients with multiorgan failure in Europe, particularly in cases requiring a holistic assessment of prognosis. However, it is not applicable to noncirrhotic patients. Additionally, NACSELD focuses on defining infection-related ACLF, making it particularly suitable for populations in North America where infections are prevalent, especially in cases of infection-induced multiorgan failure. Nevertheless, it is limited to infection-related ACLF, narrowing its scope of application, and does not emphasize liver failure itself. [ ] Although scholars around the world still have some different understanding of ACLF, the global research on ACLF is indeed gradually deepening and the understanding of ACLF is gradually improving. Thereby, a consensus for a general description of the disease definition of ACLF is gradually approaching. ACLF is different from ALF and chronic liver failure (CLF) and has unique clinical characteristics and prognostic outcomes. Therefore, establishing a clear disease definition of ACLF is of great significance for the early detection, diagnosis, and treatment of ACLF. With a deeper understanding of ACLF, global multicenter large-sample cohort studies are warranted to reach a general consensus on the definition of ACLF. Current Understanding of the Pathogenesis of ACLF In China and the Asia–Pacific region, the basic chronic liver disease in ACLF is mainly chronic hepatitis B, while in European and American countries, it is mainly alcoholic hepatitis and chronic hepatitis C. [ ] Although there are differences in the underlying liver diseases between the East and the West, the common pathological basis of most patients with ACLF is usually liver fibrosis or cirrhosis caused by long-term chronic liver injury. [ ] After suffering from acute intrahepatic or extrahepatic injury, acute decompensation of liver function occurs, such as jaundice, coagulation dysfunction, hepatic encephalopathy, and ascites, and eventually progresses to systemic multiorgan failure. [ ] At present, it is generally believed that the systemic inflammatory response induced by acute liver injury and bacterial infection, on the basis of long-term chronic liver injury, plays an important role in the outcome of ACLF. [ ] A large amount of clinical data also shows that the high short-term mortality of patients with ACLF is related to bacterial infection. [ ] In a multicenter ACLF cohort study of 407 patients, the EASL–CLIF research group found through that 37% of patients had bacterial infection at admission, and 46% of the remaining patients without infection at admission developed bacterial infection within 4 weeks of follow-up, mainly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, urinary tract infection, and pneumonia, suggesting that bacterial infection is widespread in patients with ACLF (>66%) and directly affects the clinical outcome. [ ] Alcohol-associated hepatitis is a major form of ACLF in Western countries, [ ] neutrophils are well known to play an important role in the pathogenesis of alcohol-associated hepatitis. [ ] A recent study demonstrated that the self-sustaining interleukin 8 (IL-8 + ) neutrophils are the major driver to promote alcohol-associated hepatitis disease progression and liver failure, [ ] which are potential therapeutic targets for alcohol-associated hepatitis. [ ] It would be interesting to determine whether IL-8 + neutrophils also play an important role in the pathogenesis of ACLF induced by other etiologies, such as HBV and HCV. In 2016, based on the CANONIC cohort, the EASL–CLIF research group proposed the well-known “SI hypothesis”, believing that ACLF is an acute exacerbation of the existing SI in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] The research group evaluated the systemic inflammatory response by detecting the levels of 29 cytokines in the serum of 522 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (237 patients with ACLF) and 40 healthy controls. They clinically confirmed the SI hypothesis and found that SI is the primary driving force for the progression of ACLF in patients with cirrhosis. [ ] In

other etiologies, such as HBV and HCV. In 2016, based on the CANONIC cohort, the EASL–CLIF research group proposed the well-known “SI hypothesis”, believing that ACLF is an acute exacerbation of the existing SI in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] The research group evaluated the systemic inflammatory response by detecting the levels of 29 cytokines in the serum of 522 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (237 patients with ACLF) and 40 healthy controls. They clinically confirmed the SI hypothesis and found that SI is the primary driving force for the progression of ACLF in patients with cirrhosis. [ ] In May 2020, renowned experts in the field of ACLF systematically concluded the definition, clinical features, pathophysiology, and prevention and treatment principles of ACLF caused by cirrhosis. They further pointed out that although the pathogenesis of ACLF is not entirely clear currently, systemic inflammatory response plays an important role in the course of ACLF. [ ] In patients with cirrhosis, the massive release of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) activates immune cells by binding to specific pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) of innate immune cells, leading to excessive systemic inflammatory response, causing immune-mediated tissue damage, and then causing single or multiple organ damage, and finally progressing to ACLF. [ ] Severe SI can lead to insufficient tissue perfusion, immune-mediated tissue damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction. [ , ] Among them, mitochondrial dysfunction is related to the progression of ACLF. In patients with ACLF, oxidative phosphorylation and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production are reduced, which may aggravate organ failure. Excessive release of proinflammatory cytokines consumes a large amount of energy. Coupled with the obstruction of energy production, it will eventually lead to immune exhaustion/immune paralysis. [ ] This immune dysfunction will increase the risk of secondary infection and lead to a higher mortality rate. [ ] In March 2021, core members of the EASL–CLIF research group again emphasized that the SI hypothesis is a new paradigm of acute decompensation and multiorgan failure in cirrhosis. [ ] Dr. Didier Samuel wrote an Editorial in the same issue and commented on the SI hypothesis proposed by Arroyo et al [ ] , pointing out that this hypothesis has introduced two new concepts in the field of ACLF: (1) Systemic inflammatory response is the driving factor for the development of decompensation in cirrhosis and (2) the increased incidence of bacterial infections in patients with cirrhosis is also the result of immune exhaustion or immune paralysis after systemic inflammatory response. [ ] It was further pointed out that with the elucidation of the mechanism of systemic inflammatory response in ACLF, it will lead to the application of anti-inflammatory therapies in the field of ACLF, and he also indicated that more work should be done to determine whether SI and immunoparesis are drivers or complications of decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] In conclusion, the pathogenesis of ACLF is comprehensive and complex, yet remains not fully elucidated. It is typically explained by the PIRO concept, including predisposition (P), injury (I), response (R), and organ failure (O). ACLF develops on the basis of long-term chronic liver damage caused by an underlying liver disease (predisposition). Following the sustention of various acute intrahepatic or extrahepatic injuries (injury), patients initially present with acute decompensation of liver function. This condition manifests as hyperbilirubinemia, coagulation disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, and ascites. The immune system response (response) induced by this injury can be divided into two aspects. One aspect is that, following acute liver injury, the cellular immunity and the reticuloendothelial cell system in the liver become imbalanced, and the ability of the liver to synthesize various anti-infectious proteins decreases, increasing the risk of bacterial infections (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis caused by intestinal flora translocation, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, and skin and soft tissue infections). Bacterial infections will lead to the presence of a large number of PAMPs in patients’ circulation. The other aspect is that necrotic hepatocytes release a large number of DAMPs into the systemic circulation. Circulating DAMPs and PAMPs bind to specific PRRs of innate immune cells, thereby activating the immune system. This activation then triggers the release of numerous proinflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-17, and interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which results in SI and a cytokine storm. This will stimulate a systemic inflammatory response that leads to subsequent immune-mediated tissue damage. After patients experience excessive systemic inflammatory response in the early stage of the ACLF, the late stage of the disease progresses to a state of immune exhaustion or immune paralysis, with bacterial infections further aggravated. Meanwhile, single or multiple organ dysfunction may occur. Subsequently, patients may progress to liver failure either without or with extrahepatic organ failure (Organ failure). Eventually, ACLF progresses to multiple organ failure, ultimately leading to the death of

IL-10, IL-17, and interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which results in SI and a cytokine storm. This will stimulate a systemic inflammatory response that leads to subsequent immune-mediated tissue damage. After patients experience excessive systemic inflammatory response in the early stage of the ACLF, the late stage of the disease progresses to a state of immune exhaustion or immune paralysis, with bacterial infections further aggravated. Meanwhile, single or multiple organ dysfunction may occur. Subsequently, patients may progress to liver failure either without or with extrahepatic organ failure (Organ failure). Eventually, ACLF progresses to multiple organ failure, ultimately leading to the death of the patient [Figure ]. [ ] Three-stage ACLF Mouse Model and Pathogenesis Progress At present, the existing experimental animal models for ACLF can be classified into three major categories: (1) hepatotoxic reagent-induced ACLF, (2) immune response-induced ACLF, and (3) surgical procedure-induced ACLF models. These models are designed to simulate different aspects of the disease pathogenesis by combining various induction methods. The principles, protocols, advantages, and disadvantages of these experimental models for ACLF are summarized in Table . In brief, hepatotoxic reagent-induced ACLF models include protocols using carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 ), thioacetamide (TAA), and acetaminophen (APAP) to induce chronic liver injury followed by acute insults, such as D-galactosamine (D-GalN) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). These models are widely used for studying liver fibrosis and acute injury. These models tend to have high mortality rates and short survival time, especially after the acute insult. Immune response-induced ACLF models primarily focus on immune responses by using substances, such as human serum albumin (HSA) and porcine serum (PS) for chronic injury, followed by D-GalN and LPS for acute injury. These models are particularly useful for studying autoimmune or viral hepatitis-related ACLF. While they provide valuable insights into immune-driven ACLF, they lack direct hepatotoxicity modeling and have high variability in immune responses. Surgical procedure-induced ACLF models include protocols such as bile duct ligation (BDL) with LPS, or BDL combined with hepatic ischemia/reperfusion injury. These models are suitable for studying cholestatic liver diseases and ischemic hepatitis. However, they require advanced surgical skills and have high mortality rates due to infection or complications from surgery. However, none of the existing ACLF models, whether induced by hepatotoxic reagents, immune responses, or surgical procedures, could fully replicate the entire disease course seen in patients with ACLF, making them imperfect representations of the condition. Based on the clinical characteristics of patients with ACLF, the optimal experimental animal model should be able to simulate the core pathological features of ACLF, including chronic liver injury, acute exacerbation, and multiorgan failure. Moreover, the reagents used for modeling should be easily accessible, and the induction methods should be simple and straightforward. Additionally, the model should allow for a reasonable survival period, ideally around one week, to facilitate intervention studies and better assess therapeutic efficacy. Due to the lack of optimal experimental animal models for ACLF, the progress of basic investigation of ACLF is limping. Although several experimental ACLF models have been established, none of them can recapitulate and simulate the whole pathological process of patients with ACLF. [ , ] Current research on the mechanisms of ACLF suggests that bacterial infection and systemic inflammatory response are crucial in the progression of the disease. [ , ] Based on cohort studies in patients with ACLF, it was found that the key clinical courses of most patients with ACLF can be divided into three stages: (1) long-term chronic liver injury, (2) acute liver injury, and (3) bacterial infection and systemic inflammatory response with extrahepatic organ damage. Recently, according to these three stages, our group has designed and developed a three-stage ACLF mouse model combining chronic liver injury, induced by injection of CCl 4 for 8 weeks, acute hepatic insult, obtained by injection of a double dose of CCl 4 , and bacterial infection caused through intraperitoneal injection of Klebsiella pneumoniae [Figure ]. [ , ] Using this mouse model, we were able to successfully simulat the key courses and major clinical features of patients with ACLF. Moreover, this model can also well simulate the extrahepatic organ damage that occurs during the progression of the disease, including acute kidney injury and multiple organ failure. It has an appropriate survival period for intervention research and provides a reliable tool for mechanistic investigation of ACLF. [ , ] The three-stage ACLF mouse model provides a comprehensive simulation of the key clinical features of ACLF, including chronic liver injury, acute insults, bacterial infection, and multiorgan injury. It is particularly useful for therapeutic research due to its ability to mimic the pathophysiological progression of ACLF, offering a survival window of 5–7 days suitable for preclinical intervention studies. The inclusion of viable bacterial infections, a critical feature in ACLF, further enhances its relevance. [ , ] Using the three-stage ACLF mouse model, our

[ , ] The three-stage ACLF mouse model provides a comprehensive simulation of the key clinical features of ACLF, including chronic liver injury, acute insults, bacterial infection, and multiorgan injury. It is particularly useful for therapeutic research due to its ability to mimic the pathophysiological progression of ACLF, offering a survival window of 5–7 days suitable for preclinical intervention studies. The inclusion of viable bacterial infections, a critical feature in ACLF, further enhances its relevance. [ , ] Using the three-stage ACLF mouse model, our group found that the imbalance of signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1)/STAT3 activation in the liver affecting liver regeneration is an important mechanism for the continuous progression of ACLF. It is mainly affected by excessive expression of IFN-γ and bacterial infection. Liver tissue and peripheral blood of patients with HBV–ACLF and ALD–ACLF confirmed that liver regeneration was significantly inhibited during the systemic inflammatory response. By regulating the imbalance of STAT1/STAT3 activation in the liver in the ACLF mouse model, the mortality rate of ACLF mice can be improved. Subsequently, it was found that the innate immune-related cytokine interleukin-22 (IL-22) can reverse the imbalance of STAT1/STAT3 activation in the liver and promote liver regeneration, thereby blocking the disease progression in ACLF mice. [ , ] Based on this study, a multicenter phase II clinical trial on treating ACLF with IL-22 fusion protein (IL-22Fc, F-652) is currently underway. At present, most studies on the mechanism of ACLF are related to systemic inflammatory response and immune dysfunction. Zhang et al [ ] found that the expression of V-domain Ig suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA) in peripheral blood and liver tissue of patients with ACLF was significantly reduced. The excessive differentiation of Th17 cells and the massive release of proinflammatory cytokines were related to the downregulation of VISTA expression. Using the three-stage ACLF model, activating VISTA expression in ACLF mice can inhibit the activation of CD4 + T cells, reduce inflammation, and reduce mortality. He et al [ ] found through transcriptomic studies that the expression of transcription factor ETS Proto-Oncogene 2 (ETS2) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of patients with ACLF was significantly higher than that in patients with chronic liver disease and healthy control. Moreover, ETS2 can be used to predict the 28/90-day mortality rate of patients with ACLF. It was confirmed that ETS2 has the effect of inhibiting excessive inflammatory response in mice model. Bernsmeier et al [ ] found that the expression of MER receptor tyrosine kinase (MERTK) was upregulated in patients with ACLF. MERTK is mainly expressed on monocytes–macrophages and inhibits innate immune responses. The number of monocytes–macrophages with high expression of MERTK in patients with ACLF increased significantly, inhibiting innate immune responses and increasing the risk of bacterial infection in patients with ACLF. Bernsmeier et al [ ] also found that CD14 + CD15-HLA-DR-myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) were significantly increased in patients with ACLF. This type of cell can inhibit T-cell function and weaken the antimicrobial innate immune response. It is related to secondary infection, disease severity, and prognosis of patients with ACLF. Yao et al [ ] detected the situation of T cells in the peripheral blood of patients with HBV–ACLF by single-cell sequencing technology and found that peripheral blood T cells in patients with ACLF are diverse, including naive T cells, effector T cells, and exhausted T cells. The frequency of exhausted T cells in patients with ACLF increased significantly during the progression of ACLF, suggesting that T-cell exhaustion promotes the occurrence of immune dysfunction (immune exhaustion/immune paralysis) in patients with ACLF. Peng et al [ ] used single-cell RNA sequencing to analyze liver nonparenchymal cells (NPCs) and PBMCs from healthy controls, and patients with liver cirrhosis and ACLF. They also examined a series of inflammation-related cytokines and chemokines in liver and plasma samples, as well as the lipid metabolome targeting free-fatty acids in the liver. The results revealed macrophage reprogramming in the liver during ACLF. Immunosuppressive triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) + macrophages were enriched in ACLF livers and contributed to an immunosuppressive hepatic microenvironment. The accumulation of unsaturated fatty acids in ACLF livers promoted macrophage reprogramming, highlighting the regulation of lipid metabolism as a potential target for improving immune dysfunction in patients with ACLF. [ ] Yang et al [ ] found that semaphorin-6B (SEMA6B) is significantly overexpressed in HBV-related patients with ACLF compared to healthy individuals. It mediates SI by inducing macrophages and inhibits proliferation through G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, thereby promoting hepatocyte apoptosis. These findings highlight SEMA6B as a promising early therapeutic target for patients with HBV–ACLF. [ ] Yu et al [ ] found that the levels of B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA) were significantly

fatty acids in ACLF livers promoted macrophage reprogramming, highlighting the regulation of lipid metabolism as a potential target for improving immune dysfunction in patients with ACLF. [ ] Yang et al [ ] found that semaphorin-6B (SEMA6B) is significantly overexpressed in HBV-related patients with ACLF compared to healthy individuals. It mediates SI by inducing macrophages and inhibits proliferation through G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, thereby promoting hepatocyte apoptosis. These findings highlight SEMA6B as a promising early therapeutic target for patients with HBV–ACLF. [ ] Yu et al [ ] found that the levels of B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA) were significantly increased in circulating and intrahepatic CD4 + T cells in patients with HBV–ACLF, which were positively correlated with disease severity, prognosis, and infection complications. Using the three-stage ACLF mice model, BTLA knockdown or administration of anti-BTLA antibody indicated increased cytokine secretion, reduced mortality and bacterial burden, showing a potential therapeutic target. [ ] Therapeutic Strategies and New Advances Currently, there is no specific and effective treatment for ACLF, the core principles of managing ACLF revolve around organ support and targeted interventions. [ ] Organ support aims to stabilize critical functions such as the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, while targeted interventions focus on addressing specific triggers, such as infections or SI. Early identification and treatment of these triggers are crucial for improving patient outcomes. Traditional treatment concepts for ACLF mainly include etiological treatment, supportive and symptomatic treatments, artificial liver support systems, and liver transplantation. The precise triggering factors of ACLF remain elusive; however, in 40%–50% of ACLF cases, bacterial translocation linked to SI is regarded as a critical determinant. When the trigger is identified, early recognition and targeted intervention of the causative factor would significantly improve the prognosis of patients with ACLF. However, a significant proportion of patients exhibit no identifiable triggering factors, substantially complicating the treatment process. [ ] Bacterial infection represents the most common trigger in patients with ACLF, exacerbating the disease course and significantly worsening the prognosis. A recent study revealed that approximately 37% of patients with ACLF presented with bacterial infections at the time of diagnosis. An additional 46% of patients developed bacterial infections within the subsequent 4 weeks. [ ] Regardless of the severity of ACLF, the prognosis of infected patients is significantly poorer compared to that of uninfected patients. [ ] Therefore, systematic pathogen detection and antimicrobial susceptibility testing should be performed upon hospital admission. Empirical antibiotic therapy should be initiated promptly upon the appearance of infection signs and subsequently adjusted based on pathogen detection and susceptibility results. [ ] For patients without infections, recent studies indicate that prophylactic use of antibiotics may reduce the risk of infection during the ACLF course, thereby decreasing mortality rates. [ , ] HBV reactivation is one of the most common triggers of ACLF in Asian countries and is associated with a high short-term mortality rate. [ ] Therefore, once HBV reactivation is suspected, immediate initiation of antiviral therapy with oral nucleotide or nucleoside analogues is recommended. For patients with ACLF and alcoholic liver disease, alcohol abstinence and corticosteroids remain the first-line therapeutic strategy. [ ] Artificial liver support system (ALSS) is a critical component of the comprehensive medical treatment of ACLF and serves as an essential bridging therapy for patients awaiting liver transplantation. [ ] These modalities include plasma exchange, blood/plasma adsorption, hemofiltration, hemodialysis, and various integrated blood purification systems. Extracorporeal liver support systems can rapidly improve the body’s internal environment and overall condition, mitigating further damage to the liver or other organs, while creating conditions for liver regeneration and recovery. In ACLF, liver cell injury is predominantly driven by cytokine storms and toxin accumulation. [ ] ALSS could effectively remove toxins produced during liver failure and reduce the levels of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Additionally, it also ameliorates cholestasis, enhances liver and renal function, and stabilizes hemodynamics, thereby providing patients with ACLF and improved survival opportunities or a better chance to await liver transplantation. [ ] Compared to conventional drug therapy, ALSS has been shown to significantly reduce the mortality rates in HBV–ACLF. [ ] However, according to the latest EASL clinical guidelines, extracorporeal liver support therapies, whether artificial or biological, are not routinely recommended for ACLF outside of research trials. [ ] Liver transplantation is one of the most effective approaches for managing end-stage liver failure resulting from diverse etiologies. It is indicated for patients who show inadequate response to active medical treatment and/or artificial liver support therapy, or who fail to achieve improvement or recovery with these interventions. However, the widespread application of liver transplantation is significantly constrained by factors such as donor liver shortages, high procedural costs, technical complexity, and the risk of posttransplant rejection. Recent advances in ACLF treatment have introduced several promising approaches [Table ]. Cell-based therapies Mesenchymal

routinely recommended for ACLF outside of research trials. [ ] Liver transplantation is one of the most effective approaches for managing end-stage liver failure resulting from diverse etiologies. It is indicated for patients who show inadequate response to active medical treatment and/or artificial liver support therapy, or who fail to achieve improvement or recovery with these interventions. However, the widespread application of liver transplantation is significantly constrained by factors such as donor liver shortages, high procedural costs, technical complexity, and the risk of posttransplant rejection. Recent advances in ACLF treatment have introduced several promising approaches [Table ]. Cell-based therapies Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) [ , ] and hepatocyte transplantation [ ] offer potential for liver regeneration and functional recovery, though large-scale clinical trials are needed to confirm their efficacy. Immunomodulation therapies Agents such as thymosin α1 [ ] and BTLA blockers [ ] aim to restore immune balance and enhance anti-infective capacity, addressing the immune dysregulation observed in ACLF. Cytokine-targeted therapies Drugs such as IL-22 promote liver regeneration [ , ] and have shown promise in early-phase clinical trials with good safety and a certain degree of efficiency (phase IIa in China, unpublished). Artificial liver support systems Nonbioartificial (e.g., double plasma molecular adsorption system [DPMAS] combined with plasma exchange [PE]) [ , ] or bioartificial liver systems, [ ] and novel devices like the DIALIVE liver dialysis system provide temporary support, bridging patients to recovery or liver transplantation. [ ] Gut–liver axis modulation Engineered carbon bead adsorbents reduce intestinal endotoxin levels, mitigating liver injury and SI. [ ] Pharmacological interventions Statins have shown potential in preventing the progression of cirrhosis to ACLF and reducing ACLF-related mortality, though further randomized controlled trials are needed. [ ] Despite these advancements, challenges remain, particularly in understanding the heterogeneous triggers of ACLF and standardizing treatment protocols. Future research should focus on large-scale, multicenter studies to validate these emerging therapies and refine therapeutic strategies. Conclusion and Prospect Although there is still no unified standard for the disease definition and diagnosis of ACLF worldwide, and there are still some differences in the descriptions of ACLF disease definitions by various associations or organizations around the world, with the gradual deepening of research, the clinical definition of the ACLF is more accurate and substantial progress is being made in the understanding of the pathogenesis of ACLF. ACLF has been widely recognized as a clinical syndrome different from ALF and CLF. Yet, only in recent years, key features of ACLF disease description, such as the basis of chronic liver diseases, acute intrahepatic or extrahepatic injury, acute hepatic decompensation, extrahepatic organ failure, high short-term mortality, and the reversibility of the disease course, have been systematically introduced, gradually narrowing the differences in disease definition between liver disease associations in the East and the West. However, there are still some differences in the evaluation standards for describing these key features, and it is urgent to carry out large-sample global multicenter prospective studies covering different etiologies and populations to achieve unification of the disease recognition and reach a consensus on ACLF definition in the East and the West. chunks.content: Introduction Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is one of the most effective therapeutic options for treating complications of portal hypertension. Guidance on TIPS has been published by numerous international groups, including the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) in 2005 (with updates in 2009 and 2023), the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) in 2018 and the British Society of Gastroenterology in 2020, along with the North American practice-based recommendations for TIPS from the Advancing Liver Therapeutic Approaches (ALTA) Consortium in 2021 and the Baveno VII recommendations of 2022 [ – ]. Moreover, recent advances relating to novel procedural techniques, TIPS stent technology and emerging indications for TIPS have contributed significantly to the body of evidence for the effectiveness and safety of TIPS. With this rapid evolution of knowledge, there remains a lack of consensus about which patients should receive a TIPS and an absence of dedicated guidance on TIPS referral pathways and practice guidelines in the Australian context. Consequently, Australian institutions demonstrate marked variability in practice and outcomes, with critical knowledge gaps revealed by a recent national survey of TIPS centers [ ]. One of the key aims of guideline development is to promote dialogue among and between referring teams, multidisciplinary teams at TIPS centers and proceduralists. Methods The development of the consensus statement comprised elected members of the GESA Liver Faculty, representatives from IRSA and individuals from all relevant professional groups, including specialist clinicians, nurses and researchers with expertise in management of portal hypertension-related complications and the use of TIPS. A modified Delphi ( m -Delphi) approach is used to achieve consensus (Fig. ). A consensus process was conducted in accordance with the standards outlined in the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II (AGREE II) [ ]. Evidence supporting each recommendation was derived from a structured review of English-language literature published between January 1990 and June 2023, using PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Knowledge, and the Cochrane Database. Searches combined core keywords with topic-specific terms relevant to each clinical domain. Evidence was appraised hierarchically, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, followed by meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and observational studies; high-quality case reports and existing evidence-based guidelines were considered where data were limited. Systematic reviews were assessed using the AMSTAR tool, and the quality and strength of evidence were graded according to the GRADE framework, consistent with the NHMRC 2016 standards for guideline development. Draft statements were synthesized through iterative expert discussion to ensure evidence alignment and clinical relevance. The level of evidence for all consensus statements was appraised according to Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system, as recommended by the National Health and Medical Research Council Guidelines for Guidelines [ , ]. The quality of the evidence was classified as high, moderate, low, or very low, and the strength of recommendation was classified as either strong or weak (Table ). In accordance with GRADE guidance, strong recommendations based on low-certainty evidence were permitted when one or more of the following conditions were met: (i) the balance of benefits and harms was judged to be clear and consistent across available evidence; (ii) the intervention addressed outcomes of critical clinical importance, including morbidity, mortality, or irreversible harm; (iii) there was substantial concordance between indirect evidence, pathophysiological rationale, and clinical experience; (iv) patient values and preferences were considered unlikely to vary meaningfully; and/or (v) failure to act was judged to pose a greater risk than implementation of the recommendation. In such cases, low certainty of evidence reflected limitations in study design, imprecision, or indirectness rather than uncertainty regarding the direction of effect. The rationale for issuing a strong recommendation in the context of low-certainty evidence was explicitly discussed by the panel and documented during the consensus process. Statements were categorized into four overall clinical domains related to TIPS, as follows: (1) preparation for TIPS, patients’ selection, and pre-TIPS workup, (2) best procedural practice, (3) postoperative care and follow-up, and (4) indications for TIPS. Recommendation statements were tailored to the Australian context where relevant. An 80% consensus was required for statements to progress to the modified Delphi ( m- Delphi) consensus rounds. Participants were asked in m -Delphi round 1 to rate their agreement with each statement based on a 9-point scale, with 1 being “strongly disagree” and 9 being “strongly agree”. Consensus was defined as a mean score above 7 (indicating agreement) with responses from at least 80% of participants. Statements scoring between 6 and 9, or those not meeting the 80% response criterion, were subsequently reviewed and subjected to formal voting during a hybrid online and in-person meeting. Recommendations with a mean score < 5 with/without disagreement of participants or if the number of responders is less than 5 has not automatically progressed to hybrid online–face-to face meeting (Fig. ). Statements scoring between 6 and 9, or those not meeting the 80% response criterion, were subsequently reviewed and subjected to formal voting during a hybrid online and in-person meeting. All participants completed a standardized conflict-of-interest disclosure form prior to participation. Disclosures were prospectively documented in the project record. Members were permitted to abstain from voting on any statement for which they considered themselves to lack sufficient expertise. Dissenting comments and reasons for disagreement were reviewed collectively by the panel. Statements that did not meet the predefined consensus threshold were revised based on substantive feedback and recirculated for re-rating in subsequent m-Delphi rounds. GESA convened multidisciplinary expert groups to discuss several identified topics at a hybrid online and face-to-face meeting held in Sydney on 24 May 2024. At this meeting, the preliminary ratings from the first m -Delphi round were discussed, statements with suboptimal wording were refined, and a second round of formal voting was held to re-rate statements through equally weighted voting. Participants ( n = 50) who could not attend in person were given the option to attend online via videoconferencing for real-time discussion on each proposed statement. The complete list of participants—including names, specialties, institutions, and states—is provided in Supplementary Table 1 (Acknowledgement of participation). A second online questionnaire ( m -Delphi round 2) followed the hybrid meeting. Results from both m -Delphi rounds have provided a practical approach and best practice recommendations for the clinical assessment and management of patients undergoing consideration for the TIPS procedure. Summary of recommendations can be found in Table . Following the modified Delphi process, the final recommendations underwent independent external review by international experts to confirm validity, clarity, and applicability before publication. Preparation for TIPS, patient selection and pre-TIPS workup Preparation for TIPS A multidisciplinary and team-based approach to TIPS is of crucial throughout all stages of TIPS planning, management, and evaluation [ , ]. The decision to implant a TIPS (whether emergent or non-emergent) should initially involve multidisciplinary team discussions with, as a minimum, one hepatologist and one interventional radiologist who have proven procedural expertise. Where appropriate, and based on individual factors, the multidisciplinary team discussions should also involve various other specialists, such as a liver transplant surgeon, liver transplant physician, cardiologist, anesthesiologist, intensivist, hematologist or nephrologist. Longitudinal care for patients who undergo TIPS involves a range of specialists and allied health professionals, to minimize the risk of complications and optimize patient outcomes. TIPS implantation demands a high degree of technical skill and clinical proficiency to achieve optimal patient outcomes. It should therefore be undertaken by appropriately trained and experienced proceduralists at centers with relevant experience in performing the procedure, and where specialist services for managing complications are available [ , ]. Procedural and post-procedural complications of TIPS implantation are listed in Table . Patient selection Patient selection for TIPS is a multidisciplinary decision that involves demographic, clinical and laboratory parameters and preoperative considerations, as well as standard scoring systems for patients with cirrhosis. These include the model for end-stage liver disease (MELD), Child–Pugh score, chronic Liver failure consortium acute-on-chronic liver failure (CLIF-C ACLF) score, modified TIPS score (MOTS), Emory model, Bonn TIPS early mortality (BOTEM) score, platelet–albumin–bilirubin index (PALBI) and Freiburg index of post-TIPS survival (FIPS) [ – ]. Recently, the Elderly Patients Calculator TIPS (ExPeCT) model was developed for mortality prediction in patients aged ≥ 70 years with an indication for TIPS [ ]. Prognostic scoring to assess candidacy for TIPS should be individualized to the patient’s clinical context and interpreted within a multidisciplinary decision-making framework. Historically, MELD score has been the strongest predictor of 90-day mortality after TIPS. Some studies suggest that TIPS should not be undertaken when the MELD score is ≥ 18 for patients with ascites [ ]. However, the role of MELD score in patient candidacy for TIPS implantation remains unclear. Recently, the FIPS score has demonstrated superiority to established scoring systems (Child–Pugh, MELD and MELD-Sodium scores and the bilirubin–platelet model) for identifying high-risk patients with a worse prognosis after elective TIPS implantation for variceal bleeding or refractory ascites [ , , ]. Nonetheless, the FIPS score demonstrates limited prognostic discrimination in patients undergoing pre-emptive TIPS implantation. A study in a Chinese cohort of 536 patients undergoing TIPS found that risk stratification using the Child–Pugh score appeared more favorable than using the FIPS score [ ]. Therefore, using prognostic scoring to assess candidacy for TIPS

candidacy for TIPS implantation remains unclear. Recently, the FIPS score has demonstrated superiority to established scoring systems (Child–Pugh, MELD and MELD-Sodium scores and the bilirubin–platelet model) for identifying high-risk patients with a worse prognosis after elective TIPS implantation for variceal bleeding or refractory ascites [ , , ]. Nonetheless, the FIPS score demonstrates limited prognostic discrimination in patients undergoing pre-emptive TIPS implantation. A study in a Chinese cohort of 536 patients undergoing TIPS found that risk stratification using the Child–Pugh score appeared more favorable than using the FIPS score [ ]. Therefore, using prognostic scoring to assess candidacy for TIPS implantation can only guide clinical decision-making but the potential risks and benefits should be carefully evaluated for each individual patient. The prognostic scoring systems available for predicting survival after TIPS implantation are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Pre-TIPS workup Imaging Contrast-enhanced multiphasic cross-sectional (CT/MRI) series and Doppler ultrasound examinations should include portal venous phase imaging to adequately define portal veins, hepatic veins, and the parenchyma of the liver and review any vascular and parenchymal anatomic variations to determine suitability of TIPS implantation. For patients who require emergency TIPS implantation, bedside echocardiography of the heart and Doppler ultrasound of the liver are a possible alternative [ , ]. Cardiopulmonary assessments The complex hemodynamic changes observed in cirrhosis and portal hypertension can result in impaired cardiac function, a syndrome known as cirrhotic cardiomyopathy. This includes a cluster of cardiovascular abnormalities, such as impaired cardiac contractility with systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction, as well as electromechanical abnormalities (i.e., prolonged QT interval) in the absence of other known causes of cardiac disease [ – ]. Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy complicates several therapies used for treating patients with cirrhosis and confers an increased risk of post-TIPS heart failure. Diastolic dysfunction has been identified as predictor of cardiac events post-TIPS implementation [ , ]. Therefore, cardiovascular assessment is essential before TIPS implantation, as increased portosystemic shunting is associated with worsening of hyperdynamic syndrome, as seen by a marked rise in preload and cardiac output, combined with a concomitant decline in systemic vascular resistance [ ]. Cardiac decompensation occurs in up to 20% of patients within the first year after TIPS implantation [ ]. Right-sided heart failure may be triggered not only in patients with pre-existing overt heart failure or severe tricuspid regurgitation, but also in those with subclinical cardiac dysfunction or moderate to severe portopulmonary hypertension [ – ]. Hence, a comprehensive cardiac history should be taken, and investigations to evaluate any structural or functional cardiac abnormalities should be done for all patients undergoing elective TIPS implantation. Investigations should incorporate 12-lead electrocardiography, measurement of serum N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level and echocardiographic measurement of both left and right ventricular function. Transthoracic echocardiographic assessment should include assessment of left ventricular ejection fraction and measurement of left ventricular diastolic function, left ventricular global longitudinal strain, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) and right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) [ , , ]. Bedside echocardiography and Doppler ultrasound of the liver may be indicated for patients with acute variceal bleeding who are undergoing emergency TIPS, but these investigations should not preclude or delay an emergency TIPS procedure. Nutritional assessment Sarcopenia, frailty, and malnutrition are prevalent among patients with decompensated cirrhosis [ ]. Muscle wasting is associated with an increased risk for the development of HE after TIPS implantation [ , ]. Recent international guidelines recommend that skeletal mass index be quantified by CT imaging given that this method is the most consistent and reproducible. A detailed dietic assessment can be preserved for patients at risk of malnutrition [ ]. This is even more relevant for patients with ascites, as underlying malnutrition is likely to contribute to its severity. Alcohol relapse is common after TIPS implantation, underscoring the need for careful risk assessment, especially in patients scheduled for elective procedures [ ]. Renal function assessment Physiologically, TIPS implantation may halt the decline of renal function and lead to improvement, owing to decreased effective circulating volume [ – ]. Renal function should be evaluated before TIPS, either through measurement of serum creatinine level or using glomerular filtration rate (estimated or measured), as contrast-induced injury and acute kidney injury (AKI) can occur after TIPS implantation [ ]. To date, most RCTs of TIPS have excluded patients with advanced renal disease [ – ]. However, several studies have reported that the incidence of post-TIPS AKI was about 17% [ , – ]. This proportion does not take into consideration whether these represent true cases of AKI occurring after TIPS, a result of pre-TIPS intrinsic kidney disease or an AKI from pre-existing stable chronic renal disease. ]. To date, most RCTs of TIPS have excluded patients with advanced renal disease [ – ]. However, several studies have reported that the incidence of post-TIPS AKI was about 17% [ , – ]. This proportion does not take into consideration whether these represent true cases of AKI occurring after TIPS, a result of pre-TIPS intrinsic kidney disease or an AKI from pre-existing stable chronic renal disease. The current opinion of both the ALTA Consortium and GESA is that there is no absolute serum creatinine cut-off level, chronic kidney disease stage or factors such as presence or absence of renal replacement therapy that contraindicate TIPS implantation. However, given that severe hepatic encephalopathy is common in the presence of severe (stage 4 or 5) intrinsic renal disease [ , ], we recommend against TIPS implantation in this group of patients. Mitigating post-TIPS AKI and risk of progression to acute or chronic kidney disease is crucial. For patients undergoing TIPS implantation for ascites, human albumin infusions can be considered for those having large-volume (usually > 5 L) paracentesis, to reduce the risk of paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction and AKI. Infusions may occur 24 h before, or during, TIPS implantation [ – ]. Hepatic encephalopathy Hepatic encephalopathy is a frequent complication of all portosystemic shunts, including TIPS [ ]. An episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy occurs in up to 50% of patients post-TIPS implantation [ , – ]. Numerous patient factors contribute to the development of post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy, including older age, severity of liver disease (Child–Pugh class C, Child–Pugh score ≥ 10 or MELD score > 18), prior hepatic encephalopathy, shunt size, sarcopenia, elevated creatinine level, hyponatremia and low portosystemic pressure gradient (PSPG) after TIPS placement [ , , ]. Therefore, patients scheduled for non-urgent TIPS implantation should be routinely assessed and screened for the presence or a history of overt or covert (subclinical) hepatic encephalopathy [ , ]. Typically, hepatic encephalopathy presents episodically or continuously with detectable neuropsychiatric abnormalities. In contrast, minimal hepatic encephalopathy is often overlooked in practice and can only be diagnosed with neuropsychometric testing. Screening should ideally involve at least two of: the Psychometric Hepatic Encephalopathy Score, Stroop testing, critical flicker frequency, and spectral-enhanced or quantitative electroencephalography. Covert hepatic encephalopathy carries an increased risk of falls, driving impairment and diminished quality of life [ ]. The diagnosis of covert hepatic encephalopathy in the absence of acute decompensation—a relative contraindication to elective TIPS—may guide discussions with patients, caregivers and clinical teams regarding the utility of TIPS [ , ]. TIPS implantation is among the most technically delicate interventional radiological procedures. The initial stent diameter is a key determinant in reducing the postoperative risk of hepatic encephalopathy. Controlled-expansion stents incremental and reliable adjustment of the stent diameter. Small portosystemic shunts are associated with a lower incidence of hepatic encephalopathy, though this may compromise the degree of portal pressure reduction and decompression [ – ]. For patients with a history of overt hepatic encephalopathy, receiving rifaximin before TIPS implantation may significantly reduce the risk of hepatic encephalopathy after the procedure [ ]. Despite careful patient selection and investigation for hepatic encephalopathy before TIPS implantation, the onset of hepatic encephalopathy after TIPS is common, although it is usually short-lived. Basic hepatic encephalopathy management should include correction of underlying biochemical abnormalities, cessation of night sedation and prescription of lactulose at the first episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy. Proton pump inhibitors, if prescribed, should be ceased. For subsequent episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy, both rifaximin and lactulose are recommended [ ]. If hepatic encephalopathy remains refractory to medical therapy, treatment should include endoscopy for surveillance and treatment of high-risk varices before undertaking collateral large (> 6 mm) spontaneous portosystemic shunt embolisation, followed by TIPS stent reduction (recalibration) or occlusion [ , ]. Supplementary Table 3 summarizes recent studies on HE incidences and outcomes post-TIPS implantation. Contraindications Contraindications for TIPS can be found in Table . Consent Informed consent is an essential component of patient care, including before a TIPS procedure. In accordance with local and international guidelines, health care providers must ensure that patients fully understand the risks and benefits of the TIPS procedure, as well as any available alternative treatments [ , , – ]. Patients should also be made aware of potential side effects of TIPS implantation, including hepatic encephalopathy, to ensure they can make a well-informed decision about their treatment [ ]. A fact sheet that can be provided to patients to help them understand the TIPS procedure and give their informed consent is available at: https://www.gesa.org.au/public/13/files/Education%20%26%20Resources/Patient%20Resources/TIPS/GESA%20TIPS%20Patient%20Resource.pdf . A fact sheet that can be provided to patients to help them understand the TIPS procedure and give their informed consent is available at: https://www.gesa.org.au/public/13/files/Education%20%26%20Resources/Patient%20Resources/TIPS/GESA%20TIPS%20Patient%20Resource.pdf . Section 2 Best procedural practice Anesthesia and sedation TIPS implantation should be performed either under general anesthesia or with deep sedation. Blood products Evidence regarding management of procedural bleeding risk in patients undergoing the TIPS procedure is limited, particularly for correction of thrombocytopenia, but there is some evidence that viscoelastic testing can guide correction of coagulopathy [ – ]. Procedure Stents While bare-metal stents were previously standard, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE)-covered stents have become the gold standard in routine practice, due to superior patency, better ascites control, reduced risk of rebleeding, and overall cost-effectiveness [ , – ]. We recommend using stents with an 8 mm diameter in patients with high cardiac risk (mild portopulmonary hypertension or systolic or diastolic dysfunction) to prevent worsening of cardiac function and reduce the risk of post-TIPS heart failure [ , ]. Measurement of PSPG before and after TIPS Post-TIPS PSPG is important for predicting rebleeding risk and postoperative complications, such as hepatic encephalopathy and deterioration in hepatic function. One study identified that a PSPG > 12 mmHg after TIPS implantation (> 24 h of follow-up) was associated with an 8.5-times higher risk of recurrence of portal hypertension complications (variceal bleeding or ascites) [ ]. PSPG should be measured before and after TIPS implantation, with the aim of achieving an absolute reduction in PSPG to < 12 mmHg, or a relative reduction of > 50% from the pre-TIPS baseline, in patients with acute variceal bleeding [ , ]. PSPG should be measured as the difference in pressure between the main portal vein and the confluence of the hepatic vein and inferior vena cava (IVC). If measurement of IVC pressure is not feasible, right atrial pressure can be used instead; however, this may lead to an overestimation of PSPG [ , , ]. Section 3 Postoperative care and follow-up Post-TIPS monitoring Patients post-TIPS should be followed with gastroenterologist/hepatologists and interventional radiologist to monitor for ongoing procedural complications as well as ongoing liver disease. Kidney function should be closely monitored in patients post-TIPS for contrast-related injury, or AKI. Doppler ultrasound In the era of ePTFE-covered stents, early TIPS dysfunction due to thrombosis rarely occurs. Hence, early Doppler ultrasound within about 48 h is of limited utility soon after TIPS insertion. Proactive follow-up with Doppler ultrasound typically takes place 1 week after TIPS placement, then routinely at 3 months, 6 months and 6-monthly intervals thereafter [ ]. Early ultrasound findings suggesting TIPS dysfunction should prompt endovascular evaluation especially when combined with recurrent of portal hypertension-related symptoms (e.g., ascites and variceal bleeding) [ ]. Doppler ultrasound findings suggesting of TIPS dysfunction includes alteration of intrahepatic portal vein flow direction or abnormal velocity within TIPS (A mean maximum flow velocity (mVPmax) at the portal vein < 28 cm/s when flow is hepatofugal or mVPmax < 39 cm/s when flow is hepatopetal). Venography Indications for venography include abnormal Doppler parameters, such as markedly elevated or diminished velocities within the shunt, reversed portal venous flow or the recurrence of portal hypertensive complications, including refractory ascites or variceal hemorrhage. Catheter-based venography, typically performed in conjunction with PSPG assessment, constitutes the reference standard for evaluating TIPS patency and hemodynamic function. This technique permits direct visualization of luminal stenosis, thrombosis, or structural anomalies within the shunt and facilitates immediate endovascular intervention when indicated (e.g., balloon angioplasty or secondary stent placement) if indicated [ – ]. Section 4 Indications TIPS for portal hypertensive bleeding Acute variceal bleeding and TIPS Acute variceal bleeding is a life-threatening complication of cirrhosis. Its annual incidence is 10–15%, and 6-week mortality is about 15–20% [ ]. A landmark 1981 study showed that mortality in patients with acute variceal bleeding is concentrated within the first 3 days [ ]. At present, the standard of care for patients with acute variceal bleeding includes a combination of restrictive transfusion strategy (packed red blood cells, with a target hemoglobin level of 70–80 g/L), endoscopic variceal ligation, antibiotic prophylaxis and vasoactive drugs (e.g., terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide), and salvage balloon tamponade or insertion of self-expanding metal stents [ ]. Nonetheless, initial endoscopic and medical treatment fails in 10–20% of patients, which is associated with a high short-term risk of further liver decompensation and death. Most patients with acute variceal bleeding have advanced (Child–Pugh class C) cirrhosis, and rescue TIPS implantation results in high mortality in these patients. Numerous endovascular obliteration or embolisation techniques, such as retrograde transvenous obliteration (plug-assisted, coil-assisted or balloon) or antegrade transvenous obliteration, have been used

hemoglobin level of 70–80 g/L), endoscopic variceal ligation, antibiotic prophylaxis and vasoactive drugs (e.g., terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide), and salvage balloon tamponade or insertion of self-expanding metal stents [ ]. Nonetheless, initial endoscopic and medical treatment fails in 10–20% of patients, which is associated with a high short-term risk of further liver decompensation and death. Most patients with acute variceal bleeding have advanced (Child–Pugh class C) cirrhosis, and rescue TIPS implantation results in high mortality in these patients. Numerous endovascular obliteration or embolisation techniques, such as retrograde transvenous obliteration (plug-assisted, coil-assisted or balloon) or antegrade transvenous obliteration, have been used as alternative or complementary treatments to TIPS for managing variceal bleeding. High MELD scores and lactate levels have been associated with mortality in patients with cirrhosis treated with salvage TIPS implantation [ ] (Table ). In 2004, the first study on pre-emptive TIPS implantation for acute variceal bleeding was published [ ]. In this RCT, TIPS implantation was performed for acute variceal bleeding within 72 h of diagnostic endoscopy in 26 hemodynamically stable patients, with a hepatic venous pressure gradient > 20 mmHg, who had received standard care and were likely to be at high risk of future rebleeding and bleeding-related mortality. In these patients, TIPS placement within 24 h of admission led to a significant reduction in mortality and rebleeding, compared with standard-of-care measures. However, given that routine hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement is not readily available at most institutions, pre-emptive TIPS implantation was not championed, despite this landmark trial. In 2010, a second RCT showed that pre-emptive TIPS implantation within 72 h of initial upper endoscopy in 63 patients admitted with acute variceal bleeding and Child–Pugh class B cirrhosis (with active bleeding at endoscopy) or class C cirrhosis (regardless of bleeding status at time of endoscopy) was associated with significant reductions in rebleeding and failure to control bleeding, and improved survival, with no increased risk of hepatic encephalopathy [ ]. These results were later confirmed in a larger trial of 132 patients [ ]. Further, individual patient data meta-analysis of three RCTs and five observational studies, involving 1327 patients with cirrhosis (of whom 310 received pre-emptive TIPS implantation and 1017 received vasoactive drugs and endoscopy), concluded that patients with Child–Pugh class C cirrhosis (score 10–13) or class B (score 8–9) presenting with active variceal bleeding at endoscopy are at high risk of rebleeding and are the most likely to benefit from pre-emptive TIPS implantation [ ]. Patients who do not fulfill these criteria should be evaluated for rescue TIPS [ ]. Independent of Child–Pugh class, any patient presenting with uncontrolled acute variceal bleeding at endoscopy warrants referral for salvage TIPS. However, a more recent two-center open-label RCT of 58 patients found that pre-emptive TIPS reduced variceal bleeding but had no effect on survival and, conversely, increased the risk of hepatic encephalopathy [ ]. A growing body of observational studies suggests that the presence of hyperbilirubinemia, hepatic encephalopathy or acute-on-chronic liver failure at time of bleeding has no impact on patients’ survival when they are managed with pre-emptive TIPS implantation [ , , ]. Aside from the known role of TIPS in treating variceal bleeding, a recent meta-analysis of individual patient data, including 12 controlled studies involving 2338 patients, found that TIPS implantation for prevention of variceal rebleeding and refractory ascites can reduce the overall risk of further decompensation and improve survival, compared with standard care [ ]. Secondary prevention of variceal bleeding Guidelines from prominent international liver disease societies (AASLD, EASL and ALTA) consider TIPS implantation as second-line therapy for prevention of recurrent bleeding. This is based on two RCTs demonstrating the clinical utility of TIPS in reducing variceal rebleeding risk, with an increased risk of hepatic encephalopathy and no impact on survival or quality of life [ , ]. Gastric varices Limited evidence supports the effectiveness of TIPS or BRTO (balloon-retrograde transverse obliteration) for management of GVs. Available literature has shown that TIPS when compared with BRTO is associated with higher postoperative procedure-related complications, higher rebleeding risk, postoperative HE and hepatic ischemia without any difference in patient survival [ – ]. Pre-emptive TIPS (when combined with endoscopic cyanoacrylate injection (glue) with or without NSBBs) can be used as first-line therapy for GOV2 and/or IGV1 management. A recent RCT of small sample size ( n = 21) demonstrated that the use of pre-emptive TIPS (within first 5 days of bleeding) with combined endoscopic (injection of glue) and pharmacological therapy (first, somatostatin or terlipressin; carvedilol after discharge ( n = 11) is associated with a significantly higher rebleeding-free survival in patients with gastric fundal varices (IGV1/GOV 2), when compared with standard care ( n = 10) in patients of Child–Pugh B and C scores [ ]. Importantly, in this RCT, patients had bare stents that carry much poorer outcomes.
