QUE activates the FXR/TGR5 pathway, reducing hepatic lipid accumulation [ ]. CGA promotes free fatty acid release via PPARα and facilitates the hydrolysis of exogenous triglycerides [ , ]. Tea polyphenols such as EGCG and ECG upregulate LDL receptor and SREBP-2 expression, thereby inhibiting intestinal cholesterol absorption [ , , ]. Additionally, polyphenols post-transcriptionally modulate gene expression-e.g., ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and FAS-via interactions with microRNAs such as miR-33a and miR-122 [ ]. Glucose metabolic homeostasis Polyphenols regulate glucose homeostasis through multi-target mechanisms. EC counteracts high glucose-induced insulin signaling impairment, restoring glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2) expression and insulin receptor (IR) function [ ]. RES improves insulin sensitivity and promotes skeletal muscle glucose uptake via SIRT1 activation [ ]. CA stimulates protein kinase B (AKT) and AMPK signaling, enhances glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis in hepatocytes, and inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes including phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and glucose-6-phosphatase (G6P) [ , , ]. Rutin enhances insulin receptor kinase (IRK) phosphorylation and promotes GLUT4 translocation, improving peripheral glucose uptake [ ]. EGCG facilitates GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle, restores insulin sensitivity in HepG2 cells, and suppresses hepatic glucose output via antagonism of the glucagon-protein kinase A (PKA) pathway [ , , ]. QUE reduces hexokinase 2 (HK2) expression and inhibits the AKT-mTOR axis, thereby attenuating the glycolytic dependency of HCC cells [ ]. As depicted in Fig. , the pleiotropic actions of polyphenols, detailed above, orchestrate a concerted rewiring of glycolipid metabolism, which constitutes a core mechanism for their anti-HCC properties. Modulation of mitochondrial function and oxidative stress Polyphenols critically regulate cellular energy metabolism and redox homeostasis through multiple mechanisms. RES enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and upregulates key lipid catabolic enzymes, including carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-1), thereby promoting fatty acid oxidation [ , ]. DMY modulates the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway via Bcl-2/Bak-caspase-9/3 signaling and concurrently activates the AMPK-PGC1α/ERRα-SIRT3 axis to improve mitochondrial integrity and function [ , , ]. QUE promotes PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, a process essential for clearing damaged mitochondria and ameliorating high-fat diet-induced mitochondrial dysfunction [ ]. CUR enhances peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation, inhibits NF-κB activation, and acts as a transient receptor potential melastatin 2 (TRPM2) channel inhibitor to alleviate oxidative mitochondrial damage [ , , ]. In the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, a central driver of HCC, curcumin and EGCG are potent inhibitors, with EGCG (50 mg/kg/d in DEN-induced rat models) upregulating p21 and downregulating CDC25A to suppress hepatocarcinogenesis [ ]. TME via anti-inflammatory and Immunomodulatory actions The efficacy of many polyphenols begins with gut microbiota-dependent activation and immunomodulation through two interconnected pathways. They are initially metabolized by microbial enzymes (e.g., β-glucosidases, esterases) into bioactive aglycones, and are further transformed into metabolites such as phenyl-γ-valerolactones and phenolic acids [ , ]. These compounds can enter systemic circulation via the portal vein-directly impacting the liver-or exert local effects, including enhanced intestinal barrier integrity. A meta-analysis on acute lung injury supports this, showing that polyphenol-rich supplementation reduces pro-inflammatory cytokine levels [ ]. Furthermore, specific polyphenols like Baicalin and Kaempferol directly modulate the gut’s Th17/Treg balance, underscoring a key mechanism for their intestinal and systemic anti-inflammatory actions [ ]. This gut-level immunomodulation underpins many systemic effects. For instance, chlorogenic acid (CGA) modulates the gut microbiota-TLR4-NF-κB axis. It helps maintain gut barrier integrity and enriches beneficial gut microbiota, thereby reducing the translocation of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a TLR4 ligand, into the portal circulation. This decrease in hepatic LPS exposure attenuates TLR4-mediated activation of NF-κB signaling, ultimately mitigating liver inflammation [ , ]. Similarly, pterostilbene downregulates the TXNIP/NLRP3 inflammasome, enhances PPARα signaling, and modulates the gut microbiota-TLR4-NF-κB axis to ameliorate inflammation along the gut-liver interface [ , ]. Beyond these gut-mediated mechanisms, polyphenols directly suppress multiple pro-oncogenic signaling pathways. Curcumin suppresses pathways including PI3K/AKT, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, and NF-κB, thereby impeding epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), angiogenesis, and glycolysis [ , ]. It also inhibits TLR4 signaling and the TGF-β1/SMAD7 pathway, reducing the production of key pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, IL-13, and IL-1β [ , , ]. RES not only inhibits SREBP-1c and FAS expression but also improves mitochondrial function in CD8⁺ T cells, potentially revitalizing anti-tumor immunity [ , , ]. DMY and EGCG aalleviate hepatic steatosis and inflammatory responses, partly through suppression of TNF-α [ ]. EGCG further exerts anti-HCC effects largely via modulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, concurrently inhibiting proliferation, inducing apoptosis, and suppressing metastasis [ ]. Additionally, proanthocyanidin exerts multi-target anti-HCC activity by inhibiting key inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), regulating Bcl-2/Bax-mediated apoptosis, and suppressing cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and clonogenicity [ ]. Detoxification of hepatotoxicants Polyphenols mitigate chemical-induced liver injury through multiple and often complementary mechanisms. For instance, chlorogenic acid (CGA) activates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway and inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation, protecting against liver damage induced by carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), acetaminophen (APAP), and D-galactose [ , ]. CUR not only reduces hepatic injury and fibrosis caused by carcinogens like diethylnitrosamine (DEN) and aflatoxin but also chelates iron ions to mitigate iron-dependent oxidative stress [ , , , ]. QUE confers protection by inhibiting CYP2E1, thereby reducing the formation of the toxic APAP metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), and by inducing the cytoprotective enzyme heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) [ , ]. DMY ameliorates hepatotoxicity through a multi-pronged approach involving modulation of APAP metabolism, inhibition of cell death, and promotion of liver regeneration [ ]. Furthermore, EGCG alleviates non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)-associated liver injury by concurrently inhibiting the TGF/SMAD, PI3K/AKT/FoxO1, and NF-κB pathways [ ]. Collectively, as illustrated in Fig. , these specific mechanisms are integrated into a broader protective network wherein polyphenols and their metabolites, shaped by hepatic and microbial metabolism, act through multi-organ pathways to counter hepatotoxic insults and disrupt the progression of liver disease. Bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, safety, and delivery strategies The clinical translation of dietary polyphenols is significantly hampered by their generally low oral bioavailability, a consequence of complex pharmacokinetics, extensive pre-systemic metabolism, and considerable interindividual variation. Following ingestion, most polyphenols undergo substantial phase II metabolism in enterocytes and hepatocytes, forming methylated, sulfated, or glucuronidated derivatives that often exhibit altered bioactivity and accelerated elimination [ ]. Pharmacokinetic profiles vary markedly; for instance, cocoa flavanols reach peak plasma concentration (Cmax) at 2.8 ± 0.6 h, with an elimination half-life of 4.8 ± 1.3 h [ ], whereas soy isoflavones display biphasic absorption due to enterohepatic recirculation [ ]. The food matrix further modulates bioavailability, as demonstrated by a 1.7-fold higher urinary excretion of naringenin from orange juice compared to whole oranges [ ]. Age may further affect naringenin pharmacokinetics, though clinical evidence remains limited [ ]. Advanced formulations, such as encapsulating hydrophobic compounds like eugenol into porous silica, can prolong half-life and improve release kinetics [ , , ]. Tea catechins, including EGCG, are metabolized by COMT, UGTs, and SULTs before absorption primarily via passive diffusion [ , ]. Advanced formulations, such as encapsulating hydrophobic compounds like eugenol into porous silica, can prolong half-life and improve release kinetics [ , , ]. Tea catechins, including EGCG, are metabolized by COMT, UGTs, and SULTs before absorption primarily via passive diffusion [ , ]. Anti-HCC efficacy and delivery-dependent dosing The anti-HCC efficacy of polyphenols is critically dependent on achieving effective local concentrations, necessitating optimized dosing and delivery strategies. Naringenin induces ferroptosis in HepG2 and Hep3B cells at non-toxic doses (< 0.2 mM) and suppresses tumor growth in vivo at 50 mg/kg by activating AMPK and promoting lipid peroxidation [ , ]. Clinical evidence from a trial in NAFLD patients showed that 100 mg naringenin twice daily for 4 weeks significantly reduced oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory markers via NF-κB inhibition [ ]. Synergistic effects have been achieved through nanoparticulate co-formulations, such as naringenin with ibuprofen or other botanicals, which enhance anti-angiogenic and pro-apoptotic effects in HepG2 cells [ , ]. Similarly, EGCG inhibits HCC progression through PI3K/AKT suppression and cell cycle modulation, downregulating CDC25A and elevating p21 expression [ ]. EGCG-loaded PLGA-siRNA nanoparticles further enhance apoptosis via caspase-3/7 activation [ ], and its derivative Y6 impedes tumor angiogenesis by targeting MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/HIF-1α/VEGF pathways [ ]. Eugenol also exerts anti-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic effects in HepG2 cells at 6.25–25 µg/mL, with efficacy improved by nanoemulsions [ ]. Promising candidates and advanced delivery systems Beyond the well-studied polyphenols, several emerging candidates show high potency. Pterostilbene, a resveratrol analog, exhibits ~ 4-fold higher oral bioavailability and enhanced efficacy in NAFLD-HCC models via AMPK-mediated epigenetic mechanisms [ ]. Arctigenin demonstrates remarkable nanomolar-range cytotoxicity (IC₅₀=4.74–59.27 nM) against HCC cell lines [ ]. The development of advanced nano-formulations-including lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and metal-phenolic networks-has achieved 5- to 20-fold improvements in bioavailability for various polyphenols [ , ]. These systems enable multi-targeted therapies; for example, a piceatannol-Fe³⁺ metal-phenolic network overcomes sorafenib resistance by synergizing photothermal therapy with ferroptosis [ ]. A smart nanosystem co-assembled from ursolic acid and EGCG not only enhances stability and delivery but also activates innate and adaptive immunity by stimulating IL-12/IFN-γ secretion and promoting T cell infiltration, thereby reversing immunosuppression and inhibiting HCC progression [ ]. Concurrently, gut microbiota-mediated biotransformation (e.g., of ellagic acid to urolithins) provides additional avenues for enhancing efficacy [ ]. Safety, standardization, and drug interaction risks While polyphenols from whole foods are generally safe at dietary levels, high-dose supplements require careful safety assessment. Epidemiological studies associate polyphenol-rich diets with reduced HCC risk [ , ]. However, toxicity thresholds for purified compounds vary: the NOAEL for EGCG is ~ 500 mg/kg/day in animals, with human hepatotoxicity reported at > 800 mg/day [ , ]. Curcumin (4–8 g/day) is generally well-tolerated, while resveratrol shows a favorable profile up to 1 g/day [ , ]. A major translational challenge is the lack of unified dosing and the potential for significant drug interactions. Grapefruit flavonoids inhibit CYP3A4, elevating plasma levels of statins and calcium channel blockers [ , ]. Concomitant use of garlic or Ginkgo biloba with warfarin may augment anticoagulant effects, increasing bleeding risk [ ]. Furthermore, many flavonoids inhibit CYP enzymes and affect P-glycoprotein, potentially altering the pharmacokinetics of co-administered drugs like sorafenib and regorafenib [ , ]. Standardization remains another critical barrier, with studies reporting 20–30% lower active content in commercial products than claimed, and variations in cultivation and processing leading to tenfold differences in polyphenol content [ , ]. Reliable clinical application thus mandates improved delivery strategies, systematic dose-response studies, and thorough evaluation of herb-drug interactions. Challenges and future perspectives Among the plethora of polyphenols investigated, curcumin and resveratrol demonstrate the most extensive preclinical evidence but are plagued by exceptionally low bioavailability. In contrast, EGCG has more human trial data supporting its consumption, albeit with a narrower safety margin at high supplemental doses. Pterostilbene, with its superior metabolic stability, represents a promising next-generation analog worthy of accelerated clinical translation. The clinical translation of dietary polyphenols faces several interconnected challenges that must be systematically addressed. The characteristically low oral bioavailability of many prominent polyphenols, such as EGCG and curcumin, severely limits their systemic exposure and therapeutic potential. This is compounded by chemical instability under physiological conditions, rapid metabolism and elimination, and insufficient tumor-targeting specificity. Furthermore, the scarcity of large-scale, robust clinical trials hinders the validation of their efficacy and safety in human populations, particularly in combination with standard therapeutics where pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions remain incompletely characterized. dietary polyphenols faces several interconnected challenges that must be systematically addressed. The characteristically low oral bioavailability of many prominent polyphenols, such as EGCG and curcumin, severely limits their systemic exposure and therapeutic potential. This is compounded by chemical instability under physiological conditions, rapid metabolism and elimination, and insufficient tumor-targeting specificity. Furthermore, the scarcity of large-scale, robust clinical trials hinders the validation of their efficacy and safety in human populations, particularly in combination with standard therapeutics where pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions remain incompletely characterized. Future progress will depend on integrated strategies encompassing advanced nanoformulations-such as stimulus-responsive and tumor-targeted delivery systems-to improve bioavailability and specificity. Concurrently, rigorous long-term toxicological studies, scalable manufacturing processes, and well-designed clinical trials are essential to establish conclusive efficacy and safety. Elucidating the intricate interactions between polyphenols, the gut microbiome, and host metabolism through multi-omics approaches will further enable the development of personalized, microbiota-directed polyphenol interventions. Ultimately, overcoming these translational barriers requires a collaborative, multidisciplinary effort to bridge the gap between promising preclinical data and meaningful clinical application in HCC prevention and therapy. Conclusion HCC remains a major global health challenge with limited treatment efficacy, driving the search for complementary approaches such as dietary polyphenols-flavonoids, phenolic acids, stilbenes, and lignans-which exhibit multi-target anti-HCC activity through synergistic regulation of metabolism, oxidative stress, and tumor microenvironment. However, their clinical translation is hindered by poor bioavailability and insufficient clinical validation. Future progress depends on developing advanced nanoformulations for targeted delivery, validating polyphenol-drug synergies in well-designed trials, and leveraging multi-omics to decipher polyphenol-microbiome-host interactions. Integrating these strategies will unlock the potential of polyphenols as part of comprehensive, personalized HCC management.

documents.title: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines management hepatocellular carcinoma update

chunks.content: Introduction Transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) remains the first-line standard treatment for intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in suitable candidates (ie, those with well-defined nodules, preserved portal flow and selective access); however, this recommendation may not apply to patients with extremely high tumour burden or poor liver function reserve. However, this stage is now recognised as encompassing a profoundly heterogeneous population with wide variations in tumour burden, liver function and biology, leading to significantly divergent outcomes after TACE. This realisation has rendered a uniform TACE strategy insufficient and has driven the development of subclassification systems (eg, Up-to-Seven, Up-to-Eleven, Seven-Eleven, Bolondi criteria, Kinki Criteria, Yamakado Criteria and NTAA prognostic model) to identify prognostically distinct subgroups. Building on this stratified approach, the integration of TACE with systemic therapies—particularly targeted immunotherapy—has emerged as a pivotal strategy, especially for identified high-benefit subgroups. Two recent global, multicentre, randomised controlled trials—EMERALD-1 and LEAP-012, published back-to-back in The Lancet —demonstrated that TACE plus targeted immunotherapy significantly prolonged progression-free survival (PFS) compared with TACE alone in patients with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage B HCC (LEAP-012, HR=0.57, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.77; EMERALD-1, HR=0.71, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.95) ( ). These findings provide important preliminary evidence for the efficacy and safety of TACE plus targeted immunotherapy. However, improvements in PFS do not consistently translate into meaningful OS benefits in oncology trials. This is exemplified by the LEAP-012 trial: while follow-up for OS is ongoing in EMERALD-1, mature OS data from LEAP-012 revealed no statistically significant difference (HR=0.78, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.18). This discrepancy highlights the need to identify specific subgroups of intermediate-stage HCC that may derive true survival benefit from TACE-targeted immunotherapy, whereas the true efficacy could be masked by confounding effects in heterogeneous populations. Despite differences in combination regimens between the two studies, this contradiction underscores the urgent need for precision-based risk stratification in intermediate-stage HCC. Currently, stratification models based on prognostic factors such as tumour burden, liver function, microvascular invasion (MVI), systemic inflammation or immune status, tumour markers and comorbidities are still being explored. Identifying potential responders to combination therapy has become an important challenge. By integrating evidence from recent years, this review discusses the key stratification factors for intermediate-stage HCC and their impact on treatment strategies while identifying optimal candidate populations for TACE plus targeted immunotherapy ( ). We also propose our perspectives on the application of TACE plus targeted immunotherapy in intermediate-stage HCC. Prognosis stratification and treatment decision-making for intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma Tumour burden Extensive evidence underscores tumour burden as an important determinant of prognosis in intermediate-stage HCC. Key variables of tumour burden, including tumour size and number, are closely associated with MVI risk, intrahepatic metastatic potential, reduced residual normal liver volume and impaired liver function reserve. These factors contribute to the marked heterogeneity in treatment outcomes of TACE in intermediate-stage HCC. Consequently, diversified treatment strategies tailored to distinct tumour burdens are imperative. Low tumour burden Low tumour burden is typically defined by the ‘up-to-seven’ criteria, wherein the therapeutic goal should focus on optimising local treatment modalities to improve complete response rates and long-term prognosis ( ). For resectable intermediate-stage HCC, surgical resection still demonstrates a significant prognostic advantage over traditional standalone TACE. For partially unresectable cases, resection combined with ablation represents an effective strategy to enhance prognosis, though it is often limited to ≤2 ablation sites, ablation lesion size ≤2 cm and achievement of complete ablation. Additionally, liver transplantation may serve as a viable option for intermediate-stage HCC exceeding the Milan criteria, such as those meeting the Hangzhou criteria, University of California San Francisco criteria or the ‘up-to-seven’ criteria. Furthermore, for select patients with intermediate-stage HCC who achieve downstaging through aggressive treatment, liver transplantation, resection or ablation can be attempted, although with strict patient selection. Currently, effective downstaging strategies for low tumour burden include TACE, hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) and transarterial radioembolisation (TARE). Specifically, for HAIC utilising regimens such as the modified FOLFOX (mFOLFOX, which includes oxaliplatin, fluorouracil and leucovorin) regimen, meta-analysis evidence indicates a significantly higher rate of successful downstaging to surgical resection compared with TACE (RR=2.37, 95% CI 1.54 to 3.66). Our prior research also demonstrated that TACE-based combination therapy can achieve imaging-confirmed ‘no evidence of disease’ in nearly 35% of patients with intermediate-stage HCC, significantly reducing mortality risk in this population. However, for most unresectable intermediate-stage HCC cases, TACE remains a valid therapeutic option. With advancing research, some studies have shown that for BCLC stage B HCC with limited tumour burden (≤ 5 lesions, ≤ 7 cm in size), the efficacy of TACE plus ablation markedly surpasses standalone TACE. Some investigations even advocate TACE–ablation combinations for all patients with intermediate-stage HCC, reporting superior outcomes compared with TACE alone. These findings highlight the important role of TACE–ablation synergy in unresectable and non-transplantable intermediate-stage HCC. Currently, the widely used ablation techniques

However, for most unresectable intermediate-stage HCC cases, TACE remains a valid therapeutic option. With advancing research, some studies have shown that for BCLC stage B HCC with limited tumour burden (≤ 5 lesions, ≤ 7 cm in size), the efficacy of TACE plus ablation markedly surpasses standalone TACE. Some investigations even advocate TACE–ablation combinations for all patients with intermediate-stage HCC, reporting superior outcomes compared with TACE alone. These findings highlight the important role of TACE–ablation synergy in unresectable and non-transplantable intermediate-stage HCC. Currently, the widely used ablation techniques in clinical practice include radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA) and cryoablation (CA). Specifically, the mechanism of RFA primarily involves an electrode probe emitting RF waves, which induce ionic oscillation in tumour tissues to generate heat, ultimately leading to tumour cell necrosis. For MWA, its mechanism mainly relies on microwave electromagnetic fields to heat tumour tissues, rapidly destroying cancer cells through the rotation of polar molecules. In contrast, the core mechanism of CA is the formation of an ice ball under low temperatures, resulting in tumour cell death due to cryoinjury. To date, high-quality randomised controlled trials defining the optimal ablation modality in combination with TACE for HCC are still lacking. Nevertheless, findings from a meta-analysis have indicated that TACE plus MWA yields a significantly higher OR for long-term OS and objective response rate (ORR) than TACE plus RFA or TACE plus CA. Notably, young patients with tumour lesions ≤3 cm derive the most prominent clinical benefits from the TACE–MWA combination therapy. However, standardised protocols for patient selection, treatment dosing, ablation modalities, lesion size or number thresholds and endpoint definitions remain unestablished. Addressing these gaps is imperative to avoid overtreatment and ensure guideline-adherent care ( ). High tumour burden For patients with tumour burden exceeding the up-to-7 criteria, the cornerstone of treatment lies in the synergy between systemic therapy and local interventions, while prioritising downstaging and conversion therapy potential ( ). Targeted therapy, particularly TKIs, forms an important backbone. Evidence confirms that TACE plus TKIs (eg, lenvatinib or sorafenib) and/or ablation can significantly improve outcomes compared with TACE alone, establishing TACE plus targeted therapy as a validated foundational regimen. The negative results of TACE plus sorafenib in the TACE 2 trial represent a special case, which may be associated with trial-specific design factors, such as the timing of sorafenib initiation, definition of PFS, identification of MVI-positive populations and active monitoring and management of liver function. In contrast, the integration of immunotherapy has shown a more complex efficacy profile. The failure of TACE plus durvalumab (anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)) to improve outcomes suggests that simply adding an immune checkpoint inhibitor to TACE is insufficient. Similarly, the systemic dual-combination of atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) plus bevacizumab (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor)—a regimen not containing TACE—also did not improve PFS or OS in BCLC stage B HCC. These results indicate that neither TACE plus immunotherapy nor TKI plus immunotherapy (in a TACE-free setting) alone are reliably effective strategies for this heterogeneous population. Therefore, the emerging paradigm supported by trials, like EMERALD-1 and LEAP-012, is not the replacement of the TACE-TKI backbone, but its strategic intensification. The combination of TACE, a TKI, and an immunotherapy agent (a triple-therapy regimen) leverages the established synergy of TACE with targeted therapy, while it attempts to amplify the anti-tumour immune response. This approach underscores that immunotherapy may yield the greatest benefit not as a substitute or simple add-on but as a third component integrated into a potent locoregional-systemic foundation. Future research should focus on identifying the patient subgroups most likely to benefit from this intensive triple combination. The emergence of HAIC offers a novel pathway for high-burden tumours. The mFOLFOX-based HAIC shows superior efficacy over conventional TACE in intermediate-stage HCC with tumours ≥7 cm, and drug-eluting bead transarterial chemoembolisation (DEB-TACE) combined with HAIC significantly improves local control rates for large tumours. HAIC coupled with targeted immunotherapy expands therapeutic dimensions, enabling long-term survival in select patients after downstaging and conversion. Explorations of TACE–HAIC (a treatment strategy combining TACE with HAIC) combined with targeted and immunotherapy regimens have shown preliminary efficacy, delivering potential survival benefits for high-burden intermediate-stage HCC. With the continuous advancement of locoregional therapeutic techniques, the clinical value of TARE, also known as selective internal radiation therapy, has attracted increasing attention in the management of intermediate-stage HCC with high tumour burden. This therapy involves the infusion of yttrium-90–labelled microspheres via tumour-feeding arteries to deliver targeted brachytherapy to tumour tissues while occluding the tumour blood supply through the embolic effect of microspheres, which leads to cancer cell death due to the deprivation of nutritional support. Its efficacy and safety in the treatment of intermediate-stage HCC have been verified in multiple clinical studies. of locoregional therapeutic techniques, the clinical value of TARE, also known as selective internal radiation therapy, has attracted increasing attention in the management of intermediate-stage HCC with high tumour burden. This therapy involves the infusion of yttrium-90–labelled microspheres via tumour-feeding arteries to deliver targeted brachytherapy to tumour tissues while occluding the tumour blood supply through the embolic effect of microspheres, which leads to cancer cell death due to the deprivation of nutritional support. Its efficacy and safety in the treatment of intermediate-stage HCC have been verified in multiple clinical studies. Notably, the TRACE single-centre randomised controlled trial specifically compared the safety and efficacy of TARE and DEB-TACE (typically using doxorubicin-loaded beads) in patients with unresectable HCC and relatively low tumour burden. The vast majority of the enrolled patients were at BCLC stage B, with the median tumour diameters of 4.2 and 4.7 cm in the TARE and DEB-TACE groups, respectively. The results confirmed that TARE was significantly superior to DEB-TACE in terms of time to tumour progression and OS, with a comparable incidence of adverse events between the two groups. In contrast, a retrospective exploratory study comparing TARE and TACE for unresectable HCC with relatively high tumour burden showed that for unresectable HCC lesions with diameter >8 cm, TARE achieved therapeutic efficacy comparable with that of TACE but with a significantly lower incidence of adverse events (72% in the TACE group vs 5% in the TARE group). However, this study was a retrospective analysis with a relatively low proportion of intermediate-stage HCC cases in the enrolled population; thus, its conclusions require further validation by well-designed clinical studies. With the advent of targeted and immunotherapy, the strategy of TARE plus systemic therapy has also been explored in HCC with high tumour burden. For instance, a single-arm trial conducted by Lee et al demonstrated that TARE plus durvalumab in the treatment of patients with locally advanced HCC yielded an ORR of 83.3% and an 18-month OS rate of 58.3%, which indicated that TARE plus immunotherapy holds promising clinical potential. Furthermore, Huang et al explored and compared the safety and efficacy of TARE plus targeted-immunotherapy vs TACE plus targeted-immunotherapy in patients with high tumour burden HCC. The results showed that TARE plus targeted-immunotherapy was significantly superior to the TACE-based combination regimen in terms of ORR, PFS and OS. Collectively, these findings further corroborate the potential advantages of TARE in the management of high tumour burden HCC: TARE not only exhibits a more favourable safety profile as a monotherapy but also exerts a synergistic anti-tumour effect when combined with targeted and immunotherapeutic agents. This not only provides a more optimal therapeutic option for patients with high tumour burden HCC, a population presenting great clinical treatment challenges, but also lays a solid foundation for the subsequent optimisation and exploration of clinical treatment strategies for this patient cohort. Despite these promising advances, inherent tumour and patient heterogeneity in high-burden populations remains a challenge. Future priorities include (1) identifying populations amenable to downstaging/conversion therapy (eg, biomarkers and radiomics models) and optimising strategies, (2) exploring multimodal synergy for non-downstaging candidates and (3) balancing efficacy and safety, mitigating hepatic toxicity from multisystemic combinations and immune-related adverse events ( ). Liver function reserve For intermediate-stage HCC with liver function Child–Pugh (CP) scores of 5–7, preserving liver function reserve is important, as its loss may lead to hepatic failure, treatment interruption or increased mortality; therefore, selecting effective treatment regimens must prioritise this goal to improve long-term prognosis. As noted previously, there are various combination therapy approaches for intermediate-stage HCC. However, research on the dynamic correlation is limited between different treatments and frequencies and changes in liver function reserves, especially the need to carefully evaluate the impact of local treatment combined with targeted immunotherapy on liver function reserves in intermediate-stage HCC. Although EMERALD-1 and LEAP-012 have shown that TACE plus targeted immunotherapy does not significantly increase adverse events related to liver function changes compared with TACE alone, neither study dynamically assessed the long-term effects of this combination on liver function. The significance of assessing dynamic changes in liver function lies in effectively elucidating the impact of this local combination of targeted immunotherapy on the long-term prognosis of intermediate-stage HCC. Subgroup analysis results from LEAP-012 indicate that TACE plus lenvatinib and pembrolizumab can improve PFS in intermediate-stage HCC, but it does not significantly improve OS, which may also suggest that this combination leads to a decline in long-term liver function reserves, thereby weakening its efficacy. Cancer-specific survival (CSS) as a primary endpoint may be more beneficial for evaluating the effectiveness of this combination regimen. However, the decline in liver function reserves during treatment may also act as a promoter of tumour progression, leading to no significant improvement in CSS. For patients with mid-stage HCC who have a liver function CP score of 8

from LEAP-012 indicate that TACE plus lenvatinib and pembrolizumab can improve PFS in intermediate-stage HCC, but it does not significantly improve OS, which may also suggest that this combination leads to a decline in long-term liver function reserves, thereby weakening its efficacy. Cancer-specific survival (CSS) as a primary endpoint may be more beneficial for evaluating the effectiveness of this combination regimen. However, the decline in liver function reserves during treatment may also act as a promoter of tumour progression, leading to no significant improvement in CSS. For patients with mid-stage HCC who have a liver function CP score of 8 or 9, multi-disciplinary treatment (MDT) is necessary. Laparoscopic liver resection can serve as a reference for MDT; however, the incidence of postoperative complications significantly increases, especially for patients with a CP score of 8. Additionally, for patients with a CP score of 8, adjuvant TACE after resection is a safe and effective treatment option, particularly for patients with intermediate-stage HCC with multiple lesions, tumour size >5 cm and margins <1 cm. However, whether this treatment regimen is safe and effective for patients with a CP score of 9 has not been assessed, so careful selection of the benefit population is required. Compared with symptomatic supportive care, capecitabine-based chemotherapy appears to be safe and effective for patients with intermediate-stage HCC with liver function CP score of 8 or 9. However, attention should be paid to adverse reactions such as severe thrombocytopenia and hand-foot syndrome. Anti-angiogenic combined with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) antibody therapy is also safe and effective for patients with a CP score of 8 or 9; however, these patients are more likely to experience dose reduction or discontinuation of targeted drugs. For carefully selected patients with intermediate-stage HCC with a CP score of 8 or 9, stereotactic body radiotherapy seems to be safe and effective, but special attention should be paid to the potential risk of death due to radiation hepatitis ( ). Microvascular invasion In recent years, the treatment strategy for patients with MVI-positive intermediate-stage HCC has become an important area of investigation, as this population highlights the limitations of TACE alone. TACE therapy upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor expression in tumour tissues, potentially exacerbating vascular invasion and metastatic potential in these patients. Consequently, whether combining targeted therapy with TACE is necessary for patients with MVI-positive intermediate-stage HCC has emerged as a key research focus. A recent randomised controlled trial demonstrated that sorafenib plus TACE significantly improved OS, PFS and ORR in patients with recurrent MVI-positive intermediate-stage HCC compared with TACE alone. This positive result contrasts with the negative finding of the TACE 2 trial, in which TACE plus sorafenib did not improve prognosis in a broader, unselected population of patients with unresectable HCC. The discrepancy likely stems from critical differences in the patient cohorts: the former focused on a biomarker-defined, high-benefit subgroup (MVI-positive), whereas the latter included a heterogeneous mix of patients without MVI selection. Importantly, the regimen did not enhance outcomes in the MVI-negative group, which collectively underscores MVI as a pivotal biomarker for stratifying patients who may benefit from the addition of sorafenib to TACE. Additionally, HAIC has shown preliminary efficacy in patients with MVI-positive intermediate-stage HCC. Studies have also indicated that HAIC plus sorafenib significantly improves outcomes in patients with HCC and portal vein tumour thrombi. Therefore, whether HAIC plus sorafenib further enhances survival in patients with MVI-positive intermediate-stage HCC warrants exploration in future research. MVI highlights the importance of pathological examination. However, current major guidelines, such as the European Association for the Study of the Liver, American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines, have not listed tissue biopsy as a routine diagnostic or pre-treatment essential step for unresectable intermediate-stage HCC. Therefore, obtaining tissue specimens in these patients is challenging, which hinders the development of personalised treatment for intermediate-stage HCC. However, some studies are attempting to use liquid biopsies to obtain peripheral blood circulating tumour cells and DNA to predict the efficacy of intermediate-stage HCC, suggesting that low levels of peripheral blood circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) are associated with better responses to intermediate-stage HCC. For example, in a phase Ib trial of sintilimab plus bevacizumab followed by resection for intermediate-stage HCC, Sun et al reported that lower baseline levels of ctDNA were associated with better tumour response. Biomarkers related to systemic inflammatory response and immune status Existing studies have confirmed that systemic inflammatory response and immune status are important biological factors influencing treatment stratification in patients with intermediate-stage HCC. Systemic inflammation scoring systems based on serological markers, such as the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) and other chronic inflammation-related scores including the Glasgow Prognostic Score (GPS), C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) and lymphocyte-to-C-reactive protein ratio (LCR), have been validated in multiple studies

followed by resection for intermediate-stage HCC, Sun et al reported that lower baseline levels of ctDNA were associated with better tumour response. Biomarkers related to systemic inflammatory response and immune status Existing studies have confirmed that systemic inflammatory response and immune status are important biological factors influencing treatment stratification in patients with intermediate-stage HCC. Systemic inflammation scoring systems based on serological markers, such as the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) and other chronic inflammation-related scores including the Glasgow Prognostic Score (GPS), C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) and lymphocyte-to-C-reactive protein ratio (LCR), have been validated in multiple studies as independent prognostic factors for patients with intermediate-stage HCC undergoing TACE or TACE plus ablation. For example, PLR has been demonstrated as an independent predictor of PFS after TACE, wheras GPS, CAR and LCR scores are significantly associated with OS. Further studies have shown that NLR, LMR, PLR and CAR can effectively stratify survival differences among patients receiving TACE plus ablation. These findings strongly suggest that exacerbated inflammatory responses and immunosuppressive states are closely associated with poor prognosis. Notably, these biomarkers not only hold prognostic value but also offer potential therapeutic targets for stratified treatment. For patients with high inflammatory burden and immune deficiency, combination therapies including antivirals, anti-inflammatory drugs and immunomodulators can significantly enhance treatment outcomes. Future research should focus on identifying the optimal systemic inflammatory and immune markers for precise stratification to optimise individualised treatment strategies for patients with intermediate-stage HCC. Tumour markers and comorbidities AFP is a widely used yet complex biomarker in HCC, a complexity compounded by its lack of absolute disease specificity, as serum levels can also be elevated in response to hepatic inflammation and regeneration. Its prognostic utility in intermediate-stage HCC is not defined by a single universal cut-off but is highly context-dependent, influenced by the specific clinical scenario, treatment modality and patient population. This context-dependent profile is reflected in the range of validated cut-offs applicable to different settings. For example, in broad, mixed-stage cohorts, 20 and 400 ng/mL have been established as independent prognostic factors. Notably, the 400 ng/mL cut-off is the Food and Drug Administration–approved predictive biomarker for selecting patients with advanced HCC who may benefit from ramucirumab (an anti-vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 therapy). However, these thresholds, derived from heterogeneous populations, may not be optimised for specific subgroups. Indeed, in studies focusing specifically on intermediate-stage (BCLC B) HCC, the prognostic significance of the 400 ng/mL cut-off has been inconsistent. Furthermore, the frequently cited 200 ng/mL cut-off often relies on historical benchmarks rather than contemporary, data-driven analysis. In contrast, our previous study focused precisely on the specific context of patients with intermediate-stage HCC undergoing TACE. Employing data-driven optimisation via survival ROC analysis, we identified a prognostic cut-off of 156.5 ng/mL, which has subsequently undergone internal and multi-centre external validation. These observations collectively underscore that the appropriate AFP cut-off should be aligned with the treatment pathway (eg, systemic therapy vs TACE) and disease stage. Therefore, for risk-stratifying intermediate-stage HCC within TACE-based strategies, employing a context-specific cut-off such as 156.5 ng/mL is likely to provide more accurate prognostication than applying generic thresholds. This reinforces the imperative to interpret biomarkers within a multidimensional stratification framework. Future large-scale, global collaborative studies will be valuable to further refine optimal AFP cut-offs across diverse clinical scenarios and aetiologies. Additionally, comorbidities in patients with HCC may contribute to the heterogeneity of prognosis, often closely related to underlying liver disease, metabolic disorders and decompensated liver function. These comorbidities significantly shorten the OS of patients with intermediate-stage HCC by limiting tumour-tolerant treatment, increasing treatment-related adverse events and exacerbating the malignant biological behaviour of tumours. Therefore, establishing a multi-dimensional stratification model that includes tumour burden, liver function, MVI, inflammatory–immune status, tumour markers and comorbidities can reduce clinical heterogeneity and improve the overall efficacy of patients with intermediate-stage HCC. Perspectives Overall, the combination of TACE with targeted immunotherapy marks a significant paradigm shift in the treatment of intermediate-stage HCC. This evolution is not only supported by pivotal global clinical trials but is also increasingly reflected in the principles endorsed by regional authoritative consensus statements. Notably, the recently published Chinese Expert Consensus on Sequential Surgery Following Conversion Therapy Based on Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors and Antiangiogenic Targeted Drugs for Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma (2024 Edition) systematically elaborates on a modern therapeutic principle centred on aggressive combination therapy underpinned by refined patient selection. Although this consensus primarily focuses on advanced-stage disease, the proactive treatment paradigm it establishes—‘achieving tumour control through intensive regimens such as TACE plus targeted immunotherapy to create opportunities for potential curative intervention in suitable patients’—resonates strongly with the management rationale for intermediate-stage HCC subgroups possessing high-risk features (eg, high tumour burden). Furthermore, the principle of ‘precise patient selection based on multidisciplinary team evaluation’ emphasised throughout the consensus aligns perfectly with the core thesis

and Antiangiogenic Targeted Drugs for Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma (2024 Edition) systematically elaborates on a modern therapeutic principle centred on aggressive combination therapy underpinned by refined patient selection. Although this consensus primarily focuses on advanced-stage disease, the proactive treatment paradigm it establishes—‘achieving tumour control through intensive regimens such as TACE plus targeted immunotherapy to create opportunities for potential curative intervention in suitable patients’—resonates strongly with the management rationale for intermediate-stage HCC subgroups possessing high-risk features (eg, high tumour burden). Furthermore, the principle of ‘precise patient selection based on multidisciplinary team evaluation’ emphasised throughout the consensus aligns perfectly with the core thesis of ‘multidimensional risk stratification’ advocated in this review. This paradigm shift is concretely driven by landmark trials such as LEAP-012 and EMERALD-1, which confirmed that integrating systemic therapies, including PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors and TKIs, may overcome the limitations of monotherapy, such as suboptimal response rates post-TACE and insufficient immune activation. Subgroup analyses from LEAP-012 have revealed the significant PFS advantage of TACE plus targeted immunotherapy; however, the absence of an OS benefit serves as an important reminder that this intensive combination is not universally applicable to all patients with intermediate-stage HCC; its true efficacy is likely masked by confounding effects within a highly heterogeneous population. Consequently, the paramount clinical challenge now is to precisely identify the true beneficiaries amidst this profound heterogeneity. Based on current evidence, we propose the following framework of recommendations for future research and clinical practice regarding TACE plus targeted immunotherapy in intermediate-stage HCC: Establish a stratified research framework with OS as the gold standard: future high-quality clinical trials should prioritise evaluating the efficacy and safety of combination regimens in high-benefit subgroups preselected via multidimensional models (integrating tumour burden, liver function, MVI, etc.), with OS as the primary endpoint. PFS as a surrogate endpoint requires cautious interpretation, as its improvement does not invariably translate into a meaningful OS benefit. As an illustrative example (but not an exclusive definition), a candidate profile for high benefit warranting evaluation of intensive combination therapy could include patients presenting with a combination of features such as high tumour burden (eg, exceeding the up-to-seven criteria), preserved liver function (CP A) and the presence of MVI. The integration of exploratory biomarkers like ctDNA or circulating tumour cells (CTCs) may further refine risk assessment in the context of clinical trials. Promote the exploratory integration of pathology and liquid biopsy: for patients with accessible tissue, pathological examination should be performed to clarify key information such as MVI status, histological subtype and differentiation grade. For patients without tissue availability, exploratory use of investigational liquid biopsy technologies (eg, ctDNA and CTCs) may be considered in the context of clinical trials or research settings. It should be explicitly acknowledged that these biomarkers currently lack standardised assays and prospective validation for clinical decision-making. Caution in populations with low anticipated benefit: for patients with low tumour burden and MVI-negative status (and potentially negative exploratory biomarkers like ctDNA/CTCs), treatment should prioritise optimising local therapies to improve complete response rates and long-term outcomes. The routine addition of TACE plus targeted immunotherapy in this group is not supported by current evidence and risks overtreatment. Address high inflammation response and immune dysfunction: in patients with marked chronic systemic inflammation or impaired immune status, adjuvant strategies such as antivirals, anti-inflammatory agents or immunomodulators may be considered to potentially improve the therapeutic environment and long-term prognosis. Dynamic liver function monitoring: the impact of TACE plus targeted immunotherapy on short-term and long-term liver function reserve should be dynamically assessed, particularly in patients with CP scores 7–9. Novel biomarkers with high sensitivity and specificity for real-time liver function monitoring should be explored. Develop predictive models to guide patient selection for conversion therapy: developed and validated predictive models are urgently needed to identify patients with intermediate-stage HCC who are most likely to achieve successful downstaging and pathological complete response following intensive combination therapy. Such models would enable more precise patient selection, maximising the chance of curative outcomes while avoiding futile overtreatment. Compare against other advanced treatment standards: future trials should move beyond comparing TACE plus targeted immunotherapy against TACE alone. To answer the most relevant clinical questions, the new combination should be directly compared against other contemporary, effective treatment options, such as TACE plus TKIs (eg, lenvatinib) or HAIC-based combination targeted immunotherapy. Recognise the limitation of PFS and explore composite endpoints: consistent with the principle of establishing OS as the gold standard (as outlined in Perspective 1), it is important to recognise that PFS is an imperfect surrogate endpoint in HCC, as it does not capture treatment-related liver function deterioration—an important determinant of prognosis. Therefore, future trials of TACE combination therapy should explore composite endpoints, such as time to progression or time to liver function deterioration, to provide a more holistic assessment of net clinical benefit. Foster global collaboration to validate

as TACE plus TKIs (eg, lenvatinib) or HAIC-based combination targeted immunotherapy. Recognise the limitation of PFS and explore composite endpoints: consistent with the principle of establishing OS as the gold standard (as outlined in Perspective 1), it is important to recognise that PFS is an imperfect surrogate endpoint in HCC, as it does not capture treatment-related liver function deterioration—an important determinant of prognosis. Therefore, future trials of TACE combination therapy should explore composite endpoints, such as time to progression or time to liver function deterioration, to provide a more holistic assessment of net clinical benefit. Foster global collaboration to validate and discover prognostic biomarkers: international consortia are crucial to discover and validate robust prognostic and predictive biomarkers across diverse aetiologies (eg, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease) and populations. This will ensure that stratification models are globally applicable and can identify universal principles of treatment response. Conduct context-specific health economic evaluations: cost-effectiveness analyses across varied healthcare systems are essential to guide the sustainable and equitable implementation of these advanced, often costly, therapies. Such studies will inform resource allocation and access policies, ensuring patients who stand to benefit most can receive treatment regardless of geographic or economic setting. In conclusion, the integration of TACE with targeted therapy and immunotherapy represents a paradigm shift, a strategy that is most compellingly indicated for patients with intermediate-stage HCC who are predicted to derive high benefit through multi-dimensional stratification. Future efforts must focus on refining these stratification tools and addressing the practical challenges of global implementation to fully realise the potential of this promising strategy.

The increasing prevalence of obesity and type 2 diabetes and the growing number of patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease being evaluated for LT, have resulted in a greater proportion of LT candidates presenting with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease. As cardiovascular disease is a major cause of morbidity and mortality after LT, a thorough cardiovascular evaluation pre-LT is crucial. In this review, we discuss the latest evidence on the cardiovascular evaluation of LT candidates and we focus on the most prevalent conditions, namely ischaemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias, valvular heart disease, and cardiomyopathies. LT candidates undergo an electrocardiogram, a resting transthoracic echocardiography and an assessment of their cardiopulmonary functional ability as part of their standardised pre-LT work-up. Further diagnostic work-up is undertaken based on the results of the baseline evaluation and may include a coronary computed tomography angiography in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. The evaluation of potential LT candidates for cardiovascular disease requires a multidisciplinary approach, with input from anaesthetists, cardiologists, hepatologists and transplant surgeons. Keywords liver transplantation MELD cirrhosis type II diabetes ischaemic heart disease cardiopulmonary reserve cardiomyopathy NAFLD Key points • LT candidates undergo electrocardiogram, a resting transthoracic echocardiography and an assessment of their cardiopulmonary functional ability as part of their standardized pre-LT work up. • Further diagnostic work-up is undertaken based on the results of the baseline evaluation and may include a coronary computed tomography angiography in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. • The evaluation and decision-making regarding transplant eligibility of patients at higher cardiovascular risk is not standardized and varies depending on local resources and expertise. • EF<40 %, severe valvular disease not amenable to repair prior to LT, severe pulmonary hypertension, significant coronary artery disease and symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias that cannot be controlled are all contraindications to LT. • The evaluation of potential LT candidates for cardiovascular disease requires a multidisciplinary approach, with input from anaesthetists, cardiologists, hepatologists and transplant surgeons. Introduction The increasing rates of obesity and the growing prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) as an indication for liver transplant(ation) (LT) has led to a greater proportion of LT candidates presenting with a higher risk of, or with established, cardiovascular disease. Cardiovascular complications are the leading cause of non-graft-related mortality in the early period after LT. 1 Cardiovascular morbidity and mortality is even more prevalent more than a year after transplantation, even in patients with no identified pre-existing risk factors. 2 Hence, a thorough pre-transplant cardiovascular evaluation of potential recipients is warranted. In this review, we focus on the cardiovascular assessment of LT candidates, particularly functional assessment and the evaluation and management of the most common cardiovascular comorbidities, namely coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation and arrhythmias, valvular disease, and cardiomyopathies. The evaluation and management of portopulmonary hypertension and hepatopulmonary syndrome are beyond the remit of this review. Cardiovascular risk assessment of the LT candidate LT candidates undergo an electrocardiogram (ECG) and resting transthoracic echocardiography as part of their standardised pre-LT work-up. Clinical history can identify cardiovascular risk factors, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, past history of smoking or familial history of early cardiovascular disease. Although patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-related cirrhosis are considered at high risk of developing cardiovascular events both before and after LT, there is insufficient evidence to recommend a specific risk algorithm. 3 Further diagnostic work-up is undertaken based on the results of the baseline evaluation described above. In Fig. 1 , we present an indicative algorithm for cardiovascular assessment of the LT candidate. Fig. 1 Indicative algorithm for cardiovascular work-up in patients listed for liver transplantation . Show full caption # If severe aortic stenosis, consider transcatheter aortic valve replacement. § AHA risk factors: Age (>50 years); family history of heart disease; dyslipidemia, history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, left ventricular hypertrophy, family history of premature CHD, active or past tobacco use, or prior coronary artery calcification score >0. ∗If CPET is available, the following threshold values can be used: Peak VO 2 >26 ml/kg/min (men) or >21 ml/kg/min (women): Good functional status Peak VO 2 21–26 ml/kg/min (men) or 17.5–21 ml/kg/min (women): Moderately decreased functional status (moderate risk) Peak VO 2 <21 ml/kg/min (men) or <17.5 ml/kg/min (women): Poor functional status If 6MWT is chosen, the following threshold values can be used 13 : 6MWD >450 m: Good

Assessment of cardiopulmonary reserve and functional ability Notably, baseline assessment does not provide complete information on the ability of individuals to use oxygen in stress-induced conditions such as surgery or infections. For this purpose, dynamic tests of the so-called cardiopulmonary reserve , which can be defined as aerobic exercise capacity, that integrate the responses of different systems (such as the cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurological and skeletal muscle) are required ( Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 The concept of cardiopulmonary reserve. Show full caption This refers to the ability to increase peak oxygen consumption (y axis) with increasing oxygen requirements (x axis). There are several tests to assess cardiopulmonary reserve in a liver transplant candidate, such as the cardiopulmonary exercise test, the 6-minute walk test, gait speed, short physical performance battery and the liver frailty index. It is useful to remember that in the resting state, Fick’s equation describes the different components of oxygen uptake (VO 2 ): 4 VO 2 : VO 2 = (SV ∗ HR) ∗ (CaO 2 – CvO 2 ) where SV is the stroke volume, HR is the heart rate, CaO 2 is the arterial oxygen content, and CvO 2 is the mixed venous oxygen content. Hence, VO 2 is the product of cardiac output times the arterial minus mixed venous oxygen content. Metabolic equivalents (METs) express the resting oxygen uptake in a sitting position normalised to body weight and expressed in ml per minute. One MET equals 3.5 ml/kg/min. 4 At maximal exercise, the Fick’s equation reflects the maximal capacity of the individual to take in, transport and use oxygen and defines the functional aerobic capacity of the individual: VO 2 max = (SVmax ∗ HRmax) ∗ (CaO 2 max -CvO 2 max). Functional cardiopulmonary reserve is impaired in patients with decompensated chronic liver disease; 5 in a systematic review evaluating patients listed for LT, the mean peak VO 2 across studies was 17.4 ml/kg/min, 6 which is below the threshold of 18 ml/kg/min required for normal independent living. This could result from several factors related to the decompensated stage of cirrhosis that affect different systems and organs 7 ; 8 : i) circulatory system (hyperdynamic circulation due to portal hypertension, cirrhotic cardiomyopathy [CCM]); ii) respiratory system (hydrothorax, hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension); iii) skeletal muscle system (malnutrition, sarcopenia, obesity and sedentary behaviour). In addition to the above, patients with underlying cardiovascular disease might show further decreased cardiopulmonary reserve due to features specific to their underlying disease process. Whenever cardiopulmonary reserve is impaired, mitochondrial capacity to use oxygen is reduced at a tissue level (skeletal muscle; cardiac muscle), and tissues are unable to adapt to pathophysiological stresses. Not surprisingly, several studies have demonstrated that decreased cardiopulmonary reserve (also referred to as “deconditioning”) is associated with mortality both on the LT waiting list and after LT, independently of liver function 9 ; 6 . Objective tools to study the cardiopulmonary reserve include cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET – the reference standard) and indirect tests, which have the advantage of being inexpensive and simpler to apply. In general, all the described tests are highly reproducible and have been extensively validated in the setting of chronic extrahepatic diseases and in the geriatric population. Liver frailty index, a simple test aiming at quantifying physiological reserve, will be discussed in another review from this special issue. Reference standard: cardiopulmonary exercise testing CPET is performed in an exercise/physical medicine setting, and requires dedicated resources and expertise. 4 The testee exercises on a treadmill or stationary bicycle, and during cardiac, blood pressure, pulse oximetry and expired gas analysis monitoring, the workload is increased until exhaustion. 6 The data output include the ventilatory anaerobic threshold and peak exercise oxygen uptake (VO 2 ), as well as minute ventilation/carbon dioxide production gradient and slope (the latter seems to be superior in characterising muscle deconditioning in the general population). In patients awaiting LT, the anaerobic threshold on CPET predicts pre- and post-transplant survival; however, the thresholds vary significanly among publications. 6 ;

medicine setting, and requires dedicated resources and expertise. 4 The testee exercises on a treadmill or stationary bicycle, and during cardiac, blood pressure, pulse oximetry and expired gas analysis monitoring, the workload is increased until exhaustion. 6 The data output include the ventilatory anaerobic threshold and peak exercise oxygen uptake (VO 2 ), as well as minute ventilation/carbon dioxide production gradient and slope (the latter seems to be superior in characterising muscle deconditioning in the general population). In patients awaiting LT, the anaerobic threshold on CPET predicts pre- and post-transplant survival; however, the thresholds vary significanly among publications. 6 ; 10 Data on the ability of CPET to predict intra- or post-operative cardiovascular events is not available in the current literature. The advantage of CPET is that it provides granular data on cardiopulmonary reserve. Disadvantages include the complex infrastructure required (which may not be widely available), cost, and the practicality of patients with severe decompensated liver disease performing the test. Thus, although CPET is incredibly important in facilitating our understanding of cardiopulmonary reserve in patients awaiting LT, it has not been widely adopted as a screening tool to assess cardiovascular risk across transplant centres. 6-Minute walk test As its name suggests, the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) measures the distance walked on a flat surface for 6 min. It is designed to measure functional exercise capacity in the cardiology and thoracic medicine setting, 11 and has been validated as a predictor of mortality in patients with cirrhosis awaiting LT. 12 A recent study in 694 patients awaiting LT showed that for every 100-metre increase in 6MWT, there was a significant decrease in mortality (hazard ratio 0.48). 13 A cut-off threshold of 250 m is associated with increased waitlist mortality. 12 Although the data derived is not as detailed as the CPET, advantages of the 6MWT are the ease, wide availblility and relatively low cost of the test. Disadvantages include the inability to accommodate physically impaired individuals and the challenges of testing severely ill indivduals. In conclusion, there is clear evidence that patients with poorer cardiopulmonary reserve have worse waitlist outcomes, and tests aimed at quantifying cardiopulmonary reserve are an important part of risk stratification of candidates for LT. Interventions aimed at improving cardiopulmonary reserve are needed. Published studies investigating “pre-habilitation” (including 2-50 patients, largely with well-compensated cirrhosis), utilise exercise-based interventions (mostly supervised and hospital-based) to improve debility and to some extent cardiopulmonary reserve. 14 The combination of aerobic and resistance exercises at moderate-high intensity appears most effective in improving physical debility. 14 In another small study, a 12-week home-based physical activity programme combined with essential amino acid supplementation (12 g/day) improved aerobic fitness in patients with cirrhosis and poor cardiopulmonary reserve. 15 Experience of CPET in this context is severely limited owing to limited access to the test. Thus, other functional tests should be utilised to determine who may benefit from intervention. These tests should not necessarily preclude patients as transplant candidates but serve as tools to inform risk-based discussions and to plan interventions. Evaluation of LT candidates for coronary heart disease The prevalence of coronary heart disease (CHD) in patients with end-stage liver disease (ESLD) is higher than in the general population. 16–19 This increased risk may be partly explained by systemic inflammation that contributes to thrombo-inflammation. 20 LT candidates with CHD are at high risk of intraoperative, perioperative and long-term complications, including death. 21 , 22 The term CHD refers to both macrovascular and microvascular diseases of the myocardium, although the primary focus of most practice guidance recommendations on CHD in LT candidates is on epicardial coronary artery obstruction. Herein, CHD is defined as a history of myocardial infarction, revascularisation (coronary artery bypass grafting or percutaneous coronary intervention) or known ≥50% stenosis in a major epicardial coronary artery. CHD screening refers to testing modalities ( e.g. , non-invasive stress tests) used to detect the presence of previously unknown but clinically significant CHD. The optimal approach to CHD evaluation and management in LT candidates has been debated for decades, with multiple guidelines and consensus statements published ( Table 1 ). 23–30 There remains controversy related to who to screen, how to screen, and why to screen and treat chronic CHD in LT candidates. A major goal of CHD risk stratification is to identify patients who may be at risk of perioperative death, to improve assessment of the intermediate risks and benefits of LT, and to guide better medical or interventional management for long-term risk mitigation. There are two epidemiologic trends in LT that influence current recommendations for CHD screening: changing LT demographics leading to an increasing prevalence of CHD risk factors ( e.g ., older age, higher prevalence of NASH), 31 and improved medical management of CHD leading to declining rates of CHD-related morbidity with a concurrent rise in rates

in LT candidates. A major goal of CHD risk stratification is to identify patients who may be at risk of perioperative death, to improve assessment of the intermediate risks and benefits of LT, and to guide better medical or interventional management for long-term risk mitigation. There are two epidemiologic trends in LT that influence current recommendations for CHD screening: changing LT demographics leading to an increasing prevalence of CHD risk factors ( e.g ., older age, higher prevalence of NASH), 31 and improved medical management of CHD leading to declining rates of CHD-related morbidity with a concurrent rise in rates of non-coronary cardiac events after LT. 32 , 33 Results of CHD screening in LT candidates should inform considerations regarding the benefit of LT, perceived risk of perioperative complications and projected long-term outcomes. 34 Guideline or statement Society Recommendations Initial evaluation Surveillance after listing Raval et al. Both pharmacologic and exercise stress testing have low sensitivity (13-37%) and suboptimal NPVs (75-80%) for detection of significant CHD 49 and prediction of post-operative CHD events in LT candidates. 50 This is due to blunted chronotropy (which makes it difficult to reach the target heart rate) and reduced cardiorespiratory fitness in ESLD. 50–57 Resting vasodilation in ESLD also limits the predictive accuracy of myocardial perfusion scintigraphy. 58 Cardiac magnetic resonance stress imaging has an excellent NPV of 98% in LT candidates, but its use is limited by its high cost, requirement for significant centre expertise, and overall low sensitivity (50%) for CHD. 59 , 60 In the general population, cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) with calculation of myocardial flow reserve detects coronary ischaemia with high accuracy. 61 PET perfusion imaging is highly attractive in LT candidates given its renal safety profile and the fact that it is not affected by chronic vasodilation, though data evaluating its use is limited. 62 Non-invasive angiography with coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) should be considered as the initial testing strategy in LT candidates who are at high risk for significant coronary artery disease (CAD). 30 , 31 , 49 , 63 ,

While both CCTA and ICA are associated with nephrotoxicity, the risk of nephrotoxicity may be lower with CCTA. 65 , 66 Coronary angiography may be performed in LT candidates with kidney dysfunction in consultation with a nephrologist. 26 , 28 When an ICA strategy is chosen, it may be performed despite coagulopathy in patients with ESLD. 67 , 68 However, periprocedural risks exist, so ICA should be reserved as the last test performed in an otherwise appropriate candidate for LT listing. 69 Notably, anatomic evaluations may miss functional microvascular disease that can contribute to type 2 myocardial infarction after LT. 70 , 71 However, universal functional testing is not supported by data incorporating cost-effectiveness and utility measures. 57 Therefore, stress testing alone should be reserved in intermediate risk patients ( Fig. 2 ). Under current US allocation policies based on acuity circles, some patients ( e.g ., those with model for end-stage liver disease [MELD] exceptions) may wait for over a year for LT. 72 CHD risk will not be static over that time and thus risk assessment should be considered at least yearly. The intensity of repeat testing will depend on both patient and programmatic factors, but should include assessment of change in prevalence or severity of CHD risk factors and risk factor control, at the minimum. This recommendation is in line with US practice patterns, where 85% of transplant centres repeat risk assessment with an ECG and resting echocardiography at least yearly. 31 Patients with high MELD who present simultaneously for LT evaluation and the operation can be in varying levels of decompensation, with fluctuating levels of stress-induced cardiac ischaemia and other cardiac abnormalities. 73 Studies do not distinguish between outpatient and inpatient evaluations for CHD. Therefore, the timing, selection, and interpretation of testing must take the severity of the patient’s illness and the stage of cirrhosis at the time of evaluation into consideration. Data to support or refute routine revascularisation prior to LT are limited. If CHD is identified, management decisions ( e.g . regarding medical and percutaneous interventions, or surgical revascularisation) must be made in conjuction with cardiologists and specialists in thoracic surgery, in the context of a high-risk patient population being considered for a lifesaving and resource-intensive LT procedure. 30 In LT candidates, significant CHD (≥50% luminal stenosis in ≥1 segment of the three major coronary arteries, or stenosis ≥70% in at least moderate-size branch vessels) without revascularisation options should be considered a contraindication to LT. 30 , 74 , 75 Table 3 summarises management considerations for identified CHD in LT candidates based on currently published practice guidance. Importantly, this discussion regarding the evaluation of CHD risk is not relevant to patients with symptomatic CHD, in whom immediate evidence-based interventions for acute coronary syndrome should be considered. Revascularisation There are no prospective randomised trials of CHD revascularisation in LT candidates; however, the presence of angiographically significant stenoses increases the risk of cardiac events and death after LT. 37 Revascularisation of asymptomatic significant CHD should be performed only if the patient has been deemed to be a suitable LT candidate because routine treatment is associated with significant risk without clear benefit. 30 Percutaneous coronary intervention can be safely performed in LT candidates. 133 According to recent consensus guidance, in LT candidates with significant CHD requiring revascularisation, newer-generation drug-eluting stents with a minimum of 3 months of DAPT should be used if possible. In LT candidates who cannot wait to complete guideline-recommended duration of DAPT, options include consideration of drug-eluting stents with a very short duration of DAPT (1 month), bare metal stent if available for use, or combined LT-CABG. Open table in a new tab Cardiac arrhythmias Cardiac arrythmias are common among LT candidates and recipients, and have been associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including stroke and decreased post-LT survival. 32 , 76–84 While both atrial and ventricular arrythmias occur, atrial fibrillation (AF) remains the most common arrythmia in this setting, and is the entity for which the most data is available in the LT population. Atrial fibrillation In data from systematic reviews and meta-analyses, the prevalence of pre-existing AF prior to LT (∼3-6%), as well as post-operative AF (up to 10%), appears to be higher than rates in the general population (which are reported to be 1-2% below age 65 and 9% over 65). 77 , 84 , 85 AF is likely the most common MACE to occur in the early post-operative period, accounting for 43% of MACEs in the first 90 days post-LT in an analysis of UNOS (United Network for Organ Sharing) data. 32 As LT candidates get older and develop more significant cardiac comorbidities, AF is likely to be even more common. Risk factors for pre-existing AF in LT candidates include elevated BMI, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, CHD, and prior cerebrovascular accidents. 77 It has also been hypothesised that AF may be a manifestation of underlying CCM, which is an increasingly recognised factor in LT patient outcomes. It is also notable that both isolated intraoperative 81 or new/persistent post-LT AF 82 , 86 appear to be associated with important clinical events, including MACEs, post-LT kidney dysfunction, length of hospital stay and survival. Reported risk factors for post-LT AF include age, BMI, MELD score at LT, diabetes mellitus, pre-LT AF, CHD, and perioperative factors including the use vasopressors prior to LT and pulmonary artery diastolic pressure at the end of the LT surgery. 76 , 79 , 80 , 82 , 85 , 87 Risk indices for post-operative AF have been developed, including in a large single-centre experience, wherein patients with the high-risk index had a more than 60% chance of developing post-LT AF. 82 This type of risk stratification could be used to drive monitoring or perhaps preventative therapies. In terms of screening, identification of patients with AF in the pre-LT period and/or with CCM is essential.
