Study Limitations This retrospective single-center investigation, conducted at a high-volume Romanian tertiary referral center, imposes inherent constraints on external validity, as local demographic profiles, antimicrobial stewardship practices, and operative protocols may diverge from those in heterogeneous international cohorts. Although the 1:2 matching scheme across catarrhal: chronic, phlegmonous: chronic, and gangrenous: chronic subgroups effectively controlled for age and sex disparities while enabling precise delineation of inflammatory gradients, residual confounders—including undocumented pre-operative antibiotic administration, temporal discrepancies between symptom onset and occult comorbidities such as subclinical metabolic dysregulation—may subtly modulate hematologic indices and preclude definitive causal inferences. The retrospective design of this study represents a major limitation, as it inherently restricts control over confounding variables and the completeness of clinical data. Histopathological subcategorization, despite reliance on standardized microscopic criteria, remains susceptible to inter-observer variability in assessing necrosis depth, inflammatory infiltrate density, or fibrotic remodeling, potentially attenuating the observed progression from phlegmonous to gangrenous forms. Furthermore, involvement of multiple surgeons across the study interval introduces heterogeneity in laparoscopic proficiency, which could independently elevate conversion rates beyond inflammation-driven tissue friability. The lack of formal calibration and external validation represents a limitation of the present study. Nonetheless, the cohort’s scale (759 patients) and comprehensive acute–chronic–histologic stratification establish a robust foundation for subsequent multicenter prospective validation. 5. Conclusions This study establishes that routine blood-derived inflammatory indices, particularly NLR, robustly distinguish acute from chronic cholecystitis and outperform MLR/PLR. NLR’s escalation from phlegmonous to gangrenous forms parallels immunologic progression—from innate surge to adaptive exhaustion—with histologic necrosis and surgical complexity. Mechanistically linked to neutrophil-driven immunothrombosis, these markers offer prognostic value for operative planning. Integrating NLR into preoperative assessment promises refined risk stratification and optimized outcomes in acute biliary inflammation.

documents.title: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines Management of Pediatric Hepatobiliary Disease

chunks.content: Introduction Chronic liver diseases in childhood are considered to be rare. Although advances in treatment have led to improved survival rates and prognosis for children with rare liver diseases, the transition into adulthood presents a unique set of challenges in healthcare management. , The pathophysiology and spectrum of liver diseases with pediatric onset differ substantially from those seen in adults, complicating the delivery of optimal medical care as patients transfer to adult hepatology departments. Furthermore, the lack of age-appropriate approaches exacerbates the discrepancy between the young person’s needs and the care they receive. , Suboptimal transfers from pediatric to adult services often result in poor therapy adherence and a considerable loss to follow-up. In turn, this contributes to disease progression and the occurrence of disease-related complications in (young) adulthood. To our knowledge, the transfer journey in rare liver diseases, defined as the patient’s journey from being informed about the transfer to full integration into adult care settings, is less understood and explored compared with conditions such as kidney disease and congenital heart disease. , Recognizing this gap, the European Reference Network of Hepatological Diseases (ERN RARE-LIVER) established a working group dedicated to improving transfer journeys across Europe. By identifying and addressing challenges and educational gaps head-on, this group aims to improve service and patient outcomes for young people with rare liver diseases. To further this objective, we hosted an omnistakeholder networking event to examine the critical aspects of, and opportunities in, transfer journey management for young people living with rare liver diseases in Europe. As the first of its kind, this study marks a critical step toward bridging these gaps by fostering international collaboration and developing a prioritized action plan with an emphasis on applicability, ultimately improving the lives of young people with rare liver diseases. Patients and methods Design A face-to-face omnistakeholder workshop event was hosted on 17–18 March 2023, in Belgium. The agenda of the workshop was established following a series of preparatory activities: (1) surveying European healthcare providers (HCP) to assess transfer management practices in rare liver disease (67 centers participated) (see for the survey and Madaleno et al. for preliminary results); (2) conducting interviews with young people with rare liver diseases (n = 11) and their parents (n = 7) who were unable to participate in the workshop, on challenges experienced ( ); and (3) engaging young people with liver diseases in an online forum, where they provided insights into their communication (n = 36), organizational (n = 31), and educational (n = 33) needs during the transfer period. Based on the insights gained from these activities, the ERN RARE-LIVER transition working group identified nine themes over three domains, which served as the focal points for focus sessions ( and ). The themes were presented to, and validated by, the ERN RARE-LIVER youth panel before the workshop, also improving patients’ familiarity with these topics. The event started with a plenary session discussing the state of the art on transfer journey management. A standardized workshop methodology was used across all three domains, encompassing: (1) a 25-min plenary session featuring two domain experts, who provided essential background knowledge and presented precollected data, thus establishing a foundation of best practices, while taking into account the gaps and barriers identified in our preparatory work; (2) participants were allocated to one of three parallel focus ( i.e. theme) sessions, with careful consideration of balanced representation across participant characteristics within each subgroup (n = 20–25 per focus session). Allocation was overseen by members of the ERN RARE-LIVER working group; and (3) 70-in focus sessions dedicated to identifying the most critical aspects and opportunities (actions) to establish a prioritized action plan for enhancing transfer journey management in Europe. The event concluded with a 95-min plenary session in which the results of all focus sessions were presented and discussed, providing an opportunity for participants who engaged in other sessions to offer feedback and contribute. The structure of the workshop is visualized in . Setting and participants In total, 72 individuals participated in the event. Inclusion criteria for patients were a diagnosis of a rare liver disease, aged between 18 and 25 years, and currently experiencing or having completed their transfer journey. Proficiency in English was not set as an exclusion criterion given the presence of HCPs from across Europe who could facilitate translation as needed. The inclusion criteria for non-patient participants were experience in either transfer journey management or rare liver diseases. Recruitment The ERN RARE-LIVER and professional organizations, such as the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition, disseminated recruitment leaflets via their socials. In addition, participants and patient representatives were encouraged to reach out to young people with rare liver diseases within their networks or centers. The transition working group made efforts to ensure a balanced recruitment of stakeholders, aiming for

The inclusion criteria for non-patient participants were experience in either transfer journey management or rare liver diseases. Recruitment The ERN RARE-LIVER and professional organizations, such as the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition, disseminated recruitment leaflets via their socials. In addition, participants and patient representatives were encouraged to reach out to young people with rare liver diseases within their networks or centers. The transition working group made efforts to ensure a balanced recruitment of stakeholders, aiming for equal representation of pediatricians, adult care physicians, paramedics, researchers, and patient representatives and patients. The group also aimed to engage representatives of countries under-represented within European projects. Data collection Each focus session was supervised by two experts in workshop methodologies, following a standardized protocol, along with two members of the transition working group, who provided content-related support. The protocol included the following steps: (1) focus session kickoff with instructions by the methodology experts; (2) brainstorm on theme-specific critical aspects at breakout tables; (3) presentation of results from each breakout table, and clarification; (4) voting by participants on importance; (5) brainstorm on theme-specific actions at breakout tables; (6) presentation of results from each breakout table, and clarification; (7) further voting by participants on importance; and (8) wrap-up of session by the methodology experts. Each participant was allocated three votes during voting rounds, with the stipulation that they could not allocate more than one vote to a single critical aspect or action. Participants had to take into account the real-world applicability of actions during their vote. Data analysis Critical aspects and actions identified in each focus session were ranked according to the number of votes received. Aspects and actions that received votes from at least 25% of participants were reported. Some votes were lost during the process, as indicated by (-%). In these cases, all aspects and actions identified in the session were reported. Given the diverse and distinct definitions of transition and transfer, and our findings indicating critical aspects and actions related to both, we chose to adopt the term ‘transfer journey’. This encompasses all care aspects associated with a comprehensive transfer, taking into account healthcare ( e.g. the different domains of healthcare continuity ) and psychosocial needs of patients, their significant others, and HCPs. Ensuring patient centeredness During the event, 15 young patients co-created an ERN RARE-LIVER youth panel and took part in the focus sessions. A year later, the workshop findings were revisited and reviewed from a patient perspective. All members were asked to prioritize actions individually; these were then discussed in an online panel meeting until consensus was reached, ensuring the results were meaningful and patient centered. Ethical considerations All participant data were anonymized. Results Participant characteristics This international workshop included participants from Belgium (n = 29), Cyprus (n = 3), Denmark (n = 5), Finland (n = 1), France (n = 1), Germany (n = 7), Moldova (n = 1), Poland (n = 1), Portugal (n = 2), Spain (n = 4), Switzerland (n = 1), The Netherlands (n = 5), and the UK (n = 12). Participants’ roles are presented in . Domain 1: communication Theme 1A: open communication Critical aspects: to achieve open communication, young people require clear and concise information delivered step-by-step. Establishing a strong connection between physicians and young people and allocating sufficient time during consultations are important for their full comprehension (81% of votes). Communication should be consistent throughout the young person’s transfer journey (43%). In pediatric clinics, young people also need long-term preparation, including information about potential prognoses and adult care services (31%). Strategies to enhance engagement and understanding should include tailoring communication methods to individual levels and needs (25%). Actions: key strategies could involve scheduling joint appointments with pediatric and adult care physicians to manage expectations regarding adult care services (93%), ensuring the consistent provision of information by assigning one HCP to a young person throughout the transfer journey (62%), and offering a longer initial consultation at the adult department to enhance relationship building (44%). Theme 1B: communication between pediatric and adult HCPs Critical aspects: young people need access to a single point of contact during the transfer journey (70%); loss in information when transferring between departments should be limited (60%); and strategies to facilitate communication and, thereby, a smooth transfer journey, should be implemented (30%). Actions: a specialized transition person should be assigned to manage, coordinate, and enhance communication between physicians and between departments (-%). Multidisciplinary team meetings and discussions involving pediatricians and adult care physicians should be organized to improve patient information exchange (-%). A standardized transfer document should be developed to help teams structure their information exchange, ensuring continuity of information (60%). Theme 1C: communication between HCPs

a single point of contact during the transfer journey (70%); loss in information when transferring between departments should be limited (60%); and strategies to facilitate communication and, thereby, a smooth transfer journey, should be implemented (30%). Actions: a specialized transition person should be assigned to manage, coordinate, and enhance communication between physicians and between departments (-%). Multidisciplinary team meetings and discussions involving pediatricians and adult care physicians should be organized to improve patient information exchange (-%). A standardized transfer document should be developed to help teams structure their information exchange, ensuring continuity of information (60%). Theme 1C: communication between HCPs and patients Critical aspects: discussing the patient's preferred communication channels is important to enhance access to healthcare ( e.g. e-mail, phone, or in-person meetings) (100%). Young people should have a dedicated person or team assigned to them (41%) or be knowledgeable about whom and how they may contact a professional throughout the transfer journey (59%). Actions: communication preferences should be systematically discussed and agreed upon with young people, including various methods and their appropriate uses, such as e-mail for non-urgent inquiries and calls for emergencies (100%), based on the available resources of each medical team. Young people’s expectations should be managed by informing them about response times and responsible parties (27%). Domain 2: organization Theme 2A: environment Critical aspects: young people should feel welcome in both pediatric and adult care environments. This could include using soothing colors, arranging comfortable seats, and ensuring proper internet connections (78%). Clinic visits should be efficiently organized and clustered to streamline the experience and minimize the time burden on young people, also considering tests and blood draw results (61%). Young persons’ feelings of ‘culture shock’, referring to the stress experienced when someone is suddenly subjected to an unfamiliar set of attitudes, should be prevented by bridging the gap in attitudes and expectations between departments and patients (36%). Actions: establish a formal (peer mentoring) program to introduce and guide newly transferred patients in adult clinics (93%). Provide information, such as through leaflets, and valuable insights into the adult department to young people before the transfer (85%). Theme 2B: continuity of care Critical aspects: maintaining relational continuity is vital, especially during critical or medically unstable periods. Although a dedicated transition coordinator can be helpful, ensuring continuity is more important and does not necessarily require a specific coordinator (66%). Transfer journeys should be guided by readiness, not just age, using a checklist tailored to the patient's needs (61%). Involving all stakeholders, including general practitioners and psychologists, is important (44%). Strategies to prevent young people from being lost to follow-up should be implemented, for instance by maintaining a list of young people with chronic conditions and standardized assessments of missed appointments (28%). Actions: a dedicated person, either a peer mentor, trusted family member, or HCP, should accompany young people throughout their transfer journey to ensure consistency and familiarity (-%). A joint clinic, in-person or online, could improve familiarity with adult care physicians and promote continuity of care (-%). A medical CV, drafted by patients, could empower them by providing patient-important information to adult care physicians (-%). Contact details of all stakeholders across settings should be provided before the transfer and frequently updated (-%). Theme 2C: components Critical aspects: some aspects reported above were identified as critical components in transfer journey management, including: joint appointments (70%), a dedicated someone to guide young people through the transfer journey (66%), and adequate information exchange (33%). Other critical aspects were the coordination of interdisciplinary transfers (42%) and the management of roles and responsibilities of all stakeholders to ensure accountability and promote young people’s sense of responsibility (28%). Actions: appointing a transition person to serve as a liaison between stakeholders was suggested once more (79%). Co-creating a transfer letter with patient and family involvement could improve continuity of patient-important information (48%). Regular meetings between pediatricians and adult care physicians could facilitate communication and cohesive care planning across settings (42%). Integrating age-appropriate care into the vision and mission of the organization could underscore the importance of comprehensive and coordinated care (30%). Domain 3: education Theme 3A: training of HCPs Critical aspects: young people should feel comfortable discussing sensitive topics with their HCPs, such as alcohol consumption, drugs, mental health, and sexual and reproductive health (74%). Therefore, physicians should have a basic understanding of these topics, adolescent development, and behavior (47%), along with access to information on how to address these young people’s specific needs (47%). The ERN could have an important role in training physicians and adapting training to the local level (32%). Actions: graphical prompts covering age-specific sensitive topics should be developed to equip HCPs and facilitate discussions (83%). A more patient-centered approach could be achieved by including personal information, such as hobbies and education, in health records (76%). Integrating mandatory communication skills training

consumption, drugs, mental health, and sexual and reproductive health (74%). Therefore, physicians should have a basic understanding of these topics, adolescent development, and behavior (47%), along with access to information on how to address these young people’s specific needs (47%). The ERN could have an important role in training physicians and adapting training to the local level (32%). Actions: graphical prompts covering age-specific sensitive topics should be developed to equip HCPs and facilitate discussions (83%). A more patient-centered approach could be achieved by including personal information, such as hobbies and education, in health records (76%). Integrating mandatory communication skills training into academic curricula can ensure that future HCPs create supportive environments for discussing sensitive topics (41%). Theme 3B: sharing of information Critical aspects: young people desire peer-to-peer contact for practical insights into coping, managing insurance, finances, diet, life participation, and employment (-%). They also should be empowered through information sharing from physicians to patients to make informed decisions about their care, including addressing uncertainties and providing preventive guidance (-%). Patients should also receive transparent information, accessible through various formats (-%). Actions: creating videos featuring patient experiences and establishing online forums allow young people to connect, share knowledge, and seek guidance (100%). HCPs also have a critical role in disseminating information; for example, podcasts featuring experts discussing various topics related to rare liver diseases can offer convenient access to information for adult care physicians (95%). HCPs should engage with patients to assess their knowledge and share reliable information sources (61%). Social media platforms can be used to share engaging and interactive information, such as creating Pinterest boards with disease-related content (43%). Theme 3C: peer support Critical aspects: young people have diverse preferences regarding peer support. Therefore, various mentorship formats should be offered to accommodate these differing needs (100%). The matching process between young people and mentors is considered critical for establishing constructive relationships, considering factors such as personality and experiences (66%). Peer mentors need to undergo training and guidance on how to provide effective peer support (42%). Actions: an innovative (inter)national mentorship platform should be developed and overseen by organizations such as ERNs. This platform would simplify mentor selection, enabling young people to choose based on specific needs, such as a particular disease, experience, or family situation. Offering translation in multiple languages ensures inclusivity (100%). Alongside platform development, comprehensive mentorship guidelines involving various stakeholders should be established to ensure supportive and constructive interactions (100%). Data review from a patient perspective A subset of the youth panel members (n = 8) prioritized the different domains and actions discussed above individually ( and ) and discussed these during a panel meeting until consensus was reached, ensuring the recommendations were patient centered. Their priorities were in line with the previously mentioned results. They deemed the communication domain the most important overall, with all of them stating that either 1A open communication (87.5%) or 1B communication between HCPs (12.5%) was the most important to achieve a positive transfer journey. Theme 2A organization also received a high score, with 25% naming it as the second most important and another 50% as third. They agreed with the proposed actions and deemed joint consultations (62.5%) and the appointment of a dedicated person the most important (included in top 3 by 87.5%). Furthermore, they highlighted the importance of a transfer document (ranked third by 12.5%, fourth by 25%, and fifth by 62.5%) and offering a longer initial consultation in the adult department (included in top 3 by all participants). Discussion This international omnistakeholder workshop pioneers exploring the challenges and opportunities in managing transfer journeys for young people with rare liver diseases. By emphasizing practical implications ( i.e. actions), it establishes itself as a benchmark for improving transfer journeys worldwide, applicable to not only rare liver diseases, but possibly also common liver or other rare diseases. Our findings underscore the fundamental importance of the transfer itself in maintaining continuity of care. We identified critical aspects and actions primarily related to the concept of continuity of care. Building on Haggerty et al. , three key domains can be delineated: (1) informative continuity, which stresses the importance of effective information exchange among HCPs and between patients and HCPs; (2) relational continuity, emphasizing the involvement of a trusted individual or team throughout healthcare interactions; and (3) management continuity, highlighting the need for consistency in healthcare management, attitudes, resources, and treatment, yet tailored to the changing needs of individuals. Given that most of our findings fall within these domains, we chose to organize our discussion accordingly. Notably, our research indicates that joint consultations could serve as a valuable tool for enhancing all domains of continuity of care. In line with the objective of the workshop to develop a prioritized action plan, we elaborate on the practical implications below. Continuity of care Achieving effective information

the involvement of a trusted individual or team throughout healthcare interactions; and (3) management continuity, highlighting the need for consistency in healthcare management, attitudes, resources, and treatment, yet tailored to the changing needs of individuals. Given that most of our findings fall within these domains, we chose to organize our discussion accordingly. Notably, our research indicates that joint consultations could serve as a valuable tool for enhancing all domains of continuity of care. In line with the objective of the workshop to develop a prioritized action plan, we elaborate on the practical implications below. Continuity of care Achieving effective information exchange among stakeholders requires a multifaceted approach, ensuring that communication is recurrent, consistent, coherent, and impactful. It is critical to tailor communication strategies to each stakeholder’s needs: young people should have easy-to-use channels for engaging with HCPs; pediatricians should be equipped to exchange information timely and comprehensively with both young people and adult care physicians; and both pediatricians and adult care physicians should be trained in age-appropriate communication techniques. Strategies to achieve these objectives could include ERN-hosted webinars and utilization of a standardized transfer document to enhance information exchange between departments. The ERN RARE-LIVER youth panel and transition working group co-developed such a document outlining the essential information exchange requirements ( ). However, relevant information to patients often extends beyond medical details, including how to navigate the adult care system and psychosocial topics, such coping. These experience-based insights can be shared by peers in a mentor–mentee program, where peers are regarded as experts by experience, substantially enhancing the exchange of patient-important information. , Data on mentor–mentee programs are scarce, and guidelines for developing and implementing such initiatives are lacking. Nonetheless, existing collaborations between ERNs and national patient organizations in educating and building the capacity of patient representatives could extend to training mentors and supporting mentor–mentee programs. While the concept of relational continuity might appear straightforward in theory, ensuring its realization poses challenges. Current literature and guidelines commonly recommend appointing a transition coordinator to manage the transfer journey and provide age-appropriate support. , , , However, our participants frequently stated that this approach is not feasible or applicable in their country or center. Instead, our findings suggest that relational continuity should extend beyond relying on a single HCP. The essence of relational continuity lies in establishing a familiar and accessible point of contact for young people throughout their transfer journey. However, familiarity and accessibility are distinct aspects originating from different needs. On the one hand, familiarity does not mean having a dedicated HCP, but rather someone who is trusted, supportive, experienced, and with whom young people can identify. This conclusion dovetails with the experience-based support provided in a mentor-mentee program. On the other hand, maintaining an accessible point of contact primarily concerns access to healthcare services, which should preferably not be based in one individual. Strategies should focus on informing young people about whom to approach for specific issues and where to receive care. This could be facilitated by equipping them with a patient guideline on how to access healthcare services. By providing experience-based support and facilitating access to healthcare throughout the transfer journey, we could enhance relational continuity in real-world settings. Achieving management continuity poses significant challenges resulting from variations in medical practices, infrastructure, and resources between pediatric and adult care departments, often rooted in healthcare service structures. Thus, strategies should prioritize preparing young people for management changes instead of restructuring entire healthcare systems. Participants consistently stressed the importance of providing young people with relevant information about what to expect upon transferring to adult care, including potential changes in healthcare management, and, thus, providing insights into different prognoses and therapeutical options. This information exchange should occur well in advance of the transfer to minimize the ‘culture shock’. Another potential discontinuity can stem from a lack of knowledge and guidelines, particularly on age-specific topics, such as alcohol counseling. Collaboration among the ERN RARE-LIVER guideline working group, transition working group, and youth panel is essential to identify knowledge gaps and develop guidelines or consensus papers to address them. Joint consultations: a real-world presentation of continuity of care An emerging action observed across the focus sessions was the application of joint consultations, which encapsulates all three domains of continuity of care. First, it fosters effective communication among the three primary stakeholders: young people, pediatric, and adult HCPs. This setup allows young people to participate in the information exchange and contribute patient-important details that might not have been communicated otherwise. Second, joint consultations serve as a tangible demonstration of the transfer of medical responsibility from pediatric to adult HCPs, clarifying for patients which department to approach in case of issues and avoiding care gaps. It is vital to discuss communication strategies and exchange contact details during these consultations to enhance access to healthcare. In

encapsulates all three domains of continuity of care. First, it fosters effective communication among the three primary stakeholders: young people, pediatric, and adult HCPs. This setup allows young people to participate in the information exchange and contribute patient-important details that might not have been communicated otherwise. Second, joint consultations serve as a tangible demonstration of the transfer of medical responsibility from pediatric to adult HCPs, clarifying for patients which department to approach in case of issues and avoiding care gaps. It is vital to discuss communication strategies and exchange contact details during these consultations to enhance access to healthcare. In addition, it allows young people to familiarize themselves with the adult HCP beforehand. Third, both HCPs can discuss and plan future medical management, including exploring therapeutic opportunities available in adult care settings. Although several critical aspects of transfer journey management have been identified, a well-executed joint consultation has the potential to address many simultaneously. Guidelines for organizing and implementing joint consultations are lacking, yet they should target the different domains of continuity of care. Noteworthy, transfers to HCPs outside the main organization of the pediatric department pose particular challenges because of the lack of established collaboration or different department locations; in such cases, joint teleconsultations could enhance continuity of care. Reflection on current literature and guidelines Based on the results from our omnistakeholder workshop and input from the youth panel, the critical aspects of transfer journey management are relatively practical. By contrast, current literature and guidelines often encompass a plethora of psychosocial interventions. , , , Although most programs yield positive effects on various outcomes, the participation rate is notoriously low. This might illustrate that these programs are not sufficiently meeting the needs of young people during their transfer journey. Furthermore, these programs predominantly take place in research environments; therefore, they might not speak to the needs or resources of HCPs who are imperative to implement them. As a result, the overall applicability of current guidelines is uncertain. While participants received state-of-the-art knowledge and evidence in plenary sessions, many did not consider assumed standard components, such as monitoring young people’s transition readiness, as critical actions during the focus sessions. This underscores a discrepancy between current guidelines, which might reflect an ideal, but less feasible transfer journey management, and identified critical actions, mostly structural elements that could establish continuity of care. The issue appears to be one of prioritization: only by establishing a proper structure ensuring continuity of care first can we evaluate the added value of psychosocial interventions proposed in most guidelines. Future research perspectives and initiatives The discussion has outlined several hypotheses, collaborations, and approaches. Further research is needed to assess the real-world effectiveness of strategies, such as implementing a mento–mentee program, joint consultations, or a standardized transfer document to enhance continuity of care for young people with rare liver diseases. Expanding collaborations among ERN RARE-LIVER working groups, particularly involving the youth panel in identifying challenges and developing initiatives, similar to the present workshop and the codevelopment of the transfer document, is critical. These initiatives include: (1) developing guidelines on age- and disease-specific topics; (2) creating a patient guideline on accessing healthcare services; and (3) organizing educational activities, such as webinars on transfer journeys and age-appropriate communication techniques for HCPs. These actions will further enhance the impact of the ERN RARE-LIVER on healthcare for young people with rare liver diseases and improve transfer journey management throughout Europe and beyond. Strengths and limitations We ensured a well-balanced representation of stakeholders, enhancing the applicability and relevance of our findings. Patient involvement was emphasized at every stage, from conceptualization to validation, resulting in significant contributions from young people and improving the potential impact of the workshop at the patient level. Another strength was our systemic approach, guided by methodology experts, addressing critical aspects followed by proposing feasible actions, leading to clear practical implications. This international workshop included participants from under-represented countries within European projects ( i.e. Cyprus, Poland, and Moldova), enhancing the generalizability of our findings. The preparatory work allowed voices uncomfortable in an international setting to be heard. We only engaged parents in preparatory activities, ensuring that their perspectives were incorporated when identifying the nine themes. This aimed to create an environment where young people could freely express themselves, with outcomes tailored to their specific needs. Nonetheless, we recognize the important role of parents as partners in transfer journey planning. Despite significant differences in national health policies and the absence of recruited policymakers from participating countries, the workshop focused on establishing feasible, resource-light actions to ensure the applicability of its outcomes. In the data analysis phase, voting data for 15% of critical aspects and actions could not be retrieved; consequently, no selection or prioritization was performed for these items. Implications Our results stress the importance of practical aspects of transfer journey

Nonetheless, we recognize the important role of parents as partners in transfer journey planning. Despite significant differences in national health policies and the absence of recruited policymakers from participating countries, the workshop focused on establishing feasible, resource-light actions to ensure the applicability of its outcomes. In the data analysis phase, voting data for 15% of critical aspects and actions could not be retrieved; consequently, no selection or prioritization was performed for these items. Implications Our results stress the importance of practical aspects of transfer journey management. From our findings, we have distilled fundamental and equally important recommendations designed to address these aspects, ensuring their broad relevance and applicability across diverse contexts: (1) Establish contact between pediatric and adult care services; involve other relevant HCPs ( e.g. general practitioners) in the transfer journey (see Theme 1B); (2) Provide transparent information to young people about their disease, prognosis, and what to expect on adult care services (see Themes 1A and 2A); (3) Ensure the transfer of essential information using a standardized transfer document ( ) (see Theme 1B); (4) Organize joint (tele-)consultations if possible and/or a longer initial consultation at the adult department. Alternatively, allow young people to contribute important information through co-creation of a transfer letter (see Theme 2B); (5) Proactively ask young people if they would like peer contact, and refer them to peers or patient organizations if so (see Theme 3C); (6) Provide contact details of all stakeholders and discuss communication strategies at each phase of the transfer journey, explaining to young people whom to approach for specific issues and where to receive care (see Theme 1C). These recommendations are not exhaustive but should be considered the minimum criteria for effective transfer journey management in rare liver diseases. Concluding remarks Most critical aspects and actions focused on informative continuity, relational continuity, and management continuity. Our findings highlight the need for peer support programs, communication strategies for young people, and joint consultations. The applicability of current literature and guidelines is unclear because they may not fully address real-world challenges in rare liver diseases, particularly those concerning the actual transfer process in maintaining continuity of care. Therefore, effectiveness–implementation hybrid design studies are needed to assess the real-world effectiveness of strategies aimed at improving continuity of care during transfer journeys for young people with rare liver diseases. documents.title: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines Acute on Chronic Liver Failure ACLF

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Liver failure is a severe clinical syndrome caused by multiple etiologies, characterized by acute onset, rapid progression, and high mortality, and thus poses a major threat to human health ( ). A central pathological feature of liver failure is the excessive inflammatory response, in which uncontrolled cytokine release and aberrant immune cell activation drive extensive hepatocyte necrosis and rapid hepatic decompensation ( ; ). Within the spectrum of liver failure, acute liver failure (ALF) has been widely used to investigate immune-mediated mechanisms because of its abrupt onset and prominent inflammatory features ( ). Among experimental models, the Concanavalin A (Con A)-induced murine acute liver injury model is a well-established immune-mediated hepatitis model that effectively recapitulates T-cell activation and cytokine storm-driven hepatic injury ( ; ; ). In contrast, acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) represents a distinct clinical entity characterized by acute deterioration superimposed on chronic liver disease and is associated with extremely poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options ( ; ). The key to blocking the transition to severe ACLF lies in neutralizing the acute liver insult and its powerful inflammatory aftermath ( ; ). In recent years, stem cells have emerged as a promising therapeutic approach owing to their potent immunomodulatory and regenerative properties ( ; ). Among them, urine-derived stem cells (USCs) have garnered particular attention because they can be obtained non-invasively, are widely accessible, and display favorable biological characteristics ( ; ). Nevertheless, studies specifically addressing urine-derived stem cells from ACLF patients (LF-USCs) remain scarce, and their mechanisms of action and clinical feasibility in the treatment of liver failure are largely unknown. To address this gap, the present study employed a Con A-induced murine ALF model to investigate the anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective effects of LF-USCs. These findings are expected to provide experimental evidence supporting LF-USCs as a potential autologous cell therapy and to lay the groundwork for clinical translation in liver failure. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Isolation and expansion of USCs LF-USCs were isolated from urine samples collected from three male patients diagnosed with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) at Beijing Youan Hospital, Capital Medical University. Primary baseline clinical characteristics of the ACLF patients are summarized in . Urine samples were collected after clinical diagnosis of ACLF and during routine inpatient management, before experimental cell isolation. USCs from age-matched healthy donors (H-USCs) (n = 3) were obtained as controls. Healthy donors were volunteers without a history of liver disease, chronic systemic illness, or recent acute infection. Urine samples from healthy donors were collected by spontaneous midstream urination and processed using the same protocol as that applied to ACLF patient samples. For each patient, at least three urine samples (ranging from 100 to 300 mL) were collected during the initial stage. These samples were processed independently for USC isolation rather than pooled. The resulting USC cultures were cryopreserved as individual batches and subsequently thawed and expanded as needed for downstream experiments. Sterile urine samples were first centrifuged at 1000–1500 rpm for 3–5 min, after which the supernatant was discarded, leaving 1–2 mL of pellet. The pellet was resuspended in approximately 5 mL phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), centrifuged again under the same conditions, washed, and finally resuspended in USC-specific culture medium. The resulting cell suspension was seeded into T25 culture flasks and kept undisturbed for the first 48 h, after which the medium was replaced every 2 days. After approximately 2 weeks, when large or multiple colonies appeared, cells were subcultured. All cells were maintained under standard culture conditions (37 °C, 5% CO 2 ), and cells within six passages (P6) were used for subsequent experiments, except for proliferation assays. Detailed cell culture procedures are described in . This research protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Youan Hospital, Capital Medical University (LL-2020–178-K). Written informed consent was obtained from all participating patients for the use of their medical records. 2.2 Cell activity and proliferation Cell proliferation of LF-USCs was evaluated by both CCK-8 growth curve analysis and PD kinetics ( ). For the CCK-8 assay, gradient-diluted cell suspensions were seeded into 96-well plates with six replicate wells per group. After a 2–4 h incubation for cell adherence, CCK-8 reagent was added, and cells were further cultured. Absorbance (O.D.) values were measured to generate a standard curve. Based on this curve, cells at the lowest concentration were seeded in six replicate wells and pre-incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . CCK-8 reagent was added every 24 h for six consecutive days, and O.D. values were recorded to calculate cell numbers. For PD curve analysis, passage 1 LF-USCs were seeded at 1 × 10 6 cells per 60-mm dish (N 1 ) and sub-cultured every 3 days (CT) at the same density up to passage 10. Cell counts at each passage (N n ) were obtained using
