Sex was encoded as a binary variable, with “0” representing female and “1” representing male. Together with the four previously identified differential metabolites, we incorporated the sex variable into machine learning models. The results showed that the incorporation of sex further enhanced the machine learning model’s performance. 2.6.7 Sensitivity analysis “An important consideration in our study is the inclusion of eight patients with DILI attributed to anticancer chemotherapeutic agents. Given that cancer itself can profoundly alter the host metabolome, we acknowledge the potential for confounding in our analysis. Our sensitivity analysis, which excluded these patients, demonstrated that the core metabolic signature distinguishing intrinsic from idiosyncratic DILI remained robust:the PLS-DA model still showed clear separation, and the key biomarkers retained high diagnostic power with an AUC of 0.863. This suggests that the metabolic disparities we identified are primarily driven by the mechanism of liver injury rather than the presence of an underlying malignancy. The chart can be found in the . 3 Discussion The pathogenesis of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is complex and has not been fully elucidated. It is conventionally categorized into intrinsic (dose-dependent and predictable) and idiosyncratic (unpredictable and highly variable among individuals) types ( ). In recent years, the concept of “indirect” DILI has been proposed, suggesting that some drugs may induce or exacerbate liver injury through their pharmacological effects rather than through intrinsic toxicity or immunogenicity, thereby altering the physiological state of the body ( ). However, this proposed mechanism currently lacks sufficient clinical and experimental support, and its distinction from idiosyncratic DILI remains ambiguous, making clear differentiation challenging ( ; ). Therefore, this study focuses specifically on comparing the mechanisms underlying intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI. The core challenges in this field are primarily reflected in the following aspects: First, there is a lack of objective diagnostic tools, as current clinical biochemical indicators and pathological features are insufficient to reliably differentiate between DILI caused by distinct mechanisms (intrinsic, idiosyncratic). Second, the classification of DILI mechanisms for specific drugs largely relies on empirical consensus among experts rather than well-validated objective biomarkers. Finally, it remains unclear whether fundamental differences in pathophysiological mechanisms exist between intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI, owing to the absence of in-depth and systematic experimental data. Therefore, elucidating the various mechanisms underlying drug-induced liver injury and identifying corresponding biomarkers are of crucial importance for the scientific prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of DILI. This study represents the first application of HP-CIL LC-MS-based metabolomics to investigate alterations in endogenous small molecule metabolites in the serum of patients with intrinsic versus idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The PLS-DA model demonstrated clear separation between the two groups. We subsequently integrated the results from both PLS-DA and volcano plot analyses to identify metabolites that showed consistent significance across both methods. These selected common metabolites were then used to construct diagnostic models for discriminating between intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI using multiple machine learning approaches implemented in MetaboAnalyst. Ultimately, four differential metabolites:Alanyl-Glycine (level1),N2-Acetyl-L-Cystathionine (level 2a), an Isomer of 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic Acid, and Isomer 1 of 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (level 2a)—were identified as potential biomarkers for distinguishing the two types of DILI. The initial machine learning model, which did not include sex as a feature, demonstrated that the diagnostic model constructed from the combination of four metabolites already exhibited strong discriminatory performance. This study further highlights the important influence of patient sex on model performance. Analysis of the clinical cohort revealed a significant difference in sex distribution between the two groups—the intrinsic DILI group was 76.5% female, whereas the idiosyncratic DILI group was 77.8% male (χ 2 = 12.51, P < 0.001). After incorporating patient sex as a binary feature into the original model, the results showed a consistent further improvement in the machine learning model’s performance, underscoring the value of sex as an informative variable in subtype discrimination. Metabolic pathway analysis of the differentially expressed metabolites revealed that the most impacted pathways included Tryptophan metabolism, Glycine, serine and threonine metabolism, Cysteine and methionine metabolism, and Arginine and proline metabolism, suggesting that disruptions in amino acid metabolism may play a critical role in differentiating between intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI ( ; ). The Alanyl-Glycine (level 1) screened in this study is a dipeptide formed by the linkage of alanine and glycine via a peptide bond, which has been identified in human urine. It is a degradation product of both endogenous and exogenous proteins ( ). Dipeptides play essential roles in nutritional and biological functions, and recent studies have reported their potential as biomarkers for the diagnosis and classification of various diseases ( ; ; ). Many researchers have identified differential dipeptide metabolites in different disease models using untargeted metabolomic approaches ( ). After cellular uptake, a portion of dipeptides is hydrolyzed by cytoplasmic peptidases into free amino acids, which are then utilized for cellular metabolic synthesis or transported into systemic circulation via basolateral amino acid transport systems. Another fraction of dipeptides, resistant to hydrolytic enzymes, can be transported intact into the circulation via basolateral peptide transporters, after which they are degraded into amino acids by soluble proteases in the plasma ( ; ; ). In intrinsic drug-induced liver injury (DILI), the elevation of Alanyl-Glycine (level 1) may be closely associated with its hydrolysis into individual amino acids—alanine and glycine—which subsequently enter their respective metabolic pathways. Glycine, a key component of glutathione (GSH), contributes to the detoxification process. In acetaminophen-induced intrinsic hepatotoxicity, CYP-mediated metabolism generates reactive metabolites accompanied by depletion of GSH, accelerating the formation of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species in necrotic hepatocytes. Impaired liver function or necrosis reduces hepatic amino acid metabolic capacity, leading to the release of intracellular amino acids into the bloodstream, thereby increasing plasma glycine levels ( ; ). On the other hand, alanine serves as an important gluconeogenic amino acid. Within the glucose-alanine cycle, it can be converted into glucose via gluconeogenesis. DILI impairs gluconeogenesis, disrupting glucose synthesis and ultimately resulting in significantly elevated alanine levels ( ). Additionally, DILI enhances glycolytic metabolism. As reported by Huo et al., sodium valproate—an agent known for intrinsic hepatotoxicity—increased pyruvate and lactate levels in DILI patients, indicating enhanced anaerobic metabolism, which is often accompanied by a rise in alanine ( ). Therefore, the increase in Alanyl-Glycine (level 1) may reflect concurrent metabolic disturbances of both glycine and alanine in the context of intrinsic DILI. This process not only illustrates the metabolic relationship between the dipeptide and its constituent amino acids, but also suggests that Alanyl-Glycine (level 1) (level 1) could serve as a meaningful biomarker indicating overall dysregulation of amino acid metabolism in liver injury. N2-Acetyl-L-cystathionine is a sulfur-containing amino acid derivative associated with human inborn errors of metabolism such as cystathioninuria ( ). It is likely an acetylated product of cystathionine, which serves as a key intermediate in the methionine metabolic pathway and plays a central role in the transsulfuration pathway for cysteine synthesis ( ). N2-Acetyl-L-cystathionine is a sulfur-containing amino acid derivative associated with human inborn errors of metabolism such as cystathioninuria ( ). It is likely an acetylated product of cystathionine, which serves as a key intermediate in the methionine metabolic pathway and plays a central role in the transsulfuration pathway for cysteine synthesis ( ). In the context of intrinsic hepatotoxicity induced by agents such as acetaminophen (APAP), liver injury is initiated through rapid depletion of glutathione (GSH). Metabolomic studies have shown that GSH depletion leads to the exhaustion of precursor metabolites—including cysteine and methionine—as part of the cellular compensatory response to APAP-induced oxidative stress ( ). In an attempt to restore GSH levels, the transsulfuration pathway may be upregulated, resulting in the accumulation of cystathionine. This, in turn, drives the elevation of its acetylated derivative,N2-Acetyl-L-Cystathionine (level 2a). Therefore, the elevation ofN2-Acetyl-L-Cystathionine (level 2a) may serve as a downstream metabolic marker indicative of enhanced transsulfuration activity in hepatocytes responding to glutathione depletion during intrinsic drug-induced liver injury. Amino acid metabolism, particularly involving tryptophan, has been documented in previous studies as a common biomarker associated with hepatotoxicity ( ). As an essential amino acid, tryptophan participates in various biosynthetic pathways, and its metabolic disruption is implicated in the pathogenesis of liver dysfunction. No studies have been reported to date regarding Isomer 1 of 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (level 2a) or Isomer 1 of 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (level 2a) in the context of DILI research. They identified deoxycholic acid, taurodeoxycholate, and glycodeoxycholate as biomarkers distinguishing severe from non-severe DILI. employed an untargeted metabolomics approach based on liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry to analyze the metabolic profiles of HepG2 cells treated with drugs known to cause liver injury through different mechanisms. Their findings indicated that glutathione-related metabolites, the lysophospholipid/phospholipid ratio, and intermediates of fatty acid β-oxidation served as key metabolic markers differentiating mechanisms such as oxidative stress, phospholipidosis, and steatosis. This study is the first to employ HP-CIL LC–MS based metabolomics to investigate metabolic differences between intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI, with the aim of identifying biomarkers capable of predicting these two DILI subtypes. By integrating metabolomic data with clinical variables and applying machine learning strategies, we preliminarily identified potential biomarkers associated with the mechanisms of intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI, and further developed a predictive model for distinguishing the two subtypes. Considering the limited sample size, 60% of the data from both the intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI groups were used as the training set during the biomarker screening phase, while the remaining data served as the test set. Under various machine learning strategies, the selected specific biomarkers were evaluated, and the model demonstrated reliable predictive performance based on the test set results. Following the cluster analysis, we retrospectively reviewed the clinical characteristics and medication histories of the patients within the third cluster. We found that this cluster likely consists of patients who developed DILI following the use of anticancer chemotherapeutic agents. This discovery provided a crucial explanatory clue. In recent years, the classification of DILI pathogenesis has been evolving. The traditional intrinsic-idiosyncratic dichotomy is being challenged. As the reviewer speculated, our third cluster might correspond to a newly proposed mechanism—indirect DILI. An authoritative review published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019 first systematically introduced this concept, specifying liver injury triggered by the drug’s pharmacological effects themselves, rather than its direct hepatotoxicity or immunogenicity, often manifesting in individuals with underlying liver disease or specific susceptibilities ( ). Anticancer drugs have traditionally been classified as intrinsic DILI, but recent guidelines and perspectives tend to reclassify many of their cases as indirect ( ). This is because their liver injury is often associated with indirect effects caused by cytotoxicity (e.g., immunosuppression, mitochondrial stress) rather than direct membrane dissolution. Regarding the challenge of distinguishing it from Idiosyncratic DILI: As noted in the literature ( ), indirect DILI shares similarities in clinical presentation (e.g., dose-independent nature) with idiosyncratic DILI, making practical differentiation difficult. This explains why in our unsupervised cluster analysis, the third cluster, potentially representing indirect DILI, was identified as a distinct metabolic entity rather than being merged into the cluster of idiosyncratic DILI. This suggests that, at the metabolomic level, it may possess a unique background metabolic network perturbation. This study has several limitations. First, the sample size is relatively small, and future investigations should incorporate larger cohorts to enhance the robustness and generalizability of the findings. Second, the metabolomic analysis focused solely on intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI without including the proposed “indirect” DILI subtype, primarily due to the current lack of sufficient clinical and experimental evidence supporting its distinct pathological basis and diagnostic criteria, as well as its potential overlap with idiosyncratic DILI in clinical and mechanistic features. In contrast, the intrinsic-idiosyncratic classification has been well established for over 30 years and is widely endorsed in international guidelines, offering a more solid and consensus-driven framework. Finally, the functional roles and dynamic changes of the identified biomarkers during the progression of DILI require further validation through additional mechanistic and longitudinal studies. In summary, we applied a metabolomics approach to characterize both drug subtypes and cases of DILI with well-established mechanisms, encompassing intrinsic and idiosyncratic types. This study revealed distinct metabolic profiles between intrinsic and idiosyncratic DILI and, through integration with machine learning strategies, identified potential biomarkers associated with these two mechanistic subtypes. The PLS-DA model based on serum metabolomics demonstrated promising clinical predictive value for ATB-DILI, though further validation in larger and more targeted studies is warranted. These findings may provide valuable insights for the diagnosis and treatment of DILI, as well as new perspectives on its pathogenic mechanisms from a metabolomic standpoint.

chunks.content: Introduction Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) poses a major global health burden, accounting for approximately 75–85% of all primary liver cancers and ranking as the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide [ – ]. It is responsible for an estimated 906,000 new cases and 830,000 deaths annually, with rising incidence largely attributable to chronic infections (hepatitis B virus [HBV] and hepatitis C virus [HCV]), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) [ ], alcohol consumption, dietary aflatoxin exposure, and underlying cirrhosis [ , , ]. In particular, metabolic dysfunction-related fatty liver disease-especially non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)-has emerged as a predominant risk factor in developed countries, frequently progressing from simple steatosis (non-alcoholic fatty liver, NAFL) to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventually HCC [ , ]. Pathogenetically, HCC is driven by metabolic reprogramming (e.g., enhanced aerobic glycolysis and de novo lipogenesis), oxidative stress (e.g., reactive oxygen species [ROS] accumulation), chronic inflammation (involving nuclear factor-kappa B [NF-κB], tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α], and interleukin-6 [IL-6]), and dysregulated signaling pathways such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and Wnt/β-catenin. These alterations collectively promote proliferation, apoptosis evasion, invasion, and metastasis [ , ]. The progression of HCC and its resistance to therapy are strongly influenced by the dynamic tumor microenvironment (TME). The HCC TME comprises diverse cellular components-such as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and immune cells-as well as acellular factors like extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, cytokines, and growth factors. These elements foster immune evasion, stromal activation, and angiogenesis, thereby promoting invasion and treatment resistance [ ]. Specifically, M2-polarized TAMs and immunosuppressive cytokines (e.g., IL-10, TGF-β) create an immunotolerant niche, while CAFs remodel the ECM and secrete pro-tumorigenic factors. Current HCC treatments include surgical resection, liver transplantation, transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), targeted agents (e.g., sorafenib, lenvatinib), and immune checkpoint inhibitors. However, the majority of patients are diagnosed at advanced stages, which limits the efficacy of curative interventions. Furthermore, targeted therapies frequently encounter intrinsic or acquired resistance in over 50% of patients and are associated with significant toxicity, alongside a post-resection recurrence rate exceeding 70% within five years [ – ]. In this context, dietary polyphenols-plant-derived compounds characterized by phenolic hydroxyl groups-have garnered increasing interest for their potential in HCC prevention and adjunct therapy. These are classified into flavonoids (e.g., catechins, quercetin, dihydromyricetin), phenolic acids (e.g., chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid), stilbenes (e.g., resveratrol), and curcuminoids (e.g., curcumin) [ – ]. Unlike synthetic drugs, polyphenols exert pleiotropic effects-including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-tumor activities-with minimal toxicity [ , ]. Epidemiological studies suggest that regular intake of polyphenol-rich foods (e.g., green tea, cocoa, berries, red wine, olives) correlates with reduced HCC risk, largely due to their ability to suppress malignant transformation in the liver [ – ]. Growing preclinical evidence indicates that dietary polyphenols inhibit HCC development by targeting key pathogenic pathways, modulating the TME, regulating epigenetic mechanisms, and enhancing chemosensitivity [ , – ]. Their multi-target action and favorable safety profile make them promising candidates for integration into HCC treatment strategies [ , ]. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the molecular mechanisms underlying the anti-HCC effects of dietary polyphenols, emphasizing their multi-target nature, current challenges in clinical translation, and future research directions. By synthesizing preclinical and clinical evidence, we aim to illustrate how these natural compounds disrupt oncogenic signaling and remodel the TME, offering innovative approaches for HCC management and therapy. Literature search strategy This review employed a systematic literature search to evaluate the anti-HCC properties of dietary polyphenols. Relevant studies were retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar using keywords and MeSH terms such as “dietary polyphenols,” “hepatocellular carcinoma,” “HCC,” specific compounds (e.g., curcumin, resveratrol, EGCG), and key mechanisms (e.g., apoptosis, metabolic reprogramming). Boolean operators (AND, OR) were applied to optimize the search strategy. The inclusion criteria encompassed original research on polyphenol effects in HCC models, mechanistic studies, and clinical trials, while the exclusion criteria eliminated non-English publications, non-HCC studies, reviews without original data, and combination therapies where polyphenol effects could not be isolated. Data extraction focused on experimental models, polyphenol characteristics, biological outcomes (e.g., proliferation, apoptosis, signaling pathways), and key findings. The molecular pathogenesis of liver cancer Hepatocarcinogenesis is initiated by genetic alterations triggered by various etiological factors. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) promote viral genome integration and disrupt mitotic regulatory proteins, resulting in persistent inflammation and genomic instability [ ]. Aflatoxin B1 induces DNA adduct formation, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses, with a characteristic mutation at codon 249 of the tumor protein p53 (TP53) gene [ ]. Acetaldehyde, a metabolite of alcohol, facilitates DNA adduct and reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation while impairing immune surveillance [ ]. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) contributes to hepatocarcinogenesis through oxidative stress, lipotoxicity, insulin resistance, and the establishment of a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment, ultimately resulting in genetic damage [ ]. The molecular pathogenesis follows a sequential pattern: aberrant activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is often an early event; followed by Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutations (60%), which confer limitless replicative potential through telomere elongation [ ]; TP53 mutations (35–50%) lead to chromosomal instability [ ]; and subsequent mutations in catenin beta 1 (CTNNB1) (20–40%), axis inhibition protein 1 (AXIN1) (9–13%), and AT-rich interaction domain 1 A (ARID1A) (12%) further drive malignant transformation [ – ]. These molecular alterations exhibit certain etiology-specific patterns, such as the association between HBV infection and TP53 mutations, while CTNNB1 mutations are frequently observed in HCV- and alcohol-related HCC [ ]. Accumulation of these genetic alterations contributes to considerable intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity. Based on molecular profiles, HCC is broadly classified into two subtypes: proliferative and non-proliferative. The proliferative subclass, often associated with HBV infection, is characterized by high chromosomal instability, elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels, frequent TP53 mutations, and poor prognosis. In contrast, the non-proliferative subclass, linked to HCV infection and alcohol consumption, exhibits CTNNB1 and TERT promoter mutations, relative chromosomal stability, lower AFP levels, moderate histological differentiation, and less aggressive clinical behavior [ , ]. This heterogeneity poses major challenges for personalized treatment, prognostic assessment, and contributes to therapy resistance and recurrence [ , ]. During tumor progression, multiple signaling pathways become dysregulated. These include the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) pathway, which promotes cell proliferation and survival [ ]; the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway, a cornerstone of angiogenesis [ ]; the Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (Ras/MAPK) pathway, which is hyperactivated in nearly all advanced HCCs and approximately half of early-stage cases [ ]; the insulin-like growth factor (IGF) receptor signaling pathway, active in about 20% of HCCs [ ]; the insulin-like growth factor (IGF) receptor signaling pathway, active in about 20% of HCCs [ ]. Notably, these pathways are not isolated but form an interconnected network; for instance, PI3K/AKT can cross-talk with Wnt/β-catenin and Ras/MAPK signaling, creating a robust signaling web that promotes HCC progression and resistance. As summarized in Fig. , these dysregulated pathways-alongside key genetic alterations such as TERT reactivation and TP53 inactivation-collectively form the molecular basis of HCC pathogenesis and provide a rationale for targeted therapeutic interventions. HCC remains a major cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Although therapeutic modalities-including chemotherapy, targeted agents, and immunotherapy-have advanced considerably, drug resistance continues to pose a central barrier to durable treatment response [ – ]. As schematically summarized in Fig. , this resistance arises from a complex interplay of biological mechanisms encompassing five key hallmarks: (1) Tumor heterogeneity-genomic alterations in HCC generate substantial genetic diversity, enabling the emergence of subpopulations capable of evading therapy; (2) Tumor growth kinetics-slow-proliferating or quiescent tumor cells often persist after treatment, as many therapies preferentially target rapidly dividing cells; (3) “Undruggable” genomic drivers-key mutations in genes such as MYC and TP53 currently lack effective targeted therapies, narrowing therapeutic options; (4) Selective therapeutic pressure-treatments such as radiotherapy exert selective forces that enrich for resistant HCC subclones; and (5) Influence of the immune system and tumor microenvironment (TME)-the TME promotes immunosuppression, impairing T-cell-mediated tumor clearance, while fostering a pro-tumorigenic niche through recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), M2-polarized macrophages (M2-Mφ), and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). In light of these challenges, polyphenols-naturally occurring phytochemicals with pleiotropic bioactivities-have attracted increasing interest for their potential to inhibit HCC progression and overcome drug resistance by simultaneously targeting multiple nodes within these dysregulated pathways and resistance mechanisms. and biological activities Dietary polyphenols, recognized as the “seventh class of nutrients,” are a large family of plant-derived compounds characterized by phenolic structures. They are ubiquitous in plant-based foods such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, tea, coffee, and red wine [ – ]. Their broad health benefits, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor activities, are well-documented in preclinical studies [ , ]. However, a critical factor often overlooked is that their efficacy is not solely determined by dietary intake, but by their bioavailability and biotransformation. Most dietary polyphenols are consumed as glycosides or esters and must undergo extensive metabolism-by host enzymes and, crucially, by the gut microbiota-before absorption, which significantly influences their final bioactive forms and potencies. Structurally, polyphenols are primarily categorized into flavonoids, phenolic acids, lignans, and stilbenes [ – ]. Based on their chemical structures, polyphenols are primarily classified into four major categories: (1) Flavonoids, such as flavonols, isoflavones, chalcones, anthocyanins, and catechins; (2) Phenolic acids, including hydroxybenzoic acids, hydroxyphenylacetic acids, and hydroxycinnamic acids; (3) Lignans, which comprise dibenzylbutyrolactones (dibenzylbutyrolactone lignans), furofurans (furanofuran lignans), arylnaphthalenes (arylnaphthalene lignans), and neolignans; (4) Stilbenes, exemplified by trans-stilbene and trans-resveratrol [ – ]. The anti-HCC potential of dietary polyphenols is underpinned by their diverse chemical structures, which dictate both their biological activities and dietary availability. As detailed in Table , these compounds are systematically classified into major subclasses-such as flavonoids, phenolic acids, stilbenes, and lignans-along with their common dietary sources and sites of absorption and metabolism. The structural diversity across these subclasses, ranging from the benzopyranone core of flavonoids to the simple phenolic rings of phenolic acids, is vividly illustrated in Fig. . This chemical complexity forms the molecular basis for their pleiotropic mechanisms of action against HCC. The anti-HCC mechanisms of polyphenols are pleiotropic, encompassing the suppression of proliferation, induction of apoptosis, inhibition of metastasis, and modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment [ ]. A critical synthesis of the evidence reveals that their multi-target nature often arises from the ability of different compounds (and their metabolites) to converge on key hub pathways dysregulated in HCC, such as PI3K/AKT, AMPK, and Nrf2 signaling. This mechanistic redundancy is a strength but also complicates the identification of a primary driver of efficacy for any single compound. While several polyphenol-rich traditional medicines are used clinically for other indications [ , ], their direct application in HCC requires rigorous validation, as the complex matrices of herbs present additional challenges for standardizing active components and interpreting outcomes. Phenolic acids, including chlorogenic acid (CGA) and caffeic acid (CA), demonstrate hepatoprotective and anti-HCC effects. CGA regulates lipid/glucose metabolism and attenuates liver injury induced by CCl₄, APAP, and D-galactose via Nrf2 activation and NLRP3 inhibition. A recent in vivo study showed that CGA (50 mg/kg/d, p.o., 8 weeks) significantly inhibited DEN-induced HCC progression in rats, associated with modulation of gut microbiota and host metabolism [ , ]. CA protects against APAP hepatotoxicity by activating Nrf2/HO-1 and improving mitochondrial function [ , ]. Furthermore, CA ameliorates hepatic microcirculatory dysfunction and oxidative damage, counteracts the downregulation of sirtuin 3 (SIRT3), and enhances mitochondrial respiratory chain (MRC) activity [ ]. Flavonoids represent a major subclass with diverse anti-HCC activities, capable of modulating cellular glucose uptake and metabolism in HepG2 cells [ ]. Among them, dihydromyricetin (DMY) protects against various forms of liver injury [ , ], and promotes liver health by regulating lipid metabolism, enhancing ethanol metabolism, and attenuating inflammation [ ]. Quercetin (QUE) exerts concentration-dependent dual effects: at low concentrations (≤ 10 µM), it acts as an antioxidant and cytoprotector via Nrf2 activation; at high concentrations (≥ 30–50 µM), it shifts to a pro-oxidant role, inducing selective cytotoxicity in HCC cells through mitochondrial apoptosis and inhibition of survival pathways [ ]. Its anti-HCC mechanism involves inhibition of Yin Yang 1 (YY1) and upregulation of p53, disrupting YY1-p53 interaction and promoting apoptosis [ ]. Green tea catechins, particularly epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), are widely studied. In a DEN-induced rat HCC model, EGCG (50 mg/kg/d, p.o., 20 weeks) upregulated p21 and downregulated CDC25A, suppressing hepatocarcinogenesis [ – ]. The EGCG-siRNA platform has validated its gene silencing capability in preclinical models through effective knockdown of PHD2, which stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and dampens inflammatory signal transduction. This targeted delivery system holds substantial promise for HCC intervention, with potential application against functionally diverse oncogenic drivers including anti-apoptotic proteins (Bcl-2, Survivin), transcription factors promoting proliferation (STAT3), and mediators of angiogenesis (VEGF) [ – ]. Epicatechin (EC) reduces hepatic oxidative damage via Nrf2 activation and suppresses inflammatory injury by inhibiting the HSP60-NF-κB axis [ , ]. TME via anti-inflammatory and Immunomodulatory actions The efficacy of many polyphenols begins with gut microbiota-dependent activation and immunomodulation through two interconnected pathways. They are initially metabolized by microbial enzymes (e.g., β-glucosidases, esterases) into bioactive aglycones, and are further transformed into metabolites such as phenyl-γ-valerolactones and phenolic acids [ , ]. These compounds can enter systemic circulation via the portal vein-directly impacting the liver-or exert local effects, including enhanced intestinal barrier integrity. A meta-analysis on acute lung injury supports this, showing that polyphenol-rich supplementation reduces pro-inflammatory cytokine levels [ ]. Furthermore, specific polyphenols like Baicalin and Kaempferol directly modulate the gut’s Th17/Treg balance, underscoring a key mechanism for their intestinal and systemic anti-inflammatory actions [ ]. This gut-level immunomodulation underpins many systemic effects. For instance, chlorogenic acid (CGA) modulates the gut microbiota-TLR4-NF-κB axis. It helps maintain gut barrier integrity and enriches beneficial gut microbiota, thereby reducing the translocation of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a TLR4 ligand, into the portal circulation. This decrease in hepatic LPS exposure attenuates TLR4-mediated activation of NF-κB signaling, ultimately mitigating liver inflammation [ , ]. Similarly, pterostilbene downregulates the TXNIP/NLRP3 inflammasome, enhances PPARα signaling, and modulates the gut microbiota-TLR4-NF-κB axis to ameliorate inflammation along the gut-liver interface [ , ]. Beyond these gut-mediated mechanisms, polyphenols directly suppress multiple pro-oncogenic signaling pathways. Curcumin suppresses pathways including PI3K/AKT, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, and NF-κB, thereby impeding epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), angiogenesis, and glycolysis [ , ]. It also inhibits TLR4 signaling and the TGF-β1/SMAD7 pathway, reducing the production of key pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, IL-13, and IL-1β [ , , ]. RES not only inhibits SREBP-1c and FAS expression but also improves mitochondrial function in CD8⁺ T cells, potentially revitalizing anti-tumor immunity [ , , ]. DMY and EGCG aalleviate hepatic steatosis and inflammatory responses, partly through suppression of TNF-α [ ]. EGCG further exerts anti-HCC effects largely via modulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, concurrently inhibiting proliferation, inducing apoptosis, and suppressing metastasis [ ]. Additionally, proanthocyanidin exerts multi-target anti-HCC activity by inhibiting key inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), regulating Bcl-2/Bax-mediated apoptosis, and suppressing cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and clonogenicity [ ]. Detoxification of hepatotoxicants Polyphenols mitigate chemical-induced liver injury through multiple and often complementary mechanisms. For instance, chlorogenic acid (CGA) activates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway and inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation, protecting against liver damage induced by carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), acetaminophen (APAP), and D-galactose [ , ]. CUR not only reduces hepatic injury and fibrosis caused by carcinogens like diethylnitrosamine (DEN) and aflatoxin but also chelates iron ions to mitigate iron-dependent oxidative stress [ , , , ]. QUE confers protection by inhibiting CYP2E1, thereby reducing the formation of the toxic APAP metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), and by inducing the cytoprotective enzyme heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) [ , ]. DMY ameliorates hepatotoxicity through a multi-pronged approach involving modulation of APAP metabolism, inhibition of cell death, and promotion of liver regeneration [ ]. Furthermore, EGCG alleviates non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)-associated liver injury by concurrently inhibiting the TGF/SMAD, PI3K/AKT/FoxO1, and NF-κB pathways [ ]. Collectively, as illustrated in Fig. , these specific mechanisms are integrated into a broader protective network wherein polyphenols and their metabolites, shaped by hepatic and microbial metabolism, act through multi-organ pathways to counter hepatotoxic insults and disrupt the progression of liver disease. Bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, safety, and delivery strategies The clinical translation of dietary polyphenols is significantly hampered by their generally low oral bioavailability, a consequence of complex pharmacokinetics, extensive pre-systemic metabolism, and considerable interindividual variation. Following ingestion, most polyphenols undergo substantial phase II metabolism in enterocytes and hepatocytes, forming methylated, sulfated, or glucuronidated derivatives that often exhibit altered bioactivity and accelerated elimination [ ]. Pharmacokinetic profiles vary markedly; for instance, cocoa flavanols reach peak plasma concentration (Cmax) at 2.8 ± 0.6 h, with an elimination half-life of 4.8 ± 1.3 h [ ], whereas soy isoflavones display biphasic absorption due to enterohepatic recirculation [ ]. The food matrix further modulates bioavailability, as demonstrated by a 1.7-fold higher urinary excretion of naringenin from orange juice compared to whole oranges [ ]. Age may further affect naringenin pharmacokinetics, though clinical evidence remains limited [ ]. Advanced formulations, such as encapsulating hydrophobic compounds like eugenol into porous silica, can prolong half-life and improve release kinetics [ , , ]. Tea catechins, including EGCG, are metabolized by COMT, UGTs, and SULTs before absorption primarily via passive diffusion [ , ]. Naringenin induces ferroptosis in HepG2 and Hep3B cells at non-toxic doses (< 0.2 mM) and suppresses tumor growth in vivo at 50 mg/kg by activating AMPK and promoting lipid peroxidation [ , ]. Clinical evidence from a trial in NAFLD patients showed that 100 mg naringenin twice daily for 4 weeks significantly reduced oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory markers via NF-κB inhibition [ ]. Synergistic effects have been achieved through nanoparticulate co-formulations, such as naringenin with ibuprofen or other botanicals, which enhance anti-angiogenic and pro-apoptotic effects in HepG2 cells [ , ]. Similarly, EGCG inhibits HCC progression through PI3K/AKT suppression and cell cycle modulation, downregulating CDC25A and elevating p21 expression [ ]. EGCG-loaded PLGA-siRNA nanoparticles further enhance apoptosis via caspase-3/7 activation [ ], and its derivative Y6 impedes tumor angiogenesis by targeting MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/HIF-1α/VEGF pathways [ ]. Eugenol also exerts anti-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic effects in HepG2 cells at 6.25–25 µg/mL, with efficacy improved by nanoemulsions [ ]. Promising candidates and advanced delivery systems Beyond the well-studied polyphenols, several emerging candidates show high potency. Pterostilbene, a resveratrol analog, exhibits ~ 4-fold higher oral bioavailability and enhanced efficacy in NAFLD-HCC models via AMPK-mediated epigenetic mechanisms [ ]. Arctigenin demonstrates remarkable nanomolar-range cytotoxicity (IC₅₀=4.74–59.27 nM) against HCC cell lines [ ]. The development of advanced nano-formulations-including lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and metal-phenolic networks-has achieved 5- to 20-fold improvements in bioavailability for various polyphenols [ , ]. These systems enable multi-targeted therapies; for example, a piceatannol-Fe³⁺ metal-phenolic network overcomes sorafenib resistance by synergizing photothermal therapy with ferroptosis [ ]. A smart nanosystem co-assembled from ursolic acid and EGCG not only enhances stability and delivery but also activates innate and adaptive immunity by stimulating IL-12/IFN-γ secretion and promoting T cell infiltration, thereby reversing immunosuppression and inhibiting HCC progression [ ]. Concurrently, gut microbiota-mediated biotransformation (e.g., of ellagic acid to urolithins) provides additional avenues for enhancing efficacy [ ]. Safety, standardization, and drug interaction risks While polyphenols from whole foods are generally safe at dietary levels, high-dose supplements require careful safety assessment. Epidemiological studies associate polyphenol-rich diets with reduced HCC risk [ , ]. However, toxicity thresholds for purified compounds vary: the NOAEL for EGCG is ~ 500 mg/kg/day in animals, with human hepatotoxicity reported at > 800 mg/day [ , ]. Curcumin (4–8 g/day) is generally well-tolerated, while resveratrol shows a favorable profile up to 1 g/day [ , ]. A major translational challenge is the lack of unified dosing and the potential for significant drug interactions. Grapefruit flavonoids inhibit CYP3A4, elevating plasma levels of statins and calcium channel blockers [ , ]. Concomitant use of garlic or Ginkgo biloba with warfarin may augment anticoagulant effects, increasing bleeding risk [ ]. Furthermore, many flavonoids inhibit CYP enzymes and affect P-glycoprotein, potentially altering the pharmacokinetics of co-administered drugs like sorafenib and regorafenib [ , ]. Standardization remains another critical barrier, with studies reporting 20–30% lower active content in commercial products than claimed, and variations in cultivation and processing leading to tenfold differences in polyphenol content [ , ]. Reliable clinical application thus mandates improved delivery strategies, systematic dose-response studies, and thorough evaluation of herb-drug interactions. Challenges and future perspectives Among the plethora of polyphenols investigated, curcumin and resveratrol demonstrate the most extensive preclinical evidence but are plagued by exceptionally low bioavailability. In contrast, EGCG has more human trial data supporting its consumption, albeit with a narrower safety margin at high supplemental doses. Pterostilbene, with its superior metabolic stability, represents a promising next-generation analog worthy of accelerated clinical translation. The clinical translation of dietary polyphenols faces several interconnected challenges that must be systematically addressed. The characteristically low oral bioavailability of many prominent polyphenols, such as EGCG and curcumin, severely limits their systemic exposure and therapeutic potential. This is compounded by chemical instability under physiological conditions, rapid metabolism and elimination, and insufficient tumor-targeting specificity. dietary polyphenols faces several interconnected challenges that must be systematically addressed. The characteristically low oral bioavailability of many prominent polyphenols, such as EGCG and curcumin, severely limits their systemic exposure and therapeutic potential. This is compounded by chemical instability under physiological conditions, rapid metabolism and elimination, and insufficient tumor-targeting specificity. Furthermore, the scarcity of large-scale, robust clinical trials hinders the validation of their efficacy and safety in human populations, particularly in combination with standard therapeutics where pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions remain incompletely characterized. Future progress will depend on integrated strategies encompassing advanced nanoformulations-such as stimulus-responsive and tumor-targeted delivery systems-to improve bioavailability and specificity. Concurrently, rigorous long-term toxicological studies, scalable manufacturing processes, and well-designed clinical trials are essential to establish conclusive efficacy and safety. Elucidating the intricate interactions between polyphenols, the gut microbiome, and host metabolism through multi-omics approaches will further enable the development of personalized, microbiota-directed polyphenol interventions. Ultimately, overcoming these translational barriers requires a collaborative, multidisciplinary effort to bridge the gap between promising preclinical data and meaningful clinical application in HCC prevention and therapy. Conclusion HCC remains a major global health challenge with limited treatment efficacy, driving the search for complementary approaches such as dietary polyphenols-flavonoids, phenolic acids, stilbenes, and lignans-which exhibit multi-target anti-HCC activity through synergistic regulation of metabolism, oxidative stress, and tumor microenvironment. However, their clinical translation is hindered by poor bioavailability and insufficient clinical validation. Future progress depends on developing advanced nanoformulations for targeted delivery, validating polyphenol-drug synergies in well-designed trials, and leveraging multi-omics to decipher polyphenol-microbiome-host interactions. Integrating these strategies will unlock the potential of polyphenols as part of comprehensive, personalized HCC management.

chunks.content: Core Tip: Tumoral calcification following transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) for hepatocellular carcinoma is a rare imaging finding, and its clinical significance remains unclear. This case report describes 2 patients with large hepatocellular carcinoma who developed complete radiological response after drug-eluting beads TACE, followed by progressive peripheral calcification and sustained disease-free survival for 6 years. The notable association between post-TACE calcification and long-term remission raises the possibility that calcification may serve as a late imaging biomarker of effective tumor necrosis and durable treatment response. INTRODUCTION Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most prevalent solid tumors and the fourth-leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide[ - ]. Surgical resection, liver transplantation, and image-guided ablation remain the only widely accepted potentially curative options[ - ]. However, the majority of patients present at advanced stages or with impaired hepatic reserve, making them ineligible for these treatments[ - ]. For such patients transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), transarterial radioembolization, and systemic therapies are recommended, providing palliative benefit and improved survival[ , ]. Among these TACE is the most frequently employed locoregional therapy for unresectable HCC[ , ]. Its safety and efficacy have been validated in multiple randomized controlled trials, and it is endorsed by major clinical guidelines as the standard first-line treatment for intermediate-stage disease[ - ]. In routine practice, however, TACE is applied across the entire disease spectrum, from very early to advanced stages[ - ]. Outcomes remain heterogeneous, largely influenced by tumor burden, liver function, and procedural technique with reported median survivals ranging from 13 to 43 months[ - ]. The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system is the most widely adopted framework for guiding HCC management, integrating tumor burden, liver function, and performance status into evidence-based treatment recommendations and prognostic prediction[ ]. Within this system TACE is designated as the standard first-line therapy for intermediate-stage disease, characterized by asymptomatic patients with large or multifocal tumors and preserved liver function without macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread[ ]. The updated BCLC system also incorporates the concept of treatment stage migration, allowing TACE in selected early-stage patients unsuitable for resection or ablation as well as its use as a bridging or downstaging strategy to liver transplantation. Consequently, in real-world practice a considerable proportion of TACE procedures are performed beyond the intermediate stage, reflecting the adaptability of the BCLC framework to diverse clinical scenarios[ , ]. Post-treatment tumoral calcification is a rare phenomenon that has been reported following HCC locoregional therapies. It has been described after radioembolization and very rarely after TACE. In conventional TACE, however, the detection of calcification is often obscured by lipiodol deposition[ - ]. To my knowledge progressive calcification following drug-eluting beads TACE (DEB-TACE), particularly in association with durable remission, has not been previously reported. Herein, I report 2 patients with large solitary HCCs who underwent DEB-TACE, achieved complete response (CR), and subsequently developed progressive peripheral calcification with sustained remission over 6 years. CASE PRESENTATION Chief complaints Case 1: A 74-year-old male presented with a liver mass evident on abdominal computed tomography (CT). Case 2: A 71-year-old male patient presented with a liver mass evident on abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). History of present illness Case 1 and Case 2 were asymptomatic and both underwent imaging as screening of high risk of HCC in patient liver cirrhosis. History of past illness Case 1: The patient had a known case of liver cirrhosis secondary to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Case 2: The patient had a known case of liver cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis C virus. Personal and family history Case 1 and Case 2 were unremarkable. Physical examination General and abdominal examinations were unremarkable for both cases. Laboratory examinations Case 1: Liver function test results, complete blood count, and coagulation profile were all within normal limits apart from a low count of platelets (70/µL). Seum alpha fetoprotein was within normal limits. Case 2: Complete blood count, coagulation profile, and liver function test results were all within normal limits. Seum alpha fetoprotein was elevated (420 ng/mL). Imaging examinations Case 1: The patient underwent CT with intravenous contrast. It showed a 6.5 cm segment 8 hepatic mass. The mass showed well defined delineate intense arterial phase enhancement with subsequent washout in the portal venous and delayed phases within the peripheral capsule. Findings revealed a liver imaging and report and data system (LI-RADS) category 5 lesion (Figure ). Case 2: The patient underwent abdominal MRI. It showed a 6 cm segment 7 hepatic mass. It showed intense arterial phase enhancement with subsequent washout in the portal venous and delayed phases. Findings revealed an LI-RADS category 5 lesion (Figure ). FINAL DIAGNOSIS Case 1 A case of large solitary HCC with preserved liver function and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic metastasis (early stage). Case 2 A case of large solitary HCC with preserved liver function and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic

peripheral capsule. Findings revealed a liver imaging and report and data system (LI-RADS) category 5 lesion (Figure ). Case 2: The patient underwent abdominal MRI. It showed a 6 cm segment 7 hepatic mass. It showed intense arterial phase enhancement with subsequent washout in the portal venous and delayed phases. Findings revealed an LI-RADS category 5 lesion (Figure ). FINAL DIAGNOSIS Case 1 A case of large solitary HCC with preserved liver function and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic metastasis (early stage). Case 2 A case of large solitary HCC with preserved liver function and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic metastasis (early stage). TREATMENT Case 1 TACE, as a bridging and downstaging therapy prior to liver transplantation, was recommended after discussion with the HCC tumor board. The first session of DEB-TACE was performed using 150 mg doxorubicin loaded into two vials of 100-300 µm drug-eluting microspheres (DC Bead). Due to a partial response (PR), a second DEB-TACE session was performed using 75 mg doxorubicin loaded into one vial of 100-300 µm drug-eluting microspheres (Figure ). Case 2 After discussion with the HCC tumor board, TACE was recommended as a bridging and downstaging therapy prior to liver transplantation. The first session of DEB-TACE was performed using 150 mg doxorubicin loaded into two vials of 100-300 µm drug-eluting microspheres (DC Bead). Due to a PR, a second DEB-TACE session was performed using 75 mg doxorubicin loaded into one vial of 100-300 µm drug-eluting microspheres (Figure ). OUTCOME AND FOLLOW-UP Case 1 The first follow-up CT after 6 weeks of TACE revealed PR (Figure ). The second follow-up CT after the second session revealed CR (Figure ). The 1-year follow-up CT demonstrated CR with peripheral faint hyperdensities, suggesting early calcification (Figure ). The patient was deemed ineligible for liver transplantation due to advanced age. He was actively monitored with clinical, laboratory, and imaging examinations. The 6-year follow-up CT demonstrated sustained CR with progressive peripheral hyperdensities encircling the tumor, consistent with concentric calcifications (Figure ). Case 2 The first follow-up MRI, performed 8 weeks after TACE, demonstrated PR (Figure ). The subsequent CT after the second TACE session revealed CR (Figure ). The 1-year follow-up CT demonstrated CR with peripheral faint hyperdensities, consistent with early calcification (Figure ). The patient declined liver transplantation as the tumor had achieved CR. He was enrolled in routine clinical, laboratory, and imaging follow-up. The 6-year follow-up CT demonstrated sustained CR with progressive peripheral concentric calcifications (Figure ). Serum alpha-fetoprotein normalized after the second TACE session and remained within normal limits. DISCUSSION Although traditionally considered a palliative option, TACE can achieve curative intent in carefully selected patients. A prospective cohort demonstrated durable management of early-stage HCC using super-selective TACE[ ], and several retrospective series have reported overall survival comparable with radiofrequency ablation in patients within the Milan criteria when ablation or surgery is contraindicated[ , ]. The optimal therapeutic objective of TACE is complete tumor necrosis[ , ]. Radiological CR, which is the strongest predictor of long-term survival[ , ], can even predict outcomes following subsequent curative treatments, such as transplantation when TACE is used as a bridge therapy[ ]. Imaging characteristics of HCC can predict the likelihood of response: Well-circumscribed capsulated hypervascular HCCs ≤ 5 cm supplied by a dominant arterial feeder respond best, whereas ill-defined, infiltrative, hypovascular tumors > 5 cm seldom demonstrate CR[ , ]. Assessment of HCC treatment response using response evaluation criteria in solid tumor (RECIST) based on tumor shrinkage often underestimate response in HCC as they disregard tumor necrosis[ , ]. The modified RECIST (mRECIST) criteria based on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to measure viable, enhancing tumor tissue are now the most widely accepted method and are endorsed by international guidelines[ , ]. The response is categorized as CR defined by the disappearance of all enhancing lesions or PR defined as at least a 30% reduction in enhancing tumor diameter[ ]. Multiple studies show that objective response by mRECIST, particularly CR, is strongly associated with improved overall survival, making it a reliable prognostic factor and validated endpoint in HCC trials[ , ]. The prognosis, however, depends not only on controlling the tumor burden but also on preserving underlying liver function. Achieving high objective response rates and minimizing collateral hepatic injury are equally important for improving survival and maintaining quality of life[ - ]. Super-selective DEB-TACE fulfils both aims by delivering higher intratumoral drug concentration, enhancing better local control, and reducing systemic toxicity and non-target embolization of the healthy liver[ , ]. Post-treatment tumor calcification has been described in several malignancies, including colorectal liver metastases and ovarian cancers in which it often reflects dystrophic calcification of necrotic tissue and has been associated with favorable prognosis[ ]. In HCC calcification following locoregional therapy is exceedingly rare. Calcification after transarterial radioembolization has been reported and was

response rates and minimizing collateral hepatic injury are equally important for improving survival and maintaining quality of life[ - ]. Super-selective DEB-TACE fulfils both aims by delivering higher intratumoral drug concentration, enhancing better local control, and reducing systemic toxicity and non-target embolization of the healthy liver[ , ]. Post-treatment tumor calcification has been described in several malignancies, including colorectal liver metastases and ovarian cancers in which it often reflects dystrophic calcification of necrotic tissue and has been associated with favorable prognosis[ ]. In HCC calcification following locoregional therapy is exceedingly rare. Calcification after transarterial radioembolization has been reported and was associated with better prognosis, suggesting its potential role as an early surrogate marker of CR[ ]. Conversely, only a single case report has described dystrophic calcification after DEB-TACE, likely related to treatment-induced tissue injury[ ]. In my cases DEB-TACE likely induced extensive coagulative necrosis leading to peripheral calcification that was unmasked by the absence of lipiodol. Although the exact pathogenesis remains uncertain, tumoral calcification after TACE is generally considered a manifestation of dystrophic calcification within necrotic tissue rather than a process specific to DEB-TACE. Necrotic cells release phosphate ions that combine with calcium salts in an alkaline environment, and in the absence of normal blood supply and cellular inhibitory mechanisms, these salts precipitate and deposit. This mechanism explains the peripheral sickle-like or ring-like calcification pattern observed that may serve as a surrogate marker of effective therapy as demonstrated in my cases[ , , ]. The association between calcification and long-term remission in my cases suggests that calcification may represent a late imaging marker of effective tumor necrosis. However, both patients had already achieved CR based on mRECIST prior to the appearance of calcification, and CR remains the most reliable predictor of outcome[ , ]. Thus, calcification should be considered a hypothesis-generating observation rather than a validated biomarker, underscoring the need for prospective studies to clarify whether it has independent prognostic significance. This report has some limitations. It describes only 2 highly selected patients with favorable prognostic features, limiting its generalizability. As a case report it cannot establish causality between calcification and outcome. Nevertheless, the rarity of calcification after DEB-TACE and the unusually long survival observed in my patients make these cases valuable for raising awareness of this potential imaging marker. CONCLUSION While TACE is generally regarded as a palliative option, my cases demonstrated that with appropriate patient selection and technique CR and durable remission are achievable even in large HCCs. The appearance of peripheral tumoral calcification following DEB-TACE may represent a late imaging marker of effective tumor necrosis and durable disease control although this observation remains hypothesis-generating and requires validation in larger cohorts. These findings suggest that calcification after DEB-TACE could serve as a potential imaging biomarker of treatment success. Further prospective studies are warranted to clarify its prognostic value and validate its clinical significance. All rights reserved. 2018 Indian National Association for Study of the Liver Corrigendum to “Wilson's Disease: Clinical Practice Guidelines of the Indian National Association for the Study of Liver (INASL), The Indian Society of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ISPGHAN) and the Movement Disorders Society of India (MDSI)” [J Clin Exp Hepatol 9 (2019) 74–98] 10 1 10 12 2019 99 99 Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hepatology PMC6995886 32025169 Clinical practice guidelines for Wilson's disease (WD) have been published by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and European Association for the Study of the Liver in 2008 and 2012, respectively. Their focus was on the hepatic aspects of the disease. Recently, a position paper on pediatric WD was published by the European Society of Pediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition. A need was felt to harmonize guidelines for the hepatic, pediatric, and neurological aspects of the disease and contextualize them to the resource-constrained settings. Therefore, experts from national societies from India representing 3 disciplines, hepatology (Indian National Association for Study of the Liver), pediatric hepatology (Indian Society of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition), and neurology (Movement Disorders Society of India) got together to evolve fresh guidelines. A literature search on retrospective and prospective studies of WD using MEDLINE (PubMed) was performed. Members voted on each recommendation, using the nominal voting technique. The Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation system was used to determine the quality of evidence. Questions related to diagnostic tests, scoring system, and its modification to a version suitable for resource-constrained settings were posed. While ceruloplasmin and 24-h urine copper continue to be important, there is little role of serum copper and penicillamine challenge test in the diagnostic algorithm. A new scoring system – Modified Leipzig score has been suggested with extra points being added for family history and serum ceruloplasmin lower than 5 mg/dl. Liver dry copper estimation and penicillamine challenge test have been removed from the scoring system. Differences in pharmacological approach to neurological and hepatic disease and global monitoring scales have been included. Rising bilirubin and worsening encephalopathy are suggested as indicators predicting need for liver transplant but need to be validated. The clinical practice guidelines provide recommendations for a comprehensive management of WD which will be of value to all specialties. Keywords
